title: Is a submarine a boat or a ship?
text:
Most often the difference between boats and ships is based on size and whether the vessel is ocean-going. A boat is generally a smaller vessel that can be carried by a ship. A ship cannot be carried by a boat. Other vessels that are generally too large to be carried may also be referred to as boats such as ferry boats, tour boats and fishing boats.

By this definition, submarines such as the Pampanito are technically ships. However, the original submarines were boats by the formal definition. They were carried to the point of attack and were not suitable for lengthy ocean transits. As a result, by tradition, all submarines are still referred to as boats even though some of the newer ones are huge in comparison. Submarines can be referred to both as ships and boats, with “boats” being far more common.
display_citation: DieselSubs FAQ — Is a submarine a boat or a ship?

title: Is the submarine a battleship?
text:
That depends on your definition of a battleship. These submarines were combatant ships and did go into battle. However, in WW2, there was a specific type of ship called a battleship. Those ships were large, heavy vessels with many guns. The biggest of our battleships had nine 16-inch guns and as many as 20 five-inch guns, 48 Bofors 40 mm guns in mounts of four, and 52 Oerlikon 20 mm guns each. The battleships the U. S. built in WW2 were 25 times larger, by displacement (or by weight), than the Pampanito.

In WW2, submarines were certainly in battles, but sailors did not refer to them as battleships.

title: Where is the pressure hull? Can I see it from the pier?
text: The pressure hull or “people pipe” is below the main deck and between the sets of ballast and fuel tanks on both sides of the boat. Most of the pressure hull is hidden by the tanks on both sides and the main deck above.
display_citation: DieselSubs FAQ — Where is the pressure hull? Can I see it from the pier?

title: Where do the torpedoes come out?
text:
The outer doors for the forward tubes are all the way forward and just below the first row of limber holes. It is a rectangular structure that moves in toward the boat when opened. The same is true of the after tubes although there are no limber holes near the after outer doors.

The outer doors for the top tubes, both forward and aft are visible on the Pampanito. You can see the outline of the rectangular doors. That is because the boat is currently much lighter than it was when it was operational. It does not have the 100 tons of battery cells, the nearly 400 tons of fuel, the full complement of torpedoes with live warheads, the food for the crew plus the 80 sailors and their gear. If that were all on board, the boat would be sitting deeper in the water and the torpedo doors would be under water.
display_citation: DieselSubs FAQ — Where do the torpedoes come out?

title: What should we know about before discussing what is in the boat?
text:
A few definitions for common words and phrases might be helpful, such as hatches, heads, ladders and watertight doors.

A hatch is an opening through a deck that allows a sailor to move up or down using a ladder.

In the Navy, a head is a toilet. There are four heads on board, although only two are visible.

A ladder, in Navy speak, is a set of stairs or steps on a ship. Most of the original ladders on the Pampanito actually resemble the almost straight up and down ladders used around your home. However, these ladders were not as easily moved. Surface ships have ladders that look more like stairs. Those are similar to what was added in the torpedo rooms for visitors and old docents to enter and exit the Pampanito museum.

A watertight door is the opening between the compartments on a submarine The doors are very heavy since they are designed to withstand sea pressure. This is so they can prevent flooding from moving from one compartment to the next. At a depth of 400 feet, the outside water pressure is about 175 PSI. The weight needed to withstand that pressure helps to explain their small size. There are no watertight doors on the lower level. To go from one compartment to the next on that level, one would have to go up to the main level, move to the desired compartment, and then go back down.
display_citation: DieselSubs FAQ — What should we know about before discussing what is in the boat?

title: Why are there so many doorways to go through?
text: The submarine is divided up into eight compartments on the main level. (The conning tower is a separate compartment above the pressure hull.) These compartments are designed so that if any one of them were to be flooded, the boat could still get back to the surface. (That is a theory that may never have been proven during actual operations.) The compartments are also divided functionally so that noise and light can be suppressed, particularly at night.

title: Why are the watertight doors so heavy?
text: The doors are very heavy since they are designed to withstand sea pressure. This is so they can prevent flooding from moving from one compartment to the next. At a depth of 400 feet, the outside water pressure is about 175 PSI.  The weight explains the small size.

title: What are the compartments on these submarines?
text:
We will be starting aft, or at the back of the boat, which is where both tours – online and in person - start. The following are the various compartments with more detail following:

  • After torpedo room
  • Maneuvering room
  • After engine room
  • Forward engine room
  • After battery
  • Control room
  • Pump room
  • Conning tower
  • Bridge
  • Forward battery
  • Forward torpedo room

The control room, pump room, conning tower and bridge are all in the same section of the hull so they will be discussed together.
display_citation: DieselSubs FAQ — What are the compartments on these submarines?

title: What is in the after torpedo room?
text:
The after torpedo room includes:

  • Four torpedo tubes, which would normally be loaded.
  • Four reload torpedoes.
  • Torpedo loading hatch.
  • Crew’s bunks above the torpedoes.
  • A signal gun to send out flares. After WW2, it could also be used to release decoy devices.
  • There is no lower level in this compartment since the propellor shafts pass through the area below this space outside the pressure hull.
  • This space has the unique head that discharges directly over the side and cannot be used in port or when submerged. It requires an eight-step process to flush since the water level outside the boat is significantly higher than the water and waste in the bowl. If flushed incorrectly, the user gets to clean up the dirty water.
  • After escape trunk.
  • Charging unit for the Mark 18 electric torpedoes.
display_citation: DieselSubs FAQ — What is in the after torpedo room?

title: What is in the maneuvering room?
text:
Maneuvering includes:

  • The cubicle which is where electrical power is distributed. 
  • The large levers direct the power from an engine-generator combination either to the battery charge or to operate the boat. These are separate circuits. When the boat is submerged, the levers are changed to take the power from the battery to operate the boat.
  • Main motors on the lower level to drive the propellors via the reduction gears.There are two motors per propellor shaft.
  • Motor order telegraphs. These receive the orders from the bridge or conning tower for the desired speed.They are then used to acknowledge the orders received and being executed.   There are two units, one for each propellor shaft.
  • Lathe for repairs.
  • Inverters to provide A/C power from the D/C battery or generators.
  • Log (or engineer’s) office. This tiny space is the second largest office on the boat.
display_citation: DieselSubs FAQ — What is in the maneuvering room?

title: The control room has a lot of equipment. Is it the command center?
text:
Yes, it has a lot of equipment. No, it is not the command center. 

The command center would be either the conning tower, which is above the control room, or the open bridge. The conning tower is the command center when the boat is submerged. It is always manned when at sea by a helmsman and quartermaster since steering and navigation are normally done from this space. Radar and sonar are also normally operated from this space. It would be very crowded during general quarters (battle stations) for submerged attacks with as many as 10 to 12 men in the space.

The conning tower is only about 20 feet long and 10 feet in diameter. It is made of slightly thicker steel due to its vulnerability since it is closer to the surface.

The bridge is the command center, where the officer of the deck will normally be when the boat is on the surface. When surfaced, the officer of the deck is supported by the crewmen in the conning tower and control room. This is particularly true when attacking while on the surface.
display_citation: DieselSubs FAQ — The control room has a lot of equipment. Is it the command center?

title: Are there enough heads on the boat? We only see two.
text: There are four heads on the Pampanito. Two are in the main berthing area. They have metal doors and are opposite the washing machine. There is one additional head in each of the torpedo rooms. And, yes, four heads are normally enough for the 80-man crew.
display_citation: DieselSubs FAQ — Are there enough heads on the boat? We only see two.

title: Why are the chiefs' quarters known as the goat locker?
text:
This is the space where the Chief Petty Officers, the highest-ranking enlisted men, sleep. The space is so named because the chiefs are the “old goats” in the Navy. On a submarine in WW2, they were as “old” as 28 or 30 years old. 

In this case, goat is not necessarily GOAT, as in greatest of all time. Nor does it imply that the chiefs smelled more like goats than the rest of us. After a few days at sea, we all smelled pretty bad.

The chiefs’ quarters are known as the goat locker throughout the Navy, not just on submarines.
display_citation: DieselSubs FAQ — Why are the chiefs' quarters known as the goat locker?

title: Pampanito is much bigger than I expected. I thought submarines were crowded.
text:
The boat is long but narrow. It is almost 312 feet long. However, the pressure hull, where the crew lived and worked, is only 16 feet in diameter and around 280 feet long. The bottom level is all machinery with much more equipment on the main level such as the tops of the engines and generators, fresh water stills, torpedo tubes, reload torpedoes and the boat’s controls. As a result, there isn’t much room left for the crew.


The submarine looks much bigger from the outside than it does from the inside, particularly with 80 crew members on board.

title: What is in the after engine room?
text:
The after engine room on the Pampanito includes:

  • Two Fairbanks Morse, 10 cylinder, opposed-piston main engines producing about 1,500 horsepower each.  The engines extend to the lower level.
  • Two generators (one attached to each engine) to produce the needed electrical power.
  • A smaller, “donkey” diesel on the lower level that can be used to top off a battery charge. This is a smaller Fairbanks-Morse, 7 cylinder, opposed-piston engine with associated generator. These smaller engines were removed from active submarines in the 1950s. 
  • Clean fuel tank.
  • Normal lube oil tank.
  • Associated fuel and oil pumps and filters.
  • Ladder and hatch to the main deck.


NOTE: Submarines built in commercial shipyards, such as Electric Boat and Manitowoc Shipbuilding, would likely have General Motors V-16 engines rather than the Fairbanks Morse. The GM engines would be about the same size, run at the same speed, and produce about the same power as the FM engines.
display_citation: DieselSubs FAQ — What is in the after engine room?

title: What is in the forward engine room?
text:
The forward engine room includes:

  • Two more Fairbanks-Morse (or General Motors) main engine-generator combinations that also extend to the lower level.
  • Two Kleinschmidt stills for fresh water.
  • Air conditioning on the lower level. This has been described as functioning more as a dehumidifier rather than actual air conditioning. In other words, in WW2 it removed some moisture but didn’t cool the air very well.
  • Clean fuel tank.
  • Normal lube oil tank.
  • Associated fuel and oil pumps and filters.
display_citation: DieselSubs FAQ — What is in the forward engine room?

title: What is in the after battery?
text:
The after battery includes:

  • Crew’s sinks, heads and showers. The two heads are behind the metal doors opposite the wash machine.
  • A shower near the wash machine.
  • Half of the boat’s battery, 126 cells, is on the lower level.
  • Fan unit to pull the hydrogen out of the battery well so it does not reach combustible levels when charging the battery. The air from the battery well is dumped into the engine rooms so the hydrogen is mixed with outside air and can be burned along with diesel fuel.
  • Main crew’s berthing with 36 bunks.
  • Pharmacist mate’s medical locker.
  • Locker to hang service dress uniforms.
  • Smaller lockers for personal items. Some smaller items would be stored under the mattresses.
  • Ice cream machine.
  • Crew’s mess with four tables seating six men each.Two tables have game boards embedded.
  • Galley, the small space next to the crew’s mess where meals are cooked. The third cook, the overnight baker, prepares bread, rolls, cakes and pies in this space.
  • A large coffee maker; coffee is always available.
  • The hatch to the ammunition locker is on the lower level, port side forward. The access hatch may be under the chest used for storage and seating.
  • Cold storage on the lower level.
  • Limited pantry space on the lower level.
  • Sinks to wash dishes.
display_citation: DieselSubs FAQ — What is in the after battery?

title: What is in the forward torpedo room?
text:
The forward torpedo room includes:

  • Six torpedo tubes, normally loaded
  • Ten reload torpedoes in skids (trays).
  • Torpedo loading hatch.
  • Ladder and hatch to the main deck.
  • Escape trunk.
  • Crew’s bunks above the torpedoes.
  • Sonar equipment. Sonar can be operated from here, but there is no PPI (plan position indicator) display.
  • Charging unit for the Mark 18 electric torpedoes.
  • Officers’ head and shower.
  • This space has a shallow lower level that includes two of the six torpedo tubes and two of the reloads.
display_citation: DieselSubs FAQ — What is in the forward torpedo room?

title: What is in the forward battery?
text:
Returning to the main level inside the pressure hull forward of the control room, the forward battery includes:

  • Boat’s office. This is the large office on the boat.
  • Chief petty officers’ berthing, also known as the “goat locker”.
  • Captain’s cabin with desk and depth and course indicators.
  • The other half of the boat’s battery, 126 cells, is on the lower level.
  • Fan unit to pull the hydrogen out of the battery well so it does not reach combustible levels when charging the battery. The air from the battery well is dumped into the engine rooms so the hydrogen can be burned.
  • Officers’ staterooms for berthing.
  • Wardroom for officers’ meals, meetings and work space.
  • Serving galley. Food is kept warm and served from here. It is not cooked here.
display_citation: DieselSubs FAQ — What is in the forward battery?

title: What is on the bridge above the conning tower?
text:
The bridge, the open space above the conning tower, includes:

  • Hatch down to the conning tower.
  • Target bearing transmitters.
  • Announcing systems.
  • Lookout platforms on the periscope shears.
  • Signal lamp.
  • Course indicator.
  • Ships’ guns including 20 mm and 40 mm, as installed.
display_citation: DieselSubs FAQ — What is on the bridge?

title: What is in the pump room below the control room?
text:
Unsurprisingly, the pump room, which is below the control room, has many of the boat’s pumps, including:

  • Trim pumps.
  • Drain pumps.
  • Hydraulic pumps.
  • Air compressors.
  • The low-pressure blower to empty ballast tanks of the last of the water.
  • On some boats, the classified materials safe is located here.
display_citation: DieselSubs FAQ — What is in the pump room?

title: What is in the conning tower above the control room?
text:
The conning tower, which is the enclosed space above the control room, includes:

  • Hatch and ladder down to control room
  • Helm.
  • Course indicator.
  • Rudder indicator.
  • Motor order telegraphs.
  • Alarms.
  • Announcing systems.
  • Ladder and hatch to the bridge.
  • Sonar displays and controls.
  • Search periscope.
  • Attack periscope.
  • SJ surface search radar display and controls.
  • ST surface search radar display. This radar is in the search periscope.
  • Depth gauge.
  • Telegraph key.
  • Dead reckoning tracker.
  • Torpedo data computer.
  • Torpedo firing keys.
  • Radio phone sets.
  • Sound-powered phones.
display_citation: DieselSubs FAQ — What is in the conning tower?

title: What is in the control room?
text:
This is where the crew dives the boat, controls depth and returns the boat to the surface. It includes:

  • Radio room with radios and encoding/decoding equipment.
  • Controls for the low-pressure blower, used to empty ballast tanks of the last of the water.
  • Periscope wells. The actual periscopes cannot be seen inside the wells nor can they be used from here.
  • High-pressure air manifold used to bring the boat back to the surface.
  • AC electrical switchboard.
  • Alarms – diving, collision and general quarters (battle stations) mounted on one of the pericope wells.
  • Announcing systems.
  • Trim manifold.
  • Air search radar.
  • IFF query and display.
  • Diving officer’s checklist.
  • Radar equipment.
  • Bow and stern plane control wheels.
  • Ladder and hatch up to the conning tower.
  • Hatch and ladder down to the pump room.
  • Chief of the watch station with the “Christmas tree” display of the status of key valves and hatches.
  • Controls to main ballast tank vents.
  • Controls to special ballast tanks and the main induction air valve.
  • LORAN (Long Range Aid to Navigation).
  • Gyrocompass.
  • Bathythermograph that measures water temperature at various depths.
  • Fathometer, a sonar device measuring the depth of water beneath the boat.
  • Boat’s safe topped by a ladder up to the main deck. This hatch has a small window to allow gun crews to see if the water above the hatch has drained away.
  • Backup helm.
  • Backup gyrocompass.
  • Magnetic (tank) compass.
  • Dead reckoning tracker. The display of Pampanito’s war patrols is on this DRT.

Note: The control room on the Pampanito is configured with red lights to show an example of the typical lighting at night.

The pump room is directly below the control room.  The conning tower is above the control room and the bridge is above that space.

title: Is the USS Pampanito (SS-383) really a submarine?
text: That is actually a valid question. Modern submarines, even the non-nuclear boats of other navies, don’t look anything like the Pampanito from the outside. They are sleek black shapes and are mostly underwater. Only a little of the hull shows along with the upright sail.Unlike the Pampanito, they have no guns. But, yes, this is what was described as a submarine in World War 2.
display_citation: DieselSubs FAQ — Is the USS Pampanito (SS-383) really a submarine?

title: What do you mean when you say this is what was considered a submarine?
text: This is as far as the technology could go in the early 1940s. However, these boats, and all others of that era, technically, were just submersibles. They were surface ships that could submerge for relatively brief periods (usually 16 hours or so), could fight submerged and then could come back to the surface. The first true submarine was the USS Nautilus (SSN-571) which was commissioned in 1954. With nuclear power, subs could operate underwater for a few months at a time and did not have to surface regularly for fresh air or to recharge batteries. Nautilus was designed to operate underwater for the vast majority of the time.
display_citation: DieselSubs FAQ — What do you mean when you say this is what we called a submarine?

title: How different are modern submarines?
text: Visitors who have served on our latest submarines tell us that they are completely different from the USS Pampanito (SS-383) and exactly the same. They are telling us that the functions are the same – diving, surfacing, being quiet, being sneaky, gathering intelligence, and attacking the ships of an enemy in wartime. However, the way those functions are accomplished may be very different. Buttons, switches and computers help to accomplish many tasks that were very manual on the Pampanito. In addition, modern submarines are much larger and cleaner. However, there still isn’t enough space to play basketball.
display_citation: DieselSubs FAQ — How different are modern submarines?

title: Were there crew bunks in the torpedo rooms?
text:
Were there crew bunks in the torpedo rooms?

Yes. Both the forward torpedo room and the after torpedo room had crew bunks located above the torpedoes. The torpedo rooms doubled as sleeping quarters for some crew members. In the forward torpedo room there are ten reload torpedoes in skids (trays), and the crew bunks are above them. In the after torpedo room, there are four reload torpedoes, and the crew bunks are also above the torpedoes. Sleeping in the torpedo room was an experience — as one crew member described it, his bedfellows were a torpedo on one side and a torpedo below him.

title: How were torpedo reloads handled at sea?
text:
How were torpedo reloads handled at sea?

Each torpedo room carried spare torpedoes stored on steel skids — tracks running along the sides of the room. When a torpedo was fired and a tube needed to be reloaded, the crew first had to remove the bunks that folded down over the skids. Then three or four men would slide the torpedo along the skid track until it lined up with the open tube, and pull it into the tube using a system of blocks and tackles — pulleys and rope that gave the crew enough mechanical advantage to maneuver the two-thousand-pound weapon in a confined space. It was heavy, awkward work. The Pampanito carried a total of twenty-four torpedoes — six tubes and spare reloads in the forward torpedo room, and four tubes and spare reloads in the after torpedo room. Reloading at sea after a firing could take roughly fifteen to thirty minutes depending on sea conditions and crew experience.

title: How did sonar work on a WWII submarine?
text:
How did sonar work on a WWII submarine?

WWII submarines used passive sonar — hydrophones — to listen for the sounds of enemy ships. The sonar operator wore headphones and could hear screws turning, machinery noise, and the pinging of enemy active sonar. Passive sonar gave bearing (direction) but not range. Active sonar could send a pulse and measure the echo return time to determine range, but using it revealed the submarine's position to the enemy, so boats were very reluctant to ping actively while hiding. FM sonar was a specialized system — quite separate from general active sonar — designed specifically to detect and navigate around minefields. The sound heads on fleet submarines like the Pampanito were retractable: extended below the keel for use, and pulled back up inside the hull when not needed to protect them from contact damage if the boat came near the bottom. With the heads retracted, the sonar was completely non-functional. A skilled sonar operator could identify different types of ships, estimate their speed, and track multiple contacts.

title: When was the Pampanito built and launched?
text:
When was the Pampanito built and launched?

USS Pampanito (SS-383) was built at the Portsmouth Naval Shipyard in Kittery, Maine. Her keel was laid on March 15, 1943. She was launched on July 12, 1943 and commissioned into the United States Navy on November 6, 1943. After her commissioning she moved to the Pacific Fleet and began her first war patrol in mid-1944. She was decommissioned on 1 December 1945 and eventually became a maritime museum ship in San Francisco, where she is berthed at Fisherman's Wharf (Pier 45) as part of the San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park.

title: How did submarine families know if a sailor was still alive on patrol?
text:
How did submarine families know if a sailor was still alive on patrol?

Families at home had very limited information about whether a submarine sailor was safe during a patrol. Submarines maintained radio silence for most of a patrol to avoid detection, so there were no regular communications home. Sailors could write letters, but mail moved under strict limitations. Letters written by crewmen were kept aboard the submarine until it reached a base, where they were then posted home. Letters and packages sent from home to the crew were held at the base until the submarine returned to port — the crew received their mail only when the boat came back in. When a submarine arrived in port, sailors were sometimes allowed to send a brief cable home. If a submarine was overdue and presumed lost, the Navy would notify the families that the boat was missing. The phrase "on eternal patrol" was used to describe submarines and their crews that never came home. No news was generally considered good news — families knew that if the submarine were lost, the Navy would eventually notify them.

title: What is a depth charge and how did it work?
text:
What is a depth charge and how did it work?

A depth charge is an anti-submarine weapon — essentially a canister filled with high explosive (TNT or Torpex) designed to sink to a set depth before detonating. Surface ships dropped them off the stern or launched them from projectors called K-guns, creating a pattern of explosions around a suspected submarine location. The fuse was set to detonate at a specific depth, calibrated before launching using a pressure-activated mechanism. The explosion didn't have to directly hit the submarine — the concussion and pressure wave from a nearby blast could rupture hull welds, crack pipes, shatter gauge glasses, and kill or injure crew members. A very close depth charge could tear open the pressure hull, allowing seawater to pour in faster than any crew could respond. The sound inside a submerged submarine under depth charge attack was described by survivors as deafening and terrifying — every loose object flew, lights shattered, and the whole hull shuddered with each explosion.

title: Were submarine crews paid more than regular Navy sailors?
text:
Were submarine crews paid more than regular Navy sailors?

Yes, submarine sailors received extra pay specifically because of the dangerous and demanding nature of submarine service. This was called submarine pay or hazardous duty pay. The Pay Readjustment Act of 1942 established submarine pay at 50% of base pay for both officers and enlisted men. Before that legislation, qualified submariners received $10 per month and non-qualified submariners $5 per month, plus $1 for each day spent submerged. Rather than a personal food allowance, ration money was allocated to the boat itself to buy food for the crew — managed by a Supply Officer who was typically a regular line officer carrying supply as a collateral duty, not a specialist. That arrangement gave the cook real purchasing authority, which is one reason submariners were famous for eating better than most sailors in the Navy. The combination of higher pay, better food, and a strong sense of camaraderie made submarine service attractive despite the obvious dangers.

title: Who steered the submarine and where was he stationed?
text:
The helmsman steered the submarine and was stationed in the conning tower.  He could not see where he was going even when the boat was on the surface.  However, he was not the sailor who decided where to go.  The helmsman’s job was to steer the course given to him by the captain or the Officer of the Deck.  Even on Navy surface ships, where the helmsman could see out through the windows on the bridge, he was just steering the course given to him.  The helmsman had a compass repeater and rudder indicator to help steer the course that had been ordered.

There was an advantage on a surface ship in that there might have been external references in the sea itself to indicate when the ship was drifting off course.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What was a position fix?
title: What was a position fix?
text: A position fix was the process of determining where the submarine was on the ocean.  This may have been done using stars or known geographic landmarks, if available.  Late in the war, this could have been done using LORAN.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How did navigators determine where the boat was?
title: How did navigators determine where the boat was?
text:
In the middle of the ocean, when no land was in sight, submarines navigated using the stars at dusk and dawn.  If they were close to land, the navigator would take bearings to known landmarks or features.

To fix their position in the middle of the ocean, navigators used celestial navigation.  (The sub was already on the surface to charge the battery and to get fresh air in the boat.)  Shooting the stars meant that navigators used sextants to measure the location of multiple stars.  If the sky was clear enough, the goal was to locate at least three of the brightest and best-known stars.  Navigators determined the elevation above the horizon of these stars and noted the time.  They then took those values to a reference book which provided values for lines on a chart.  Where those three lines intersected on the chart was where the boat was.  Ideally, the three lines gave the navigators a single point or, at worst, a small, tight triangle.  A large triangle meant that the boat could be anywhere within those lines and that might not have been accurate enough.

Celestial navigation is not unlike the GPS on your phone.  Submariners knew where they were based on references to known positions of stars in the sky.  GPS does the same thing using satellites, although GPS does the calculations for you.

To illustrate basic celestial navigation with a familiar example, you can find your way while hiking at night by finding the North Star in the Big Dipper.  However, one star can only provide general directions.  By itself, it can be very helpful but it is not enough to know your exact location.

When submarines were in sight of land, navigators used a periscope to get the bearings to known features such as mountain peaks, lighthouses, buoys, shorelines or tall buildings.  A minimum of two bearings was needed, but it was far better to have at least three.  Then the navigators drew bearing lines to those features on the chart.  Where the lines converged indicated where the boat was.  Again, the hope was for a single point or a tight triangle.  Using these geographic features generally made it easier to get definite results.  Because of the shallower water near land, it was even more important to know their exact location.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What did navigators do when the sky was overcast?
title: What did navigators do when the sky was overcast?
text:
In those cases, navigators used the dead reckoning tracker or the DRT.  Dead reckoning used the course and speed after the last known position to estimate where the boat was.  If the boat had been on a course of 270 degrees for five hours at 12 knots, the DRT assumed the sub was 60 nautical miles due west of their last known position.  However, that was just an estimate that degraded over time since it could not account for currents or wind.  Seasoned navigators would have been able to estimate those effects in the short term, giving them a better idea of the boat’s location.

If it had been cloudy for days, confidence in their exact position may have been fairly low.  If so, caution was probably required, particularly if the boat was operating in relatively shallow waters.  In this case, the fathometer could have been helpful.

It is important to remember that the U. S. did not have good charts for all of the Western Pacific during WW2.  For some areas, we had no charts at all.  One of the missions of submarines was to gather intelligence including geographic information about areas of the Pacific where good charts were not available to us.

There were two DRTs on these WW2 submarines, one in the conning tower and one in the control room.  They were automatically updated for the movement of the boat from the gyrocompass and speed log.  The DRT in the control room of the USS Pampanito (SS-333) has the map of her patrol routes.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Were other tools available?
title: Were other tools available?
text: Yes.  Navigators could also take sun lines or use the fathometer.  These weren’t likely to be as accurate as a star fix, but they were better than nothing.  Late in the war, navigators would also have LORAN to help them navigate.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What were sun lines?
title: What were sun lines?
text: Sun lines were similar to star fixes but using our sun as the only star.  The elevation is measured as during a star fix.  Since it is only one source, it could not provide an exact location.  Instead, it would be compared to the dead reckoning location.  Another option would have been to take a series of sun lines.  The sun might have burned through the clouds at midday, even though it had been overcast at dusk and dawn.  A sun line could be done through the periscope.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What was a fathometer?
title: What was a fathometer?
text: A fathometer was a downward pointing sonar which indicated the depth of the ocean bottom at that location.  If navigators had charts with accurate depth readings, they could use the fathometer to compare the reading with the chart.  That likely would not have been sufficient for a position fix, but it could have been enough to let boats know if they were sailing into danger.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What was LORAN?
title: What was LORAN?
text:
Another tool that would be available later in the war was LORAN, a Long-Range Aid to Navigation.  LORAN was a system that used signals from land-based radio stations to determine the ship’s location on the ocean.  It was similar in concept to GPS but used radio waves.  It was introduced first in the Atlantic in early 1943.  It took longer to establish the radio stations in the Pacific.

It appears likely that Pampanito would have had LORAN installed during the overhaul in 1945.  In that case, it would only have been used for navigation to and from Hawaii after the overhaul and would not have been available during the war patrols.  The LORAN unit was in the control room, near the “Christmas tree.”

LORAN-C is still in use, primarily by small vessels.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Wasn’t the lack of a position fix a concern?
title: Wasn’t the lack of a position fix a concern?
text:
It was, but how much of a concern depended on the general area where the boat was operating and what it was trying to accomplish.  If the boat were in shallow water, it was a significant concern.  If it were to rendezvous with other friendly ships, it was a concern.  If it were close to the operating area of another allied submarine, it was a concern.  If it were trying to intercept enemy ships, it was a concern.  If it were in the middle of a lengthy transit and in deep water, it was a bit less of a concern.  Of course, submarine captains always wanted to know where they were.  However, knowing their exact location was more important at some times than at others.

In a related situation, the U. S. had broken some of the Japanese naval codes.  The Japanese broadcast messages to their convoys telling them where their ships were supposed to be at noon on any given day.  However, that intelligence didn’t mean that our boats could show up along that projected course and find the convoys.  Sometimes the Japanese were not very good navigators.  Sometimes our navigators weren’t as good as they hoped.  Sometimes the weather didn’t cooperate and there were no recent star fixes.  Many things had to come together for our submarines to be in the right place at the right time.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What do submarines use now?
title: What do submarines use now?
text:
Submarines now have GPS.  For a time, the U. S. Naval Academy did not teach celestial navigation assuming ships would use GPS.  However, after realizing that GPS satellites could be very vulnerable in a war, the Academy is again teaching celestial navigation.

GPS was developed in part to support submarine-launched missiles.  In order to hit their targets, submarines need to know where they are when launching missiles.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What was a gyrocompass?
title: What was a gyrocompass?
text:
A magnetic compass didn’t work very well enclosed in a steel pipe.  As a result, there was a large gyrocompass in the control room as well as a smaller backup.  There was a “tank compass” as well, but it was a second backup.

A gyrocompass was a series of spinning wheels that tended to remain steady in space, pointing in the same direction – likely north - regardless of the course of the submarine.  The information regarding the course of the boat was automatically fed from the gyrocompass to the Torpedo Data Computer and to the two DRTs.

A familiar example of a gyroscope is a bicycle.  It is difficult to balance on a bicycle when you are stopped but that becomes easy once you are in motion.  The wheels are acting as gyroscopes, tending to spin in the same plane, upright.  You turn a bicycle in motion by leaning in the direction you want to turn and that is another principle of a gyroscope.

The gyrocompasses on submarines do need to be reset periodically.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What was the speed log?
title: What was the speed log?
text: The speed log was a probe, lowered below the hull, that indicated the actual speed of the boat through the water.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Why were there red and green lights on the sail?  What lights were required?
title: Why were there red and green lights on the sail?  What lights were required?
text:
Those were the running lights.  All ships and airplanes had them and still do.  Of course, no combatant ships used the lights during the war since any lights gave away the ship’s position.  Only ships entitled to free passage, such as hospital ships or ships of neutral countries and not carrying war materials, would use those lights.

The purpose of running lights in peacetime was to allow ships and planes to determine where other craft were going in order to avoid collisions.  It didn’t usually take long to learn to translate the visible lights into the general direction that the other ship was heading.  There had to be a red light on the left or port side of a vessel and a green one on the right or starboard side.  A ship also had to have a white masthead light and a white stern light.  Again, these are peacetime requirements.  Submarines were built with the lights installed even if they weren’t used during the war.

In peacetime, submarines on the surface at night could be confusing.  Since the lights were generally close together – and higher up on the sail for visibility - subs could be mistaken for small fishing boats.  On submarines, the officer of the deck always had to be cautious and defensive.  He assumed that other vessels did not know how big the boat actually was.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What were true and relative bearings?
title: What were true and relative bearings?
text:
True bearings were absolute in that they were always based on true north.  North was always north, or 000 degrees, no matter which way a ship was heading.  East was always 090 degrees, etc.

Relative bearings used the orientation of the ship as their basis.  A relative bearing of 000 degrees was directly in front of the ship no matter what its course.  If the ship was sailing west, on a course of 270, the relative bearing of another ship due north of it was 000 true but 090 relative.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How were courses and bearings stated?
title: How were courses and bearings stated?
text:
Contrary to many movies, the numbers on a compass rose were not stated the same as other numbers.  For example, 315 was not spoken as “three hundred fifteen.”  It was too easy to confuse 315 with 350 if stated that way.  Instead, a course or bearing of 315 was stated as “three, one, five degrees.”  This way it was easier to clearly understand the bearing being given.  Other examples were due north stated as “zero, zero, zero degrees” and west stated as “two, seven, zero degrees.”

It was important to be precise and clear when stating courses or bearings to objects.  Failing to do so could have put the boat in danger.  As the saying goes: “A collision at sea can ruin your whole day” - or a career.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Why are there guns on the submarine?
title: Why are there guns on the submarine?
text: Visitors today are used to seeing images of sleek submarines with clean, uncluttered decks. That is why people are often surprised to see guns on an old WW2 submarine. However, submarines in World War 2 did have guns on the deck and in the superstructure. These guns were intended for self-defense, although this would evolve during the course of the war. Most of the guns on the deck were standard U. S. anti-aircraft weapons.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What guns did U. S. submarines have?
title: What guns did U. S. submarines have?
text:
Early in the war, the typical complement of guns was one cannon, one 40 mm Bofors anti-aircraft machine gun and twin 20 mm Oerlikon anti-aircraft guns. These were permanently installed on the decks, although the barrels of the 20 mm guns may have been stored with the ready ammunition.

Initially, the standard cannon was 3-inch. That would soon be replaced with a 4-inch gun and eventually a 5-inch. The cannon currently on the USS Pampanito (SS-383) is the 5-inch gun designed for submarines. The barrel is shorter than similar U. S. Navy guns and was galvanized to resist corrosion.

In addition, there were smaller machine guns that could be mounted around the sail. These were .30 caliber early in the war and were replaced with .50 caliber by war’s end. Various small arms were stored below decks.

There were three larger submarines at the beginning of the war that had two six-inch cannons each. However, these subs were large, slow and cumbersome. Those boats were often relegated to minelaying operations and occasional shore bombardment.

The number of guns on the boats increased during the later part of the war. It appears that the Pampanito had a second 40 mm Bofors added during her overhaul in 1945. Some other submarines had a second 5-inch gun added instead.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What does the caliber of the 5-inch gun mean?
title: What does the caliber of the 5-inch gun mean?
text: In this case the caliber was not the width of the shell. For these larger Navy guns, the caliber indicated the length of the barrel. The length of the barrel was the diameter of the bore multiplied by the caliber. In this case, the length of the barrel was 5 inches multiplied by 25 caliber or 125 inches, just over 10 feet.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did the guns get submerged?
title: Did the guns get submerged?
text: Yes, the guns were submerged. Remember that our WW2 submarines were rated to dive to at least 300 feet. (Many, in fact, went deeper due to battle damage or to avoid depth charges. Pampanito went deeper than 400 feet at least twice.) As a result, the guns were definitely well under water.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How did the guns fire after being submerged?
title: How did the guns fire after being submerged?
text:
These guns required regular maintenance in advance. The guns had to be ready to fire very quickly upon surfacing since the enemy tended to shoot back. There was no time for maintenance before loading and shooting.

A few of the guns were designed to resist or avoid corrosion. The barrel of the five-inch gun was galvanized to resist corrosion. The .50 caliber machine guns were stored dry in special deck lockers. The barrels of the 20 mm Oerlikons could be removed and placed in one of the ready ammunition storage lockers. The 40 mm Bofors were too big to be stored but they could be maintained in place. All of the guns needed maintenance as often as practical. Even though all of these guns were designed for a naval (salt water) environment, none of them took well to being submerged.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Where would the .50 caliber guns be mounted?
title: Where would the .50 caliber guns be mounted?
text: Near the sail, there are 10 stanchions that have sockets to hold the .50 caliber gun mounts. There were two stanchions on each side of the main deck. There were three more on each side of the gun deck where the Bofors guns are located on the Pampanito. The guns used an aircraft mounting in the stanchions.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What small arms would be carried?
title: What small arms would be carried?
text:
Small arms might have included:

  • One .22 caliber pistol.
  • One .22 caliber rifle.
  • Six .30 caliber Carbine M-1s.
  • Twelve .45 caliber Colt pistols.
  • Two .45 caliber Thompson submachine guns.
  • Two 12-gauge Winchester Riot Guns.
  • One .45 caliber line throwing rifle.
  • Two Very (flare) pistol guns.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Were the guns now on the Pampanito always the configuration on WW2 submarines?
title: Were the guns now on the Pampanito always the configuration on WW2 submarines?
text: No. The cannons were originally 3-inch. These were replaced by 4-inch guns and then by the 5-inch. Pampanito began with a four-inch gun that was upgraded in 1945. The cannon could be forward of the sail or aft. Most submarines had just a single Bofors 40 mm gun, with a second one added late in the war.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did any U. S. submarines shoot down Japanese aircraft?
title: Did any U. S. submarines shoot down Japanese aircraft?
text:
There is no record of the Pampanito shooting down any planes. In fact, there are very few indications that any of our submarines shot down enemy aircraft in WW2. Their best option was to dive. Those were the instructions given to the captains – to get deep quickly if any aircraft was sighted.

The only clear record of an American submarine shooting down a Japanese aircraft occurred during the attack on Pearl Harbor that brought the U.S. into the war. Most accounts of the war did not even address the topic of submarines shooting back.

There were four U.S. submarines tied up at the Pearl Harbor Submarine Base at the time of the December, 1941 attack: the USS Narwhal (SS-167), the USS Dolphin (SS-169), the USS Cachalot (SS-170) and the USS Tautog (SS-199). Naturally the submarine crews did what they could to help fight off the attack. The only boat to get credit for shooting down a plane was the Tautog. Even that may have been shared with some other defenders. Narwhal may have hit two other aircraft, but there was no clear indication that she brought them down. Other than that day, there are only a few indications that captains used the guns to fend off a plane in order to buy some time for other purposes such as a rescue.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did any other country use submarines to shoot down planes?
title: Did any other country use submarines to shoot down planes?
text: At one point in the Battle of the Atlantic, when allied aircraft were sinking a large number of U-boats, the Germans created anti-aircraft submarines by adding more machine guns. Admiral Doenitz ordered those U-boats to stay on the surface to shoot it out with the aircraft. Some of these boats were used as escorts to try to allow other U-boats to make it out to their patrol areas. This was mostly for the U-boats sailing from the German submarine pens in France, such as Brest and Lorient, into the Bay of Biscay. Some allied planes were shot down but at a terrible cost in U-boats. At least 57 aircraft were shot down by U-boats but 12 U-boats were lost in these attacks. Doenitz soon had to cancel the order.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — If the guns weren’t normally used for anti-aircraft defense, how were the guns used in WW2?
title: If the guns weren’t normally used for anti-aircraft defense, how were the guns used in WW2?
text:
It appears that the main use of these guns was to attack small shipping later in the war. U. S. subs had destroyed many of Japan’s larger ships. The Japanese were reduced to using sampans, junks, sea trucks, and wooden ships to help move what cargo they could. The smaller ships were not worth the cost of an expensive torpedo. Since torpedoes would normally need to run at a depth of at least six feet, they would likely pass under these small ships without exploding.

The guns worked reasonably well to attack the smaller ships. The cannons and the 40 mm guns could be used to set fire to them and to sink them. The 20 mm and smaller machine guns might be used to suppress enemy fire, assuming the submarines were close enough. Small arms were used if a boarding party was needed.

Guns were also used to try to detonate mines that had broken away from their moorings and were adrift. (Somehow, Pampanito’s crew were able to hit these mines but couldn’t seem to sink or detonate them.) The guns would be available if needed for special missions such as bombardments, rescues, and when inserting or extracting coast watchers or guerrillas.

The Pampanito does not appear to have ever fired her guns at Japanese aircraft or shipping.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did all captains use the guns against small ships?
title: Did all captains use the guns against small ships?
text:
No. Some did and some did not. Rather unusually, the senior commanders of the submarine forces in the Pacific did not provide any firm guidance to the sub skippers in this regard. Commanders left it to the conscience of each captain to determine his own course of action.

Some captains understood that the small ships were usually family businesses and that the crews were not Japanese. These captains generally decided not to attack the small vessels.

Other captains considered them, also correctly, to be a part of the war effort and did not want the supplies to make it through. Most of these small vessels did have war materials along with a few Japanese soldiers on board. These captains did attack. Some of the skippers then tried to provide food and water to the non-combatants along with information about the nearest land.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Why were some guns added?
title: Why were some guns added?
text: The assumption was that, if the Allies had to invade Japan, submarines would act as pickets and would attempt to intercept suicide boats and aircraft. In this case, the boats would have needed the guns. U. S. subs would have needed to spend more time on the surface and needed more guns to defend themselves. Fortunately, the war ended without needing to invade Japan.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Why don’t our submarines have guns now?
title: Why don’t our submarines have guns now?
text:
Guns on modern submarines aren’t needed and have too many disadvantages. The guns aren’t needed because submarines now submerge once after leaving port and get to deep water. Modern boats normally stay submerged until returning home or visiting some other port. The new boats do not normally need to spend time on the surface to charge batteries or get fresh air into the boat, so there is little need for this type of anti-aircraft defense.

One of the disadvantages of having the guns is that the irregular shapes add drag to the submarine making it slower and less efficient. That means that a little more fuel was used. The shapes also cause water to swirl and make noise. Modern sonars would detect the additional noise. In addition, there is no longer a flat deck surface for the gun crews to operate safely.

The types of attacks that were done using these guns in WW2 can now be done by other ships, aircraft or, if secrecy is needed, Navy SEALs.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How many submarines did the U. S. have in WW2?
title: How many submarines did the U. S. have in WW2?
text:
The U. S. started with about 50 operational submarines. The U. S. built 221, lost 52 and ended the war with about 179 boats in service. There were about 40 more in sea trials or still being completed. Definitions vary so it can be difficult to get consistent, definitive numbers. Contracts for many more of the Balao and Tench class boats were cancelled when it became apparent that the subs would not be needed for the war.

This refers only to operational boats. At the beginning of the war, the U. S. still had some old R-class boats and most of those were being used for training. Some S-class boats were being used for training while others were still operational boats at that time. (The R-boats go back to the early part of WW1 and the S-boats were built during and right after that war.) However, both classes had shorter range and many other limitations. The operational S-boats would become training boats as new construction could replace them.
category: U. S. WW2 Subs in General

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What was built after the R and S class boats?
title: What was built after the R and S class boats?
text:
The U. S. had built about 40 “fleet boats” in the 1930s. This includes the Porpoise, Perch, Salmon, Sargo, and Tambor classes. These are the boats that were built as new technologies became available and designers learned from operational experience. These boats were larger than the S-boats, had greater range and carried more torpedoes. They were almost the size of the Gato/Balao/Tench boats built during the war and had similar capabilities. A table, below, compares the sizes of U. S. submarine classes in WW2.

The fleet boats were operational at the start of WW2 along with some of the S-boats. About 16 of the fleet boats were lost during the war. Many of the others were still in active service at the end of the war.

NOTE: The name “fleet boats” generally refers to the various classes of U. S. submarines built between WW1 and WW2. The reference is to the fact that these boats were intended to sail with the fleet, or ahead of it, and engage the enemy first. Although it wasn’t practical for these boats to sail with the fleet, and it rarely if ever happened, the name stuck. The name was sometimes also applied to the Gato/Balao/Tench classes that were built during the war.

There were also a few larger boats built after WW1. These larger boats had two six-inch guns and they were slower and less maneuverable. Therefore, these boats were more likely to be used for minelaying and for special operations.
category: U. S. WW2 Subs in General

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What classes of submarines did the U. S. build during the war?
title: What classes of submarines did the U. S. build during the war?
text:
The first of the newest WW2 classes, the Gato boats, were just being commissioned when the Japanese attacked Pearl Harbor. The design had been set in 1939 and then the U. S. started building this new class. This class and the Balao and Tench classes were what were built during the war. All three classes were very similar, other than the thickness of the hull. The different classes look the same to most observers. Sometimes all three classes are referred to as Gato boats.

The Balao class boats had a thicker hull, at 7/8 inch rather than 11/16 inch for the Gatos. The hull was also strengthened to allow the boat to sit on the bottom. The Tench class kept those improvements and had some ballast tank piping rerouted for safety.

The U. S. completed a total of about 77 Gato class, 119 Balao class and 25 Tench class boats during and shortly after the war.
category: U. S. WW2 Subs in General

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What is a class of ships or submarines?
title: What is a class of ships or submarines?
text:
A class is a group of ships built to essentially the same design. There may be some small differences, often depending on the shipyard where the vessel was built.

Classes are normally named after the first ship in the design that was ordered. In an oddity, the USS Drum (SS-228) was the first Gato submarine completed and commissioned. However, the USS Gato (SS-212) was the first of the design ordered and the class is named after her.
category: U. S. WW2 Subs in General

title: How do these classes of submarines compare to each other?

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What did the U. S. do with all these submarines at the end of the war?
title: What did the U. S. do with all these submarines at the end of the war?
text:
The U. S. had a huge Navy and decided to keep only about half of it active. That included aircraft carriers, cruisers and destroyers as well as submarines. Many of the ships that the U. S. didn’t keep in active status were added to the reserve fleet. Others were used in live weapons tests or sold to friendly nations.

The boats that were kept active after the war would be upgraded starting in the early 1950s. Guns were removed; the sail was streamlined and made more efficient. Snorkels were added so that boats did not have to surface to recharge the batteries or get fresh air in the boat. With a snorkel, that could now be done from periscope depth. Later, there would be a GUPPY program to improve battery capacity.
category: U. S. WW2 Subs in General

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What was the reserve fleet?
title: What was the reserve fleet?
text: The reserve fleet, sometimes called the “mothball fleet”, was a number of inactive boats and ships that the U. S. kept on hand in case of new hostilities. The vessels were unloaded, covered in protective coatings and then sealed up as much as practical. The idea was that it would be cheaper and faster to reactivate them and upgrade them to current standards than it would be to build new ones. U. S. reserve fleets are currently being dismantled and the ships sold for scrap.
category: U. S. WW2 Subs in General

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did the U. S. use any of the reserve fleet submarines after WW2?
title: Did the U. S. use any of the reserve fleet submarines after WW2?
text:
Yes. The U. S. reactivated and recommissioned a number of these boats for service during the Korean Conflict in the early 1950s. A few of those were kept active after the fighting ended but most went back into the reserve fleet.

Other boats were sold to allies and friendly nations. Some of those were given upgrades first. Other boats from the reserve fleet were used as targets when testing new torpedoes. Still others were used in the atomic bomb testing in the Pacific. Lastly, some of the WW2 boats became museum submarines, such as the USS Pampanito (SS-383) here in San Francisco.

By the late 1950s, the U. S. was building nuclear powered submarines. That meant that the WW2 boats were quickly outdated. By the end of 1973 nearly all of the WW2 submarines had been decommissioned. However, some of the new classes of diesel submarines that we built after the war were still in service in the U. S. Navy as late as 1988.

Two U. S. WW2 submarines, the USS Tusk (SS-426) and the USS Cutlass (SS-478) were transferred to Taiwan and are still in service as of 2026. However, since these two boats are now 80 years old, they are limited in their capabilities. Taiwan is currently building new, non-nuclear submarines.

NOTE: Some of the battleships that were in the U. S. reserve fleet were returned to service as late as the First Gulf War. They had been upgraded to carry and launch tomahawk missiles. All of the Iowa class battleships, the last class, are now museums.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Why was there such a difference in the numbers of boats built in each yard?
title: Why was there such a difference in the numbers of boats built in each yard?
text:
The first reason is that Electric Boat and the Portsmouth Naval Shipyard were established yards and could ramp up production more quickly. Those yards were experienced in building submarines. The Manitowoc Shipbuilding Company had not been building Navy ships at all. That shipyard did not finalize their first contract, for just 10 boats, until October of 1940.

Mare Island Naval Shipyard was an experienced yard and had built submarines as well as Navy ships of various types. However, it soon became apparent that the shipyard would be needed for submarine overhauls. That limited the amount of new submarine construction that could be completed there.
category: U. S. WW2 Subs in General

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What is different about a U. S. naval shipyard, like the ones in Portsmouth and Mare Island?
title: What is different about a U. S. naval shipyard, like the ones in Portsmouth and Mare Island?
text: Naval shipyards are owned and operated by the government. Costs for building ships are based on the total costs for labor, materials and overhead. Civilian shipyards, such as Electric Boat and Manitowoc Shipbuilding, are profit making ventures. They add a reasonable profit to their estimated costs when entering into a contract with the government.
category: U. S. WW2 Subs in General

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How much did these submarines cost?
title: How much did these submarines cost?
text:
The numbers vary. The cost for boats from Portsmouth or Mare Island during WW2 is generally quoted at $5 million. The first contract for the boats from Manitowoc was for about $3 million and the second was for $3.2 million per boat, plus incentives for early completion. That doesn’t necessarily mean that the boats built in the civilian yards are that much less expensive. It seems unlikely that the accounting is consistent. For example, did the private yards include the costs for the propellers, engines and batteries, which the shipyards didn’t actually build? It seems likely that Navy yards included all costs while the contracts with the private yards may have only included the hull, wiring, piping, and installation of the engines and other large items.

These prices are in 1940s dollars. $5 million in 1943 would be the equivalent of over $112 million today.
category: U. S. WW2 Subs in General

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How long did it take to build these submarines?
title: How long did it take to build these submarines?
text:
In the period between the two world wars, it could take as much as two to three years to complete a submarine. There was little urgency and architects were likely making changes to the designs as they learned more about how prior boats performed. There was also some incentive to take longer in order to improve planning and to maintain staffing levels in the shipyards. However, by the late 1930s, as the war was on the horizon and more boats were being ordered, the typical time to complete a submarine was down to about a year and a half.

When the war had broken out in Europe, contracts were being let to begin building ships either as an effort to keep us out of the war or to be able to fight it effectively if the U. S. was eventually in it. Construction had already begun, but not on a pace that would soon be needed.

By the time the U. S. was in the war, in December of 1941, construction had continued to speed up. Submarine designs had been set and soon shipyards were operating 24 hours per day, seven days per week. Shipyards would also have multiple boats under construction at any one time. There would be some boats where the work had just begun and others farther along but still in drydocks. Others may have been launched but still needed a few months for more work to be completed. During the war, boats would usually be commissioned less than a year after construction began.

For example, construction on the Pampanito began on March 15, 1943. She was commissioned on November 6, 1943. The submarine USS Picuda (SS-382) was started on the same day, in the same drydock. The boats were both launched on the 12th of July. Picuda was commissioned about three weeks before Pampanito. The Portsmouth Naval Shipyard commissioned 32 of these submarines in 1944 alone.

When a submarine is commissioned, there is still more to do before it is fully functional. It is true that construction work has generally been completed, builders’ trials have been completed and the full crew is aboard. The Navy has accepted the work done on the boat so far.

However, further sea trials are still pending, along with the need to fix any of the issues discovered at that time. Generally, those issues are minor leaks, squeals or equipment not quite performing up to specifications. Most of these problems would be resolved quickly.
category: U. S. WW2 Subs in General

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Were all new U. S. submarines identical in WW2?
title: Were all new U. S. submarines identical in WW2?
text:
As mentioned above, the three classes built during WW2 – Gato/Balao/Tench – were very similar but not quite identical. The Balao and Tench classes had thicker hulls and Tench boats had improved piping. This enabled the Balao and Tench boats to have an approved depth limit (test depth) of about 400 feet vs. 300 feet for the Gato boats.

In addition, there could be some slight variation in equipment location. One tall skipper had the forward battery layout changed a bit so he could have a longer bunk and be able to stretch out. These variations were generally minor and were limited by functionality. Some changes depended on the preferences of the captains, most often on the commissioning (first) commanding officer.

One of the more apparent variations was the location of the large cannon. It could be located either forward or aft of the sail. It depended on whether the captain expected it to be used more often offensively (usually forward) or defensively (aft of the sail). The gun could get moved after commissioning if the current captain could talk the shipyard into making the change during a refit or overhaul.

If a sub sailor knew one of these boats - or even an older fleet boat - and qualified on it, he wouldn’t need much time at all to qualify on another.

The differences among these three classes are not usually apparent to most observers.
category: U. S. WW2 Subs in General

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How could a shipyard build submarines in Manitowoc on Lake Michigan?
title: How could a shipyard build submarines in Manitowoc on Lake Michigan?
text:
The family-owned Manitowoc Shipbuilding Co. was an experienced shipyard. The yard had built many ships, such as ore carriers, that operated on the Great Lakes. When the war broke out, the leadership wanted to assist in the war effort and keep staff employed. Although the yard had no experience building submarines, and originally turned down the project, the shipyard worked with Electric Boat in New London to prepare. This shipyard then built 28 submarines as a subsidiary of Electric Boat. The sailors in Manitowoc boats generally appreciated the high quality of the work.

However, Manitowoc Shipbuilding did face multiple challenges:

  • In order to understand how each piping or wiring system fit within the whole, and the order of installation for each one, the shipyard first built a full-sized model of a submarine out of wood.
  • The shipyard was building ocean-going submarines in a fresh water environment. Fresh water is less dense than sea water meaning that it doesn’t support as much weight. That, in effect, makes the completed submarine act as if it were tons heavier. The shipyard had to compensate for that so the boat wouldn’t go straight to the bottom when it submerged the first time.
  • Manitowoc submarines had to be launched sideways at commissioning due to the location on a river. That had never been done with these boats. There was concern that the sudden roll would damage some of the battery cells or that the boat would roll over. The engineers decided to launch without the battery cells installed and calculated the expected roll of the boat. The calculations were exactly correct and everything worked out as designed.
  • Winter conditions on the Great Lakes are harsher than in Portsmouth, New London or Mare Island. The submarines undergoing sea trials in winter collected quite a bit of ice when on the surface. Much of that had to be removed before diving because of the added weight. It made the boat top heavy and less stable. This was also an issue, although to a lesser extent, in Portsmouth and New London.
  • The boats then had to be sailed or transported to salt water.

In spite of all the things Manitowoc had to do just to be able to build these boats, the yard completed nearly all of them ahead of plan and under budget. All but one of the boats were completed ahead of schedule, entitling the shipyard to performance bonuses. The shipyard accepted some of the bonuses but not all, since the owners thought it improper to make too much profit during the war.

The shipyard was also building landing craft and heavy cranes at the same time. That construction did not interfere with building submarines or vice versa.

Today, getting boats from Manitowoc to the ocean would be straightforward. The boat would just sail to the Atlantic Ocean using the St. Lawrence Seaway. However, that wasn’t completed until 1959. In 1941, the locks in the Erie Canal could not accommodate a ship longer than 300 feet and the locks on the St. Lawrence River were even shorter. These submarines were nearly 312 feetlong. Therefore, the only water route available was through the Chicago Sanitary Canal to the Illinois River and then the Mississippi down to the Gulf of Mexico. (Yes, the Chicago sewage canal.) The crews would sail the boats to Chicago. Then the subs were towed through Chicago to Lockport, IL, loaded onto a floating drydock (somewhat similar to a barge) and towed (pushed) down the rivers. The Manitowoc shipyard needed to buy or build the drydocks.

Chicago had built drawbridges which would have allowed the drydock to navigate the Sanitary Canal had they all been finished. The bridges were all functional for road traffic, but some of them didn’t open. The shipyard needed to complete the rest of the mechanisms to raise the bridges.

The completed submarines on the floating drydocks still would not fit under all the bridges on the Mississippi. To solve that, the periscope shears, periscopes and radar masts were removed before entering the Chicago Sanitary Canal and were reinstalled in New Orleans.

One interesting story concerns a delay due to high water in spring on the Mississippi. The tows had to wait several days for lower levels of water in the river in order to get under bridges. There was no alternative other than to tie the tug and floating drydock up to trees on the river banks and wait. At times, submarine builders needed to be as resourceful as submariners.
category: U. S. WW2 Subs in General

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did “Rosie the Riveter” help build submarines?
title: Did “Rosie the Riveter” help build submarines?
text:
She certainly did. However, just for clarification, submarines were no longer riveted as they had been in WW1. Now the hulls were welded. As a result, it might be more accurate to say that “Wendy the Welder” helped build submarines.

In any case, many women went to work in defense plants during the war. Some did administrative work and some did drawings and blueprints. But many others were welders. In fact, after initially resisting having women in the shipyards, management often found that women were better welders than the men. The women were more patient and some skills, such as sewing, did make the training easier.

Two of Pampanito’s engines were named, somewhat unflatteringly, after two of the women who worked in the Portsmouth shipyard.
category: U. S. WW2 Subs in General

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How big were U. S.  submarines in WW2?
title: How big were U. S.  submarines in WW2?
text:
Most of our submarines were about the same size as the Pampanito. The boats built during the war were almost 312 feet long (311 feet and 9 inches) and 27 feet wide at the widest. The pressure hull (sometimes referred to as the people pipe) is 16 feet in diameter in most places, around 275 to 280 feet long and is tapered at the ends. The Conning Tower is about 20 feet long and 10 feet in diameter.

Surface displacement is about 1,550 tons and submerged is about 2,400 tons.

These newer boats had 10 torpedo tubes – six forward and four aft – and a full complement of torpedoes was 24.

The boats had four main engine/generator combinations, plus a smaller diesel in the lower flats of the after engine room. The main engines produced around 1,500 horsepower each, whether they were built by Fairbanks-Morse or General Motors Winton.

The 40 or so “fleet boats” that were most of our submarines at the outset of WW2 were about 10 feet shorter than the Pampanito, a bit narrower and lacked the hard bulkhead to divide the engine rooms.

Some fleet boats had only eight torpedo tubes and others had ten. Generally, these earlier only carried 20 torpedoes but some could carry four more in external containers. Their speed and range were comparable to the Gato/Balao/Tench boats. Many of them served throughout the war. These older boats had a higher loss rate than the Gato/Balao/Tench boats, due to the length of time they were in combat.

Initially, one significant drawback to these pre-war boats was in the engines. Some of these boats were outfitted with 9-cylinder Hooven-Owens-Rentschler (HOR) diesels. These engines turned out not to be reliable. (The sailors thought the engines lived up to their name –HORs.) The main problem was the failure of the timing chains. After a while, these engines would be removed and replaced with the larger diesels being used in the Gato boats.

The few S-class boats still in use at the beginning of the war were significantly smaller and had less range. That is why they became training boats as soon as it was feasible to do so. The S-class boats varied in size. Length was generally from about 220 ft. to 240 ft. Beam was 21 to 22 feet. Displacement was 850 tons to 903 tons on the surface. Submerged displacement was 1,060 to 1,230 tons. Maximum speed on the surface was 13 to 15 knots. Range was 5,500 nautical miles at 6.5 knots.
category: U. S. WW2 Subs in General

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How many submarines did the U. S. lose in WW2?
title: How many submarines did the U. S. lose in WW2?
text:
The U. S. lost a total of 52 submarines from all causes or about 23%. That included about 3,500 submarine sailors with their boats. This was the highest loss rate of any of the major American service branches during the war. (However, some of the smaller units, such as the Eighth Air Force over Europe, may have had a higher loss rate.) As bad as this loss rate was for our boats, most other countries in the war lost a higher percentage of their submarines.

The most frequent cause of our submarine losses was due to enemy action, either aircraft, anti-submarine warship attacks, or a combination of the two. Some were lost to mines. Over the course of the war, four were lost by running aground on reefs although those crews were all rescued. At least two boats were lost when they were struck by their own torpedoes running in a circle, likely due to gyroscope failures. The first U. S. submarine lost in WW2, the USS Sealion (SS-195), was struck by bombs while it was being repaired in the Philippines on one of the first days of the war. In a few cases, no one knows why the boats were lost. It could have been enemy action, mines, torpedo circular runs or even operational errors, with no survivors to tell the story.

A few notes about unusual losses:

When the submarine USS Pompano (SS-181) was reported overdue, there was some confusion as to the name of the boat. It was sometimes reported in local papers as the Pampanito, which caused unnecessary grief for a few families until the error was corrected.

Two older boats, the USS Salmon (SS-182) and USS Halibut (SS-232) were so badly damaged that they had to be taken out of operational service. Salmon became a training boat. Halibut was just scrapped. However, these two boats are not included in the count of 52 since they did make it home.

It has not been definitively established but the USS Dorado (SS-248) may have been sunk by one of our own PBM flying-boats when in a safe area. Other possible causes have been put forward as well but none have been substantiated.

The USS Corvina (SS-226) is the only U. S. boat known to have been sunk by a Japanese submarine. She was lost in November of 1943.

The USS Robalo (SS-273) was probably sunk by a mine in 1944. 77 men died in the sinking. Apparently, four others survived and were captured but died in captivity.

The USS Seawolf (SS-197) was sunk in late 1944 with 82 crewmen plus 17 U. S. Army personnel while en route to Samar. There was apparently a great deal of confusion in the area. In any case, Seawolf did not, or could not, respond to interrogation signals and was sunk by U. S. forces.

The summary of our submarine losses in WW2 is as follows:

5
