display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Was everyone on board lost when a submarine sank?
title: Was everyone on board lost when a submarine sank?
text:
In WW2, that was often the case but not always. When the USS S-36 (SS-141), USS S-27 (SS-132), USS S-39 (SS-144) and USS Darter (SS-227) had each run aground, all of the crews survived. The crew of the Darter was transferred, en masse to the USS Menhaden (SS-377), then still under construction.

Nine other boats were lost with some, but not all, of the crew surviving:

The USS Sealion (SS-195) was lost at the very beginning of the war in the Philippines. Four men were killed when she was hit by two bombs from an aircraft attack. The boat was in maintenance. (One man from the USS Seadragon (SS-194) died from the shrapnel from Sealion.) The rest of the crew survived and were evacuated from the Philippines.

All 62 men of the crew of the USS Perch (SS-176) survived the damage to their boat. The men also survived the scuttling of the boat but nine died in captivity.

The USS Grenadier (SS-210) was damaged and then scuttled. All 76 men survived the loss of the boat, but four died in captivity.

The USS R-12 (SS-89) was recommissioned at the beginning of the war for use as a training boat. She was still being used as a training boat when she was lost in 1943. 42 men died when the boat went down, including two Brazilian Naval Officers. Five men were rescued and, fortunately, 18 others were on liberty that day and were not on board.

The USS S-44 (SS-155) was lost in 1943 along with 55 of her crew. Two crewmen survived.

In a very unusual case, 43 men initially survived the loss of the USS Sculpin (SS-191). The survivors were picked up by the Japanese and split into two groups and put aboard Japanese carriers for the trip to Japan. One of those carriers was sunk by the submarine USS Sailfish (SS-192) and only one of that group of Sculpin sailors survived. A total of just 21 men from the Sculpin survived the war. Captain John Cromwell, who was aboard Sculpin as wolfpack commander, had opted to go down with the boat rather than taking a chance that he might give away the Ultra secrets under interrogation. He was awarded the Medal of Honor posthumously.

The USS Tullibee (SS-284) was sunk by her own torpedo when it made a circular run. 79 men were lost and just one survived. Approximately 23 circular torpedo runs were reported in WW2, although there could have been more.

78 men were lost when the USS Flier (SS-250) was sunk by a mine. Eight others made it to Mantangula Island where they made contact with friendly natives. The natives radioed Australia, and the survivors were extracted by the USS Redfin (SS-272).

The USS Tang (SS-306) was hit and sunk by a circular run of her own torpedo. It was her last torpedo at the end of the patrol. Nine men survived the sinking and were taken prisoner. All nine survived the war including her captain, Richard O’Kane, who was later awarded the Medal of Honor.

In the other 39 cases, the entire crew went down with the boat.
category: U. S. WW2 Subs in General

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How were engineers able to design such a complex submarine?
title: How were engineers able to design such a complex submarine?
text:
Submarines evolved. These boats weren’t conjured up out of someone’s imagination as fully formed vessels in the 1930s and 40s. These WW2 submarines were the result of a rather lengthy process going back hundreds of years. Here is a (relatively) quick summary, up to the beginning of WW2.

The idea of a submersible, naval warship appears to go back at least to the reign of Alexander the Great. That was 300 years BCE. Leonardo da Vinci also designed a submarine, although it did not appear to be workable.

The first attack in American submarine history was on a British ship during our Revolutionary War. It was attempted by David Bushnell in his submarine Turtle. Like most of the designs at this time, Turtle was a small, one-man submersible powered by the man inside it. The weapon was called a torpedo but it was what we now think of as a mine. It was to be attached to the target and detonated after the submersible pulled away to a safe distance. Because the speed and endurance were so limited, the attempted attack against a British ship failed.

The USS Alligator was the first known U. S. Navy submersible, purchased during the Civil War. (The Turtle, above, was apparently operated by the Continental Army.) It was also small and powered by the 12 men inside, first with oars, then with a hand-cranked propeller. Alligator did not contribute to the Civil War effort, and sank off Cape Hatteras with no loss of life in 1863. ("The Innovative, Mysterious Alligator" by Chuck Viet, Naval History magazine, August 2010.)

The first successful attack by a submarine was the sinking of the USS Housatonic. The Confederate submarine CSS Hunley successfully approached the Housatonic and detonated the spar charge. The Housatonic sank. Unfortunately, the Hunley was not able to get far enough away and the crew was all killed when the submarine also sank. This was the third crew of the Hunley to die when the vessel sank.

A breakthrough occurred in the late 1800s. Robert Whitehead had developed his motor torpedo, a self-propelled device that was a natural fit with the submarines being built. Shortly after that, at about the turn of the century, John Holland and Simon Lake were able to create workable submarines here in the U. S. Their boats had gasoline engines and were no longer dependent on human power. They were larger and Holland’s boats carried torpedoes.

It took years but Holland was finally able to get the Navy to approve his designs and buy his submarines. These would be the first mechanically-powered attack submarines. When he ran short of capital because of all the delays, Isaac Rice came to his rescue. Rice had been looking for more applications for his Exide battery business. Submarines were a logical application for batteries since that was their source of power when submerged. Rice bought out Holland’s patents and the rest of his financial interests. Holland was eventually squeezed out of the company altogether. This was the beginning of the Electric Boat Company which still builds U. S. submarines today. It was also the last of Holland’s designs.

Some nations bought Holland’s boats. Others bought the designs and developed their own boats. Britain and Germany built their own submarines based on what they learned from the Holland designs and Lake’s work. Many navies wanted to have their own input into the designs of their boats. Holland and Lake had done their own designs and offered the boats for sale.

By the time of World War I, there had been many improvements. Boats had periscopes and both bow and stern planes for depth control. The boats were larger. They were still somewhat primitive but more habitable. Germany, in particular, had created very effective boats. This became apparent in September of 1914, only about six weeks into WW1, when Otto Weddigen in command of the U-9 attacked three obsolete British cruisers in the space of about an hour. All three sank rather quickly with the loss of almost 1,500 men.

Germany then proceeded to show how effective a weapon of war a submarine could be. Germany almost severed the supply lines to Britain and France. British ships could find German submarines with ASDIC, which the U. S. calls sonar. However, the British were still developing weapons to attack subs in the depths. Escorts could only hope to ram submarines or force them to the surface and attack with guns. Sometimes, it was good enough to just keep the U-boats down and unable to attack while the convoy escaped.

Eventually, the Allies managed to defeat the Central Powers on land to end the war. As the spoils of war, the Allies received examples of the German U-boats. After the war, when the U. S. compared our new submarines to the German U-boats, the U. S. realized how limited our boats were. One analysis found that in every category the German submarines were superior. In many aspects the U-boats were far superior. The U. S. had no choice but to begin the work of improving our designs.

The two most basic issues were first to determine what types of submarines were needed and then finding an appropriate and effective means of propulsion for them. Some of the other lesser challenges that had to be addressed were the quality of periscopes, communications, detection gear (sonar) and habitability over long distances

Perhaps the most important outcome of the analysis in 1926 was the creation of the Submarine Officers Conference. This was a group of experienced submarine officers that included force commanders, naval engineers and officers who had commanded boats. For the first time, American submarine officers would have input into the needs of the submarine force and the designs of the submarines themselves.

By 1934, the conference had settled on a design of approximately 1,500 tons surface displacement. This would provide the range needed to carry the fight across the Pacific and Atlantic. The boats needed to be large enough to carry the fuel for a long journey and to carry enough torpedoes to make the trip worthwhile. This would be the eventual size of the Gato/Balao/Tench class boats of WW2, such as the Pampanito.

The propulsion issue wasn’t easily solved. The surface navy at the time was primarily steam-driven and had difficulty imagining anything else. However, steam isn’t practical in a submarine dependent on fossil fuels. Restarting a steam plant after being submerged takes way too long. Keeping a steam plant running while submerged makes the submarine too hot for the crew.

NOTE: Our modern submarines do use steam for propulsion. However, since nuclear powered subs do not use fossil fuels to produce the steam, they don’t need oxygen for combustion. The turbines are always using the steam, and the boat is most often at a reasonable temperature.

Gasoline was also impractical as a fuel source. It is too volatile; it tends to catch fire too easily and the fumes in a closed space are toxic and can be explosive.

The answer came from improvements in diesel engines. Then it was a question of the cost of designing and producing these specialized engines. Fortunately, railroads were also looking for diesel engines that would fit in their locomotives and produce a similar amount of power. The requirements for railroad engines were similar to those for our submarines. As a result, the development and manufacturing costs could be spread across many more units.

The Submarine Officers Conference opted to design the power transfer, from the engines to the propeller shafts, as mostly electrical. On U. S. WW2 boats, the engines are not connected physically to the propellers. They were essentially electric submarines with four large engine/generator combinations to provide the electrical power. The arrangement and the flow of power is:

[Engine] [Generator] 🡪 [Cubicle] 🡪 [Main Motors] [Reduction Gear] 🡪 [Propellor Shaft]

This arrangement provides multiple advantages:

  1. There is no clutch to be engaged or to break down. A clutch would have been needed when diving to disconnect the engines from the propellor shafts.
  2. The engines can be run at a high speed for efficiency.
  3. The engines can run at a consistent speed even when the propellors need to turn slowly.
  4. It allows for four engines to be installed in two separate engine rooms.
  5. Four engines can provide a higher maximum speed for a larger submarine.
  6. Any combination of engines can be used depending on power requirements.
  7. The batteries can be recharged on a circuit separate from the one operating the boat.

At this point, the U. S. had a workable design for a long-range submarine with space for sufficient fuel and weapons. It was also large enough to provide some measure of habitability for the crew. This is what was built just before and during WW2.
category: U. S. WW2 Subs in General

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What was the primary mission of U. S. submarines in WW2?
title: What was the primary mission of U. S. submarines in WW2?
text:
The primary mission for U. S. submarines was to sink Japanese shipping of all types. The early emphasis was on sinking Japanese warships and troopships. However, cargo ships and tankers were also worthy targets.

As mentioned elsewhere, the original assumption was that submarines would operate with the fleet. The boats would be scouts and they would attack the enemy first and do as much damage as they could before the main battle fleets engaged each other. However, in hindsight, that was rather naïve. At a maximum speed of 20 or 21 knots, submarines couldn’t keep up with carriers, new fast battleships and destroyers. Even if the boats could keep up with the fleet, they would be on the surface and give away stealth, their greatest advantage and defense. Once carrier battles were fought with opponents hundreds of miles from each other, there was no practical way to have submarines accompany the fleet.

NOTE: The Japanese held the same view of submarines as part of the fleet. In fact, some Japanese submarines carried aircraft (float planes) in hangars that would be launched as scouts and recovered. The Japanese never really gave up the idea of submarines as scouts for the fleet. However, late in the war they used many of their larger boats to resupply their bases that the U. S. had simply bypassed. We were fortunate that the Japanese did not use their boats with their superb torpedoes as effectively as they could have.

As the war progressed, the U. S. realized that tankers were the most important ships for the Japanese. If those ships were sunk, Japanese warships and aircraft would be starved of fuel and wouldn’t have been able to operate effectively. Therefore, the primary emphasis shifted and many of the Japanese tankers were sunk.

Submarines comprised only about 3% of the U. S. Navy in WW2. Yet they sank about 55% of the Japanese shipping. They did so at a cost of 52 boats. The 23% loss rate was the highest of any major branch of the American armed forces during the war.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did U. S. submarine missions in WW2 include assignments in addition to finding and sinking enemy ships?
title: Did U. S. submarine missions in WW2 include assignments in addition to finding and sinking enemy ships?
text:
There certainly were other missions for these submarines. Submarines were very versatile ships. The fact that the boats could submerge and approach an assignment without being seen made them the best vessel for many other types of missions.

One of the more common missions was what was called “lifeguard duty.” Early in the war, someone suggested that submarines might be used to rescue our airmen whose planes were damaged in attacks on Japanese bases. Tests were successful and in 1943 the U. S. began to put submarines near Japanese bases when our aircraft attacked. Submarine captains did not like lifeguard duty. They thought they should have been out sinking ships rather than staying on the surface in dangerous waters for a few days at a time. Naturally, the aviators had a different view.

Pilots were told that, if they could not safely get back to their carriers or bases, they should try to get close to the submarines. There the airmen needed to get out of their planes. They could ditch (crash land in the water) or bail out of the plane. If they couldn’t get close to the boats, the submarines would try to come to them. It was helpful if a wingman could circle over the downed pilot for protection and to direct the submarine to the aviator.

Lifeguard operations were very successful. Over the course of the war in the Pacific, U. S. submarines rescued more than 500 airmen. The most famous rescued airman was a young LTJG torpedo bomber pilot by the name of George Herbert Walker Bush. He was rescued by the USS Finback (SS-230) in September of 1944 off the island of Chichi Jima. His crewman had been killed, and LTJG Bush was in the water for about 30 minutes before being rescued. The result was that submarines were responsible for two American presidents. (George W. Bush wasn’t born until 1947.)

Pampanito did lifeguard duty twice on her first war patrol. The first was near Yap Island and the second was in the Marianas. This was during the build-up to the invasion of the Mariana Islands. However, no pilots needed assistance from Pampanito on either mission.

Other submarine assignments included:

  • Intelligence gathering, which is still one of the primary missions of our submarines. In some cases, during WW2, the U. S. needed better charts. As part of the patrols, submarine force commanders sent submarines to certain areas to fill in gaps in our knowledge. In other cases, the commanders needed information about the movements of Japanese ships. The most famous examples of these were the Battles of Midway, The Philippine Sea and Leyte Gulf. Submarines were able to provide critical information for our fleet and, sometimes, sink a few enemy ships before the big battles.
  • Rescue of the crews of our four submarines that had run aground.
  • Insertion, resupply and extraction of coast watchers or guerillas on isolated islands in the Pacific. In a few instances, submarines inserted raiding parties onto Japanese held islands. Later in the war, this became more common for boats stationed at Fremantle, Australia. Commandoes there were anxious to carry out these raids, and found a sympathetic ear in Admiral Christie, then commander of submarines in the Southwest Pacific. Caution was the order of the day and there were concerns about intelligence losses. Many of the raids were successful.
  • Shelling of Japanese installations. The U. S. originally had three older submarines with two six-inch guns each, the USS Argonaut (SS-166), USS Narwhal (SS-167) and USS Nautilus (SS-168) and they could be more effective on these missions. The USS Barb (SS-220), under the command of LCDR Gene Fluckey, had rocket launchers installed for one patrol and attacked factories, a communications hub and a shipyard which built wooden transports. The hub was hit and the factories and shipyard were duly set ablaze.
  • Barb was also responsible for a very creative commando style attack which destroyed a train and did serious damage to the railroad track. The train was added to the Barb’s battle flag.
  • Minelaying. Any submarine could be used for these missions, but the size of the Argonaut, Nautilus and Narwhal allowed them to be more effective at this task.
  • Shortly after the war started, force commanders sent submarines to the Philippines with ammunition for MacArthur and his troops. One of the boats, the USS Trout (SS-202), then took much of the gold and silver from the Philippine treasury off the islands to safety in the U. S. This resulted in a humorous story when the inventory at Pearl Harbor came up one gold brick short. The brick was found in the galley, where the cook was using it as a paperweight holding his cookbooks open. The cook proclaimed his innocence, saying that he didn’t realize what the brick was. (Of course, he didn’t!)
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What were “Ultra” messages?
title: What were “Ultra” messages?
text: For most of the war, U. S. intelligence had broken some of the Japanese naval codes. This often allowed us to know Japanese ship movements and commanders could deploy our submarines – and other warships – to attack. (Sometimes Japanese messages were decoded too late for us to respond.) These messages were classified as top secret or “ultra” sensitive. If the Japanese learned that the U. S. had broken their codes, the enemy would change their coding systems and the U. S. would lose a significant advantage.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How did the U. S. find out that our submarines had been sunk?
title: How did the U. S. find out that our submarines had been sunk?
text:
Since submarines were frequently operating alone, it would often take some time before their loss was recorded. If the boat was part of a wolfpack, the other members of the pack would likely figure out relatively soon that something was wrong. However, since there was still a chance that the problem was a communications issue, commanders did not immediately give up hope.

The usual procedure was to identify the submarine as overdue about three weeks after it was scheduled to return to a base. After a couple more months, it would be declared missing and presumed lost. Families would then be notified.

The U. S. might also get confirmation from the Japanese. Both sides were required to notify the other of the prisoners of war in their custody. However, the Japanese chose not to notify us of POWs in their worst and most punitive camps. These were the camps where submariners and pilots were initially assigned for interrogation and sometimes for lengthy detention. The U. S. might not know about survivors until these prisoners were transferred to less punitive camps. That could take a long time. In the worst case, the U. S. did not know about survivors from the USS Perch (SS-176) until the end of the war, 1,297 days after the boat had been sunk in 1942.

Another reason that the U. S. withheld the information about our submarine losses for some time was to avoid providing useful information to the enemy. Japan claimed to have sunk more boats than the U. S. ever had. There was no reason to provide the actual information any sooner than required.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Was it possible to escape from a sunken U. S. submarine?
title: Was it possible to escape from a sunken U. S. submarine?
text:
Yes, it was possible but only in limited circumstances. There were two escape trunks on the WW2 era boats, one in each torpedo room. The escape procedure was generally thought to have been workable down to 200 feet. Experienced divers could escape from as much as 300 feet down. However, most sailors had only had experience in the 100-foot escape towers in New London or Pearl Harbor. Even that was in controlled circumstances with Navy divers available in case of problems. In addition, during the war, not all submarine sailors went to Sub School where they would have gone through an escape tower.

Another limitation was that, inconveniently, most of the ocean is far deeper than 200 feet. The average depth of the Pacific Ocean is around 13,000 feet deep. The greatest depth is the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench at about 36,000 feet or seven miles deep.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Has anyone escaped from a sunken WW2 type U. S. submarine?
title: Has anyone escaped from a sunken WW2 type U. S. submarine?
text:
The forward escape trunk has been used twice on boats similar to the Pampanito. The first time was before the war when the USS Squalus (SS-192) went down off the East Coast in 1939. She was quickly found by her sister ship, the USS Sculpin (SS-191), in about 200 feet of water. The Sculpin radioed for help and the Navy rushed the submarine rescue ship USS Falcon (ASR-2) to the scene. The Falcon then used a McCann rescue bell to bring the surviving crew to the surface through the forward escape trunk. It took four trips and, despite a frayed lifting cable on the last trip, the 33 survivors all made it out. The 26 men in the after part of the boat died in the initial flooding.

It was unclear how the flooding actually happened. When the boat was salvaged, the main induction valve was found to be open. That would certainly have been enough to flood the boat. However, when the Squalus dove, the main induction indicator on the Christmas tree was green, showing a closed valve. In addition, in those days, submarines didn’t do crash dives as was done during and after WW2. Instead, the crews closed up everything until they had a green board – everything was secured. Then they would add some pressure to the air in the boat. Only after they verified that the pressure held, confirming that everything was closed, would the chief of the watch actually open vents and start the dive. The Squalus appears to have been buttoned up for the dive. No one knows how the main induction opened after the pressure test.

Because of this incident, valves were added to the air induction piping in the engine rooms. These were flapper valves that held any unwanted water in that piping and out of the engine rooms. A locking mechanism was added to the main induction to ensure it stayed closed. In addition, the divider between the two engine rooms would be a hard bulkhead on future boats, instead of a soft divider. That way, flooding could be isolated to just one compartment. These upgrades would matter to the Pampanito on her first war patrol.

The other time the forward escape trunk was used somewhat successfully was in 1944 when the USS Tang (SS-306) was sunk by a circular run of her own torpedo. Tang was on the surface in the South China Sea and had just fired the last torpedo she had on board. In spite of drastic turns to try to get the boat out of the way, that torpedo hit Tang around the after torpedo room or maneuvering.

Similar to the Squalus, everyone aft of the control room died in the initial explosion and flooding. Of the crew on the bridge or in the conning tower, five managed to get clear of the boat. One officer decided to swim the few miles to China but was never seen again. The rest of the surviving crew gathered in the forward torpedo room. Due to the severe up-angle, it was difficult to do anything about an escape. One of the survivors made it back to the control room and opened the vents on the forward ballast tanks. This put the whole boat fairly level on the bottom at around 200 feet. Now the remaining crew could move about and try to escape.

Only about 13 of the men actually tried to get out via the escape trunk. Some went into the escape trunk but couldn’t bring themselves to try the free ascent to the surface. (Not everyone had gone through the escape tower training.) The first one out was a young ensign who, unfortunately, went too far aft of the escape door, got trapped under the deck in the superstructure and drowned. At least two others ascended too quickly and didn’t get enough air out of their lungs. They died on the surface of ruptured lungs. Only six of the 13 made it to the surface safely. For some reason, the Japanese only picked up five survivors.

The nine rescued survivors all lived through their experiences in Japanese prisoner camps to the end of the war. However, it was estimated that the captain, LCDR Dick O’Kane, would not have survived another month in the camps. The Japanese reserved particularly harsh treatment for pilots and submariners.

There is no record of anyone successfully using the after torpedo room escape trunk to get out of a sunken submarine.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How did the escape trunks work?
title: How did the escape trunks work?
text:
The after escape trunk was one-time use only. The boat must truly be lost since this process makes it almost certain that the submarine would not surface again. In order to use the after escape trunk during the WW2 era, the crew must:

  • Gather as many crewmen as possible together in the space and close the watertight door to maneuvering.
  • Charge Momsen rebreathing hoods with air and distribute them.
  • Flood the compartment with water up to the lower lip of the escape trunk.
  • Pressurize the compartment to exceed the outside sea pressure if it doesn’t already. At 200 feet, this was about 90 PSI. The higher pressure in the compartment was needed to be able to open the hatch against the sea.
  • Launch the marker buoy.
  • One sailor would need to climb up into the trunk to open the hatch. (Everyone would be treading water already, so no ladder was needed.)
  • Each man then would duck and go out and follow the line up to the buoy.
  • Each man needed to exhale most of the way up to get the excess air (up to 90 PSI) out of his lungs. Yell “ho, ho, ho” on the way up.
  • Stop at each knot in the buoy line for a minute to decompress.
  • The men should not ascend faster than their air bubbles.
  • At the surface, stay together, preferably near the buoy.

Again, this escape trunk has never been used successfully. The two times that sailors were able to escape from the forward trunk on a boat like this, the after part of the boat was flooded from the initial incident and everyone aft had already died.

The forward escape trunk works on the same principles but holds far fewer people and could be used multiple times. The boat didn’t have to have been sunk. The different steps were:

  • After the trunk was full with just a few men, it was flooded to just above the side door. It was pressurized, as above. That door would be used to leave the boat rather than the hatch at the top.
  • Exit out the side door and follow the buoy line up.
  • The last person out closed the door behind him. If he failed to do this, there was a long lever in the torpedo room that could be used to close the door.
  • The escape trunk would then be drained into the torpedo room and depressurized so the next group can begin their escape.

Part of the reason that this escape trunk was designed differently was so that it could be used for both exit and reentry. In WW2, divers and UDTs could exit the boat, accomplish their missions and have been recovered all without the submarine needing to surface. The boat would be much less likely to have been discovered and the boat and the divers were safer. Later, Navy SEALs could use this escape trunk.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How fast could these WW2 submarines go?
title: How fast could these WW2 submarines go?
text:
Top speed on the surface was 20 or 21 knots, about 23 miles per hour. However, this was an inefficient use of fuel. In WW2, boats departing from Pearl Harbor, Hawaii would usually run at top speed to locations such as Midway Island or Johnston Island. There the boats would top off fuel and then proceed at efficient speeds (10 to 12 knots) to their assigned patrol area.

WW2 submarines were much slower under water. Top speed submerged was 9 or 9 ½ knots or a bit over 10 miles per hour. However, top speed was limited to less than an hour before the battery was completely drained of power. The more common speed submerged was 2 to 3 knots. Higher speeds might have been used for brief periods to gain attack position. Higher speeds could be used to try to escape when being attacked but that usually made too much noise. Slow, silent and clever was more effective.

The boat’s battery was usually rated at 48 hours if the boat was going 2 knots. The ratio of speed to power needed was cubic. Generally, when the speed was doubled, eight times the power was needed, 2X2X2. If the speed went from 2 to 4 knots, the battery would only last approximately six hours. Double it again, and the battery likely won’t last an hour. It was called the “one-hour rate.”
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How far could these submarines go?
title: How far could these submarines go?
text: The range of the boats built during and shortly before the war was about 11,000 nautical miles at a speed of 10 knots. Initially, the boats carried over 90,000 gallons of diesel. That was increased later by converting another main ballast tank (MBT) to a fuel ballast tank (FBT), boosting the total to 110,000 gallons.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What does that mean?  How far could the submarines operate from San Francisco?
title: What does that mean?  How far could the submarines operate from San Francisco?
text:
U. S. submarines did not operate from the West Coast all the way to Japan or to the shipping lanes in the South China Sea. It was too far and would take too long just to get to the patrol area and back. That wouldn’t leave much time to find and attack Japanese ships. From the approximate mileage chart, below, it would have taken 36 days just to get from San Francisco to Japan and back. It would have taken about 50 days to get to the South China Sea and back.

Instead, home port for most U. S. boats was in Pearl Harbor, Oahu, Hawaii. That shortened the transit time significantly. By creating a refueling stop at Midway Island, the range of the boats was extended even further. Now, instead of taking 18 days to get to Japan from San Francisco or San Diego, it would only take nine from Midway. Instead of 25 days to get to the South China Sea, it would only take 16.

The numbers in the following table are rounded approximations. Some notes regarding the table:

  1. San Francisco was used as an approximation for the West Coast. The distance to Hawaii from San Diego was actually a bit greater than that from San Francisco.
  2. Hainan Island, China was used as an approximation for the South China Sea. The distances to the Luzon Strait and the Formosa (Taiwan) Strait, where many U. S. attacks were concentrated, were somewhat shorter.
  3. Pampanito’s first war patrol was initially to Johnston Island to refuel and then to Yap in the Caroline Islands. Therefore, those distances are included.
  4. On Pampanito’s third war patrol, she rescued 73 British and Australian soldiers from the South China Sea near Hainan Island. She then proceeded at best surface speed to Saipan in the Mariana Islands where the nearest forward base was located.
  5. The number of days required was estimated using 250 nautical miles per day, traveling at about 10 or 11 knots. The journeys from Hawaii to Johnston Island or to Midway, and from Hainan to Saipan assume 400 miles per day. Those transits were at higher speed and an average of 17 knots was used.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What if the boat ran out of fuel?
title: What if the boat ran out of fuel?
text:
The boats were very careful not to. There were no fueling stations other than our forward bases and there were few of those early in the war. There was no plan to refuel at sea. Although there was no apparent documentation of a boat running out of fuel, it likely was possible to arrange an emergency refueling or a tow to the nearest base if needed.

Inside the boat, there were clusters of small black valves. Those were used to tell how much fuel was left in each of the fuel tanks. The result isn’t an exact number of gallons remaining, but it was a good indication as long as the crews had been paying attention. They always did. The least bad thing to happen if they weren’t paying attention to fuel levels, and ran out, was serious embarrassment. The worst was to find themselves stranded, adrift and nearly helpless in hostile territory.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How long were war patrols?
title: How long were war patrols?
text:
These WW2 boats were designed for war patrols of up to 75 days. A few patrols even went a bit longer. However, from what we can tell from the histories, most patrols were between 45 and 60 days each. If fuel was used quickly, because of the need to run at higher but less efficient speeds, the patrol would be shorter. If the torpedoes had all been fired or the boat suffered significant damage, the submarine would also return to port sooner.

Returning to port early, because the captain had used up all of his torpedoes, didn’t always get the crew all of the usual rest break. There were instances where skippers found abundant targets and fired all their torpedoes fairly quickly. Occasionally, when those skippers returned to a base, they opted to just reload torpedoes, top off food, fuel and other supplies, and head back out quickly to finish the patrol.

War patrols did appear to get shorter as the war progressed and the U. S. pushed the Japanese back to the west. The U. S. established advance bases as we defeated the Japanese. After the Battle of Midway, the U. S. was confident enough to do maintenance and resupply at that island rather than just refueling. After defeating the Japanese in the Marianas, the U. S. established bases at Saipan and at Guam even while some Japanese soldiers were still fighting on those islands. The same was true of the Philippines where there also was still fighting in the islands when the sub tender was established in Subic Bay. With the reduction in transit time to the combat zones, and with more and more submarines in commission, the patrols could be shorter.

Five of the six Pampanito’s war patrols were between 42 and 59 days. However, her fifth patrol was only a bit over two weeks. (Sources differ on the exact length.) She was almost out of torpedoes and had a very short transit to her next port, Subic Bay in the Philippines.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How long could these submarines stay at sea?
title: How long could these submarines stay at sea?
text:
The primary limitations were food and fuel. Other things like spare parts could become an issue, but that would be an unusual case. Hopefully, running out of torpedoes was a good thing, assuming they hit their targets. Those situations aren’t part of this discussion.

Food was loaded out for the expected duration of the patrol, up to 75 days. A few patrols went a bit over 80 days. That required creativity by the cooks and patience by the crew. The menus for the last few days would likely have been strange combinations of whatever was still left on board.

Fuel was the most frequent limitation. These submarines carried up to 110,000 gallons of diesel fuel. The question then was how efficiently it was being used. A boat may have needed to run at higher, inefficient speeds to be in a newly assigned area on time. A boat may have had targets make an unexpected course change and get away. In that case, the boat may choose to make a high-speed end-around to get in front of the targets again. These were all appropriate uses of fuel, but they were less efficient. As a result, the fuel may not have lasted as long as planned.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What was an “end-around”
title: What was an “end-around”
text:
An end-around was a maneuver used to get back ahead of a target without being seen. It was used most often when a target turned away from its expected course and stayed out of effective torpedo range. The maneuver bears a slight resemblance to the football play of the same name.

Once the target has gotten far enough away from the submarine so the boat was not readily seen, it would surface. It would then sail away from the target at 90 degrees. When the boat was far enough away from the target that only masts could be seen, it would then turn to a course that paralleled the target. After getting far enough ahead, the boat would turn back toward the target’s expected track and submerge. This maneuver would be done at full speed in order to get ahead of the target.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did American submarines resupply at sea?
title: Did American submarines resupply at sea?
text:
No, the U. S. did not refuel submarines or transfer torpedoes at sea. In order to resupply, our submarines returned to a base. Early in the war this usually meant Hawaii or Midway Island for boats in the Central Pacific. For boats homeported in Australia that meant Brisbane or Fremantle. Again, as the U. S. pushed the Japanese back to the west, we were able to add bases so that submarines had shorter journeys for resupply.

NOTE: the German Navy did sometimes transfer supplies at sea and designed specific submarines for that purpose. Most often this was fuel, but it could include food, torpedoes or spare parts.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How did U. S. submarines receive messages during a patrol?
title: How did U. S. submarines receive messages during a patrol?
text:
Although submarines couldn’t send messages over long distances, the boats could receive them using a very low frequency which had a much longer range. The fleet (or Fox) broadcast was sent from very long antennae and could reach submarines thousands of miles away.

Messages in the Fox broadcast were all transmitted in a sequence and were repeated a couple times during the night. This allowed each submarine to pick off their own messages. Perhaps, the radio operators might also pick out messages for other boats in their wolfpack or others in the general area to gain more information about what was going on around them. The boats would not attempt to acknowledge receipt unless specifically ordered to do so.

Submarines did not broadcast messages using the long, low frequency antennae running along much of the length of the boat. They could only use the higher frequency, medium range radios. Their messages would often have to have been relayed in order to reach commanders at Pearl Harbor, Midway or Australia.

There might occasionally have been a very limited amount of positive, personal information in these messages. The ship’s office on the Pampanito displays one such message regarding the birth of a child. It appears that Pampanito was returning from patrol when the message was received. Generally, care was taken not to send messages with bad news since the sailor couldn’t do anything about it at the time. There was no sense in distressing the sailor needlessly.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What kinds of messages would U. S. submarines send during a patrol?
title: What kinds of messages would U. S. submarines send during a patrol?
text:
Submarines did not often transmit messages because doing so revealed their presence, and could give away their exact location. However, there was still the need to get the most important messages out.

The most important messages were those regarding enemy convoys or warships that got past the submarine. This might allow other boats in the area to find the targets and attack. The message would be brief but would need to include the number and types of ships, last known base course (without zigs and zags) and estimated effective speed.

Other messages could include results of attacks. These would normally have been sent when the boat was clear of the attack area or in relatively safe waters. Boats would also report when they were headed back to port because they were out of torpedoes, short of fuel or had serious damage and needed to end the patrol.

Submarines would also communicate with each other. This would normally have been done using high frequency radios with limited range so that it would be less likely to have been intercepted. Once our boats started operating in small wolfpacks in the fall of 1943, communications between boats became very important. Boats had to coordinate operations to be more effective.

To assist with this, a radar was added to the search periscope with a Morse Code (telegraph) key. The radar transmission would be very directional, thus reducing the chances of it being intercepted. It would appear on the receiving boat as radar interference. Another option was to rendezvous and discuss tactics verbally using bullhorns.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did submarines spend the whole time submerged?
title: Did submarines spend the whole time submerged?
text:
No. In fact, overall, the boats spent the majority of their time on the surface.

When in their patrol area, early in the war, submarines were on the surface when it was dark and submerged when it was light. However, as crews became better at spotting Japanese planes and ships, some captains tended to stay on the surface longer. Since the boats were so much faster on the surface, that would give them a better chance of being able to get in front of targets.

Additionally, the transit to and from the patrol area was done mostly on the surface. There was a brief trim dive every day to get the boat back into neutral buoyancy. However, the transit time, often a few weeks, plus the time surfaced at night in the patrol area, meant that the majority of the time for the full patrol would be spent on the surface.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What was a trim dive?
title: What was a trim dive?
text:
The actual weight of the submarine matters a great deal when it was submerged. If it were too light, it would tend to rise and broach the surface. If it were too heavy, it would tend to go deeper, possibly to unsafe depths. Therefore, the crew worked to keep the boat in neutral trim which was safer and made depth control easier. The goal was to have the boat weigh the same as the water it displaced.

The challenge was that the weight of an operating submarine was constantly changing. Consuming food and using supplies made the boat lighter. Burning fuel made the boat heavier. (See the section on diving and surfacing the submarine.) Changes in the temperature or salinity of the water made the boat seem heavier or lighter.

As a result, at least once each day, the submarine would be submerged so that the diving officer could get the boat back into neutral trim. That was the trim dive. It probably took no more than 10 or 15 minutes. Once the boat was back in neutral trim, it would surface and resumed previous operations. Trim dives were most common during lengthy transits from one location to another.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How long were these boats normally submerged in the patrol area?
title: How long were these boats normally submerged in the patrol area?
text: If possible, these submarines would be on the surface every night for multiple reasons. The boat would likely come up to the surface at dusk and dive again at dawn. If it was in the tropics, the day/night split would be close to 12 hours each. However, if it was in higher or lower latitudes, the split could be very uneven and the boat may have wanted to remain submerged during the added hours of daylight in summer. That left less time to recharge the battery.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Why was it important for submarines to be on the surface at night?
title: Why was it important for submarines to be on the surface at night?
text:
The primary goals were to get fresh air into the boat, to charge the battery, to receive messages and to get a star fix to update the ship’s position – knowing the ship’s location.

The air on the submarine was only intended to last 16 to 18 hours. Since most of the crew smoked, the air was probably only good for about 16 hours. (Cigarettes were given away free to servicemen in WW2.) A primary need, therefore, was fresh air.

The battery also needed to be recharged. Fortunately, running the engines to recharge the battery also pulled fresh air into the boat. Most of the air from the main induction went directly to the engine rooms. However, some of the fresh air was fed to the ends of the boat and was pulled toward the engine rooms. That way, all compartments would get fresh air.

The next need was to check for messages to the boat on the fleet broadcast. This broadcast was sent to all submarines, and was repeated during the night. It may contain operational orders for the boat. It may also include messages to other boats that would be useful for a submarine to know about.

Finally, the navigator would want to get a position fix. In WW2 this would be very dependent on the weather. If it were cloudy, there were no stars to shoot, and therefore no updated position fix. Ideally, there would be a clear enough sky at dawn and dusk to see the horizon and find the brightest stars as they appeared. The elevations of those stars above the horizon would be measured with a sextant. The resulting numbers, along with the times, were then translated into the location of the boat.

Sun lines, usually at local apparent noon, could help update the boat’s position but wouldn’t usually be as accurate as a star fix. Sun lines could be done through the periscope.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How long could these submarines stay submerged?
title: How long could these submarines stay submerged?
text:
It depends. There were two limitations that determined the answer to this question, battery power and air quality. The limits on both depended on how fast the boat used them. A short answer is that a practical limit was about 30 hours, but that was still difficult.

Submarines could stay submerged for more than the 16 hours that the fresh air would last, as indicated above, but it took some extra steps. The record during WW2 was just short of 38 hours by the USS Puffer (SS-268). At that point both the battery and the crew were in bad shape. The boat was being depth charged and tracked, and the captain had no choice. Fortunately, the boat was eventually able to get away and return to base.

As discussed above, battery duration depends very much on the speed. At two knots (about 2.3 miles per hour), the battery was rated at 48 hours. (You probably walk faster than that.) If the boat doubled the speed to four knots, the time the battery would last would be divided by about eight. The ratio of speed to battery power was cubic. If the boat doubled the speed again to eight knots, after dividing the time by eight again, the battery would last less than an hour. This was called the “one-hour rate”. At maximum speed submerged, about 9 ½ knots, the battery may only last about 30 to 40 minutes. As a result, captains tended to use the battery very conservatively.

Air quality also depended somewhat on how fast the crew used it, although the differences aren’t as drastic. Again, the air in the boat was intended to last 16 to 18 hours. However, since most of the crew in WW2 smoked, the air would likely last 16 hours. How can it be used more slowly? One way was to put everyone not actively operating the boat in their bunks. Expending less energy uses less oxygen. Another way would be to put the smoking lamp out. That didn’t usually turn out to be practical due to nicotine addiction. Still, it could be done in a real emergency.

Fortunately, there were some other options to extend the air limitation. There were six oxygen bottles on the Pampanito, and they could be bled into the boat to drive up the O2 percentage. There were also many canisters in the overhead marked “Do Not Paint.” These contain lithium hydroxide or soda lime which was a CO2 absorbent. The canisters would be opened and spread on bunks or decks to reduce the CO2 in the air even though the chemicals are caustic. These steps added a couple hours of habitable air to the boat.

If more time were needed after the above steps, it was possible to bleed air into the boat from the high-pressure air banks. It seems unlikely that any boat had to go to this extreme but it was possible to safely double the air pressure in the boat. The oxygen and CO2 percentages were about half way back to normal and the pressure was not extreme. The pressure would be about the same as swimming at about 25 feet. This would not have been very uncomfortable and would not require decompression.

However, now another challenge arises due to the increased pressure. When the boat surfaces, the captain wanted eyes on the bridge as soon as possible. He needed to know for sure that there isn’t anything up there that had been missed on sonar and periscope sweeps. Although there isn’t a great overpressure in the boat, that increased pressure was in all of the pressure hull that was 16 feet in diameter and about 275 feet long. It all wanted to go out the bridge hatch at once. When a man goes up through that small hatch, he could be pushed out much the way a bullet is pushed down the barrel of a gun, albeit more slowly. To keep him from being launched, a big sailor holds on to the sailor’s ankles as he opened the hatch. Really! The procedure was not uncommon. The overpressure could also be an issue after just launching multiple torpedoes which brings more air and water into the boat.

There were some other steps that could be taken to reduce the pressure in the boat such as running the low-pressure blower or the air compressors. However, that would usually take too much time and the captain didn’t want to introduce a vacuum.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How did the crew know that oxygen was getting low?
title: How did the crew know that oxygen was getting low?
text:
Even without a gauge of some sort, there were signs that oxygen was getting low. Probably the first would be labored breathing. Men would need to breathe deep in order to get enough oxygen into their lungs. This began to be the feel as if there were an elephant sitting on their chests. Added to that would be headaches which could be intense and painful when oxygen was very low.

Another indicator was that the air no longer supported combustion. It becomes impossible to light a cigarette because the match or lighter can’t burn. This puts the “smoking lamp” out and slows the rate of oxygen consumption slightly. There was still free oxygen in the air, but the level has definitely decreased. It would certainly have been time to do something about the poor air in the boat, if that were possible.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Were there any windows on U. S. submarines?
title: Were there any windows on U. S. submarines?
text:
This may seem to be a laughable question. However, it isn’t like asking about screen doors on a submarine, which there obviously aren’t. After all, it looks to many people as though there were a whole series of windows along the side of the boat. Those were not windows They were actually limber holes to facilitate diving the boat and they are discussed under “Diving, Surfacing and Buoyancy.”

In fact, there was just one small window on the Pampanito. (This was in addition to the periscopes.) It was located in the control room at the Chief of the Watch station. Near the Christmas tree, in the forward port corner, there was a safe and a ladder above it leading up to a hatch. That hatch had a small window in it, about two inches in diameter. The purpose of the window was to let the gun crews know when the water has cleared enough to be able to open the hatch safely and head up on deck.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did these submarines always have a window in the Control Room hatch?
title: Did these submarines always have a window in the Control Room hatch?
text: During the war, the boats did. However, in the early 1950s, most WW2 boats still in service had the guns removed. The window was no longer needed once the guns were removed.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Were U. S. submarines successful during the war?
title: Were U. S. submarines successful during the war?
text:
U. S. submarines were very successful by the end of the war. They comprised only three percent of our Navy, yet subs sank 55% of all the Japanese shipping sunk during the war. By the end of the war, Japan was nearly starved of fuel and was short of food and many other supplies.

However, the war didn’t start out that way. There were many issues with submarines that limited their effectiveness. Some of these were specific to submarines and others also applied to the Navy in general.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What were the Navy’s problems at the beginning of the war?
title: What were the Navy’s problems at the beginning of the war?
text:
In no particular order, some of the issues for submarines were a shortage of combat-ready ships; submarine captains who had been trained to be too conservative; significant torpedo problems; a faulty assumption that submarines would sail with the fleet; and the need to learn how to fight a modern war. In more detail:

The shortage of combat-ready ships of all types. President Franklin Roosevelt had been walking a tightrope between trying to keep the country out of the war, as most of the public preferred, and preparing to fight in a likely global conflict. Fortunately, he managed to get funding from Congress to start building the ships the U. S. would need. Unfortunately, it would take time to complete the ships that were ordered as well as to build enough facilities to increase production after the attack on Pearl Harbor. The first submarine of the new Gato designs to be completed, the USS Drum (SS-228) , had just been commissioned on November 1, 1941, in Kittery, Maine and was still on shakedown, post construction repairs and crew training. She wouldn’t be ready for combat until the spring of 1942.

Submarine captains had been trained to be conservative. Pre-war training taught that if the boat was sighted, it was assumed to have been sunk. Being sighted in combat wasn’t a good thing, but it wasn’t always fatal either. As a result of the conservative approach, captains were taught to fire torpedoes based on sonar bearings rather than risking having the periscope being seen. The U. S. quickly established that sonar bearings alone weren’t good enough. Visual bearings to the targets were needed, particularly until sonar capability improved.

In order to overcome these mistakes in training and procedures, the U. S. would wind up replacing about one-third of the officers who were in command of submarines at the beginning of the war.

Not every good commanding officer in peace time would be aggressive enough for command in the war. A general rule was that if a captain didn’t produce results within two war patrols, he would likely have been reassigned. Still, some captains who “washed out” of submarines went on to distinguished careers in surface ships.

The U. S. had significant torpedo problems. These are detailed in the section on torpedoes. Generally speaking, testing was woefully inadequate and the Torpedo Bureau refused to believe that the problems were in the torpedoes. The main issues were that the torpedoes ran too deep; the magnetic exploders generally did not work properly; and the contact exploders didn’t always work either. It would take almost two years to identify, acknowledge and then fix the major problems with our torpedoes. It appears that, even then, no one was held accountable.

The assumption that submarines would sail with the fleet and engage the enemy before the big gun battles. That’s why these subs were referred to as “fleet boats”. In hindsight, there were obvious problems with this theory:

  1. After the attack on Pearl Harbor, there wasn’t much of a fleet for submarines to sail with.
  2. As mentioned above, our newest WW2 submarines could not, in practical terms, keep up with the fleet.
  3. The idea of sailing with the fleet ignored the lessons of the Atlantic War where the German U-boats were beginning to cut the supply routes to England, another island nation. Japan was just as dependent as Britain for the imported supplies needed to fight a war.

The U. S. needed to learn to fight a modern war. The United States was barely involved in the naval parts of WW1. There was a great deal of new equipment and technology that we needed to learn to use most effectively. Japan had already been at war in China for over five years. The Japanese had a great deal of combat experience and had been actively training for the war that the U. S. still wanted to avoid. It would take us about 18 months for us to fully catch up and become a truly effective fighting force.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Why was the submarine service known as the “Silent Service”
title: Why was the submarine service known as the “Silent Service”
text:
Silence, or being quiet, was a fact of life on submarines. In combat, it could mean the difference between making it home or being lost at sea. Modern submarines are designed to be as quiet as possible. That doesn’t mean the crew can’t talk, but it was a very bad idea to drop a wrench.

The lack of publicity about our submarines was a great advantage. Sailors’ lives could be saved if the enemy was kept in the dark about capabilities and intended operations. Large fleets with frequent communications could be difficult to disguise or hide. It was much easier for single submarines. The boats could submerge and severely limit radio, radar and sonar emissions.

When attacking the enemy or evading attack, being quiet was even more important. The enemy’s use of sonar was how submarines could be located. Quiet boats were harder to find. There were routines to run more quietly by shutting off as much equipment as possible. When needed, hydraulic systems, such as the bow and stern planes, were operated manually to avoid the noise of the pumps. Even fans would be shut off to lower the noise level in the boat as much as possible.

Submarines took various steps to keep hidden when on patrol. The captains were very aware of the dangers of using radar often. The Japanese were listening and could locate a submarine by listening for radar sweeps. Boats even learned to sink their trash so that it couldn’t be found by the Japanese.

Steps such as these deprived the enemy of a great deal of information. “Silence is golden.”
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Why did submarines limit the use of active sonar and radar?
title: Why did submarines limit the use of active sonar and radar?
text:
The main reason was that radar and sonar gave away the submarine’s presence and location long before the pulses provided information that was useful to the boat. For example, let us assume that the effective range of radar was no more than ten miles early in the war. That meant that the radar pulse was strong enough to travel 20 miles – to the enemy ship or plane and back. The issue was that the radar pulses sent out, that didn’t hit a target and return, were still going to travel out 20 miles. That meant that the enemy could be aware of the submarine’s presence when the enemy was still 20 miles away but the boat’s radar wouldn’t pick up enemy ships until they were within ten miles.

Active sonar had the same issues as radar, although at much shorter distances.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Does that mean submarines never used active sonar and radar?
title: Does that mean submarines never used active sonar and radar?
text:
Not necessarily. It meant that the boats used it sparingly and cautiously. Subs would always be listening on sonar, but it has always been very rare to use the active mode to send out search pulses. That is likely even more true today since passive sonar has improved so much. For reference, recall the scene in “The Hunt for Red October” where the captain asks his second in command to send out a second “single ping”. The second in command looks at the captain in total disbelief, as if he had lost his mind. The movie was fiction, but that part of it, and much more, was quite accurate.

In WW2, radar was used by submarines more often than active sonar. Aircraft were a main concern. An air search radar was available early in the war. It didn’t provide much information beyond the presence of an aircraft. It was also on a frequency that the Japanese could easily detect. Since the information was still important, captains would use the air search radar very sparingly. When a new surface search radar became available, and it included some aircraft detection, it was used more often. However, it was still used sparingly and often wasn’t trusted to locate aircraft in the area. (Refer to section on electronics for more information.)

Late in the war, a radar was added to the search periscope to provide accurate range information. This would be a narrow beam and a single pulse making it hard to determine the location of the source. More importantly, it was a different frequency, making it that much less likely that the enemy was listening for it.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did loose lips really sink ships?
title: Did loose lips really sink ships?
text:
During WW2, there was a saying, also on many posters, that “Loose Lips Sink Ships.” It reminded everyone that intelligence mattered a great deal during war, and people never knew who might have been listening. Certainly, information about major fleet and troop movements mattered a great deal.

However, does that mean that the U. S. may have actually lost ships due to “loose lips?” Admiral Lockwood, commander of submarines in the Central Pacific, believed there was at least one time when we did.

In June of 1943, U. S. Congressman Andrew Jackson May of Kentucky was Chair of the House Military Affairs Committee. He held a press conference on returning from a war zone junket. He let it be known that our boats were able to evade Japanese depth charges because they would explode at shallow depths. Early in the war, the Japanese depth charges had only two settings, 30 meters (98 feet) and 60 meters (197 feet.) Even our pre-war classes, which were 250-foot (depth) boats, could get far enough below that to avoid major damage.

The Japanese weren’t nearly as incompetent as the Allies wanted to believe early in WW2. The Japanese did pick up this information from Congressman May. Then the Japanese modified their depth charges to add depth settings for 90 and 120 meters as well. In the next few months, the U.S. lost more boats than usual. Admiral Lockwood believed that Congressman May’s “loose lips” cost us as many as ten boats and 800 men.

Representative May did not suffer any serious consequences for his security breach. However, he failed to win reelection in 1946 and spent nine months in prison for unrelated bribery charges. He was pardoned by President Truman in 1952 but was unable to revive his political career.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How were the trash and sewage removed from the boat?
title: How were the trash and sewage removed from the boat?
text:
In WW2, trash and garbage were usually thrown over the side when at sea for an extended time. The trash was bagged and weighted so that it would sink to the bottom. The objective was to be sure that the trash didn’t give away the boat’s identity or location. This also meant that someone had to come up on deck the throw the trash over the side. That could be dangerous and in heavy seas the trash would be retained in the boat until the seas calmed.

Sewage was the human waste that goes through the heads (toilets). The sanitary tanks for three of the heads were emptied overboard each morning, usually between 05:00 and 06:00. High pressure air was used to blow the tanks dry. This was done by the auxiliaryman who was part of the engineering department. It was critical that the sanitary tanks then be vented to eliminate air pressure. Failure to do so results in a very nasty surprise to the next person flushing the head.

The head in the after torpedo room was different. This head flushes directly overboard since there was no room for a sanitary tank below the deck. (The propellor shafts were below that space.) The challenge was that the water level outside the boat was above the top of the torpedo tubes while the toilet was maybe a foot and a half off the deck. The toilet sits well below the outside water level. The issue then is: how did a sailor flush a head uphill without the contents and seawater coming back into the boat? He did that by first moving the contents to a small intermediate tank.

It was a multi-step process to flush this head. And if the sailor got it wrong, he’d get to clean up the mess. The basic process is:

  • Ensure that the bowl flapper valve was shut.
  • Add water to the bowl through the sea and stop valves.
  • Shut both valves.
  • After using the head, operate the flapper valve to empty the contents of the bowl into the intermediate chamber.
  • Shut the flapper valve.
  • Charge the volume tank until the pressure was 10 pounds higher than the sea pressure.
  • Open the gate and plug valves on the discharge line.
  • Operate the rocker valve to discharge the contents of the expulsion chamber overboard.
  • Shut the gate and plug valves.
  • Vent any remaining pressure.

The process worked but was not for the faint of heart. By the way, this head would only have been used when on the surface and not at all when in port.

Current environmental regulations require that ships no longer discharge waste into harbors. Therefore, modern submarines need to have holding-tanks for all heads and a means to discharge the tanks to a sewage treatment system when in port.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — When would the signal tube in the after torpedo room have been used?
title: When would the signal tube in the after torpedo room have been used?
text:
If it were needed for signaling, the boat would launch flares from that tube. This would be used mostly when doing training exercises with other U. S. ships and planes. The color of the flare contained the message. For example:

  • A green flare was fired by the submarine when the boat would have launched torpedoes if this weren’t an exercise. That would mean that the boat had sunk the carrier or tanker.
  • A red flare was fired by the submarine when it was in trouble and needed to surface quickly. All surface ships needed to get clear of the area as soon as possible.
  • Recognition signals would vary and the prescribed colors and sequence would be followed.

After the war, the signal tube could also be used to launch a decoy which was fairly basic. It consisted of a bubble generator made of calcium hydride. When it contacted water, it generated a large volume of bubbles. Air bubbles reflect sound (sonar) just as the submarine’s hull would. It was the change in density that reflects the sound. A fictional example can be seen in the movie “The Hunt for Red October.” When the Russian aircraft drops a torpedo to try to sink “Red October,” the boat releases a pair of decoys that tumble and generate bubbles in an attempt to confuse the torpedo’s sonar.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Was there a specific paint color for submarines?
title: Was there a specific paint color for submarines?
text:
There were specific colors and patterns for most Navy ships. For surface ships, this was fairly complex. Patterns act as camouflage and could even have confused the eye about which direction the ship was going.

Paint colors also mattered to submarines. The captains wanted to be less visible on the surface. Initially, submarines were all black. This was thought to be the best color when on the surface at night as well as when submerged. That turned out not to be the case.

Black was the best color for horizontal surfaces. Seen from above, the deck and other surfaces can blend in with the depths of the ocean. Those surfaces remained black in the new paint schemes.

The vertical surfaces of the submarine were a different matter. Someone pointed out that black was actually too dark at night. Submarine captains were skeptical, but experiments were done to determine which shade of dark grey would be less visible. Captains were convinced when they saw that a dark grey submarine was actually harder to spot than a black one.

After the war, submarines were painted all black again once snorkels were added and boats could be submerged most of the time.

The old Navy adage - if something moves, salute it; if it doesn’t move, move it; if you can’t move it, paint it gray – didn’t always apply.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Do submarines leak?
title: Do submarines leak?
text:
It may be a bit disconcerting to learn that submarines did leak and that was intentional. Some parts of the boat that extended through the hull also needed to move. These include the propellor shafts, the bow and stern planes and the periscopes. It was possible to tighten the packing around these structures so that the leak was stopped entirely. Unfortunately, that also would stop the devices from moving; they would no longer rotate. The small amount of water that was leaking into the boat also acts as a lubricant.

The rate of the leak was normally not a concern. It was easy to pump the water out periodically.
category: Operating U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How many men were assigned to a U. S. submarine in WW2?
title: How many men were assigned to a U. S. submarine in WW2?
text:
The typical complement of boats like the USS Pampanito (SS-383) during the war was 80 men. This includes all of the submarines we built from 1940 and forward. During the last year or so of the war, that number gradually increased to 85. After the war, it returned to 80.

The fleet boats from the 1930s had slightly fewer than 80 crewmen on board. The earlier S-boats had far fewer men on board. However, the S-boats were generally no longer in active combat by the middle of the war.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Does that mean there were bunks for all 80 men?
title: Does that mean there were bunks for all 80 men?
text: Not exactly. There were probably 70 bunks for 80 men. That is enough bunks even though not everyone would have a bunk to himself. However, other facilities, such as the mess decks and heads, were adequate for 80 men.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Why weren’t the Gato/Balao/Tench boats designed for the number of men assigned?
title: Why weren’t the Gato/Balao/Tench boats designed for the number of men assigned?
text:
Actually, the boats had been designed for the expected number of men at the time. These submarines were originally expected to have 70 men on board to operate the equipment available when they were designed. However, new equipment – often electronics - was added even before the war. It was this equipment, added after the boat design was complete, that required more than 70 men in a crew. Soon after the war started, a crew of 80 men became the standard.

Although the number of men in the crew had increased, the basic design of the boats didn’t change. At that point, there was simply no place to put additional bunks.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Why did the number of crewmen increase further in the last year of the war?
title: Why did the number of crewmen increase further in the last year of the war?
text:
The best estimates are that it was due to the addition of the second 40 mm Bofors gun or possibly because of added electronics or other equipment. However, confirmation of these reasons is hard to find.

The U. S. expected to need to invade Japan in order to force a surrender. After the Pacific island-hopping campaign, we didn’t expect Japan to surrender without a desperate, even suicidal, fight. We knew that an invasion would be a very costly undertaking in both men and ships. We expected that the fleet would be harassed constantly by kamikaze aircraft and suicide boats. Our submarines were likely to be assigned as pickets to warn and help defend the fleet. Therefore, a second 40 mm Bofors was added to many boats. The increased staffing may have been for that gun since five men were needed to load and operate it. Fortunately, Japan surrendered after the second atomic bomb was dropped and we no longer needed to invade.

Throughout the war, new equipment was added to the boats to make them more effective. That new gear often needed more operators and maintenance. That was particularly true of the new radars and sonars as well as navigation equipment such as the new LORAN.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Why does it take so many men to staff the submarine?
title: Why does it take so many men to staff the submarine?
text:
The first thing to remember is that three full shifts were needed to operate the boat all day and night at sea.

On the surface at sea, there were a number of jobs to do and there would be one person awake in each compartment to monitor the space for problems or danger. For example, on the surface there would have been:

  • The officer of the deck with three or four lookouts on the bridge.
  • A helmsman and quartermaster (navigation) along with the sonar and radar operators in the conning tower.
  • The Chief of the Watch plus an IC electrician and a messenger in the control room.
  • A radar operator for the air search and IFF equipment.
  • A radioman on watch in the radio room.
  • Two electrician mates in maneuvering.
  • A motor machinist mate (engineman) and an oiler in each engine room.
  • Normally there would have been a cook in the crew’s mess. There would often have been a mess cook there as well.
  • A steward in the forward battery.
  • A torpedoman on watch in each torpedo room.
  • There are other duties, such as an electrician monitoring the battery, particularly during a charge.
  • A gunner’s mate to maintain the guns

This was a total of about 24 per shift, and there were three shifts.

When submerged, the duties for some of these men would change. For example, the officer of the deck (OOD) would become the diving officer and there would be a new OOD in the conning tower. The oilers in the engine rooms would man the trim manifold and air manifold in the control room. The lookouts would man the bow and stern planes. In total they needed about the same number of men when submerged as on the surface.

Submarines also needed to have additional personnel on board to allow for trainees, injuries and illness. Gun crews also needed to be staffed during battle stations. In addition to these functions, the captain and the executive officer rarely stood watches. The yeoman and pharmacist mate may not have been on the watch list. These last two might have stood some watches as their primary duties permitted.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Since submarines had limited space, were there height and weight limits?
title: Since submarines had limited space, were there height and weight limits?
text:
There was a height limit on these boats. During WW2, it was six feet, four inches or 1.93 meters. That meant two things. First, if the sailor was six feet or taller, he probably wasn’t able to stretch out on his bunk. He would sleep on his side curled up a bit. Second, it meant there were multiple obstructions available for a submarine sailor to locate with his head. In that case, some important medical advice applied: “if it hurts when you do that, don’t do that”. A tall crew member who has been on a submarine even for a short time may have appeared to pay no attention to those painful obstacles. However, he had already located them all - and not all the hard way. Submariners tend to be reasonably bright.
