Location memory helped. For example, in the dark in your home, you know where the furniture is and you avoid it. Unless, of course, someone has just added something or rearranged everything. At least the obstructions on a submarine didn’t get rearranged very often.

Weight was a different issue. There were weight limits, adjusted for height, to be met when joining the Navy. During WW2, there were no official weight limits for serving sailors after that. However, there might be informal pressure if a sailor carried too many pounds. He might not want to struggle through the watertight doors if he was seriously overweight. There have also been reports that the general stench on the boats tended to suppress appetites.

At some point after the war, the rules changed. Sailors then had to be under the weight limits in order to reenlist.

Those were the maximums. The minimum height and weight limits for submarines were the same as those for everyone in the Navy when enlisting. There were no separate requirements for submarine service.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did that mean submarines wanted all smaller sailors for the crew?
title: Did that mean submarines wanted all smaller sailors for the crew?
text:
Not really. It might have been helpful to have some smaller sailors who could get into tight spaces to do some of the maintenance work. However, submarines needed some bigger men to push (technically to pull with pulleys and ropes) the 3,200-pound torpedoes into the tubes. Someone also needed to lift the heavy cylinder liners for the engines. The shells, with the casing, for the 5-inch gun weighed over 70 pounds. In short, submarines needed a number of good-sized sailors in the crew to do some of the heavy lifting and pulling.

The result was that there would be men of various sizes in the crew. It probably reflected the variety of the population in general, although with fewer basketball players.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — With all the negatives, why would anyone want to be on a submarine in WW2?
title: With all the negatives, why would anyone want to be on a submarine in WW2?
text:
Certainly, life on a diesel submarine can be primitive. The boats did stink, were cramped, and didn’t ride well in heavy seas. Sailors may not have been able to get a full shower during the entire patrol. Engineers in particular may not have seen the sky for weeks at a time. Even if a crewman was a lookout, he still may not have seen the sun for weeks since the boats were often submerged during daylight while in the patrol area. Living conditions on diesel boats were rather unpleasant.

Still, sub sailors did think it was good duty. There were many advantages in being aboard a submarine. Those advantages are different in peacetime than they were in WW2, but there were and still are many reasons to volunteer.

During WW2, the main advantages appear to have been:

  • Because of the Great Depression, a significant attraction was probably the extra submarine pay. That appears to be about 50% added to the base pay for sub sailors, at least for the junior ranks. This was very important to sailors if their families were still struggling financially. This extra pay would often be sent home and could be very helpful.
  • Submarines were the only ships that could take the fight back to the Japanese early in the war. Even as the war progressed, it would take a while for the rest of the Navy to take the fight to Japanese waters. There was a real desire to avenge the attack on Pearl Harbor, and service on submarines was the quickest way to start getting even. Although there were the occasional air attacks on the Japanese islands, such as the Doolittle/Halsey raid on Tokyo, submarines were providing a more sustained fight.
  • This may seem a bit morbid, but some men thought that the worst thing that could happen to them would be to come home maimed. Submariners were less likely than soldiers or other sailors to be maimed, to lose an arm or a leg. The odds were greater that sub sailors wouldn’t come home at all, but they weren’t likely to come home maimed. For some sailors, that was preferable.

Some advantages still applied after the war:

  • The crews were better. There were normally more volunteers for submarines than there were billets (positions) available. Naturally, the submarine service took the best available. Currently, reports are that candidates have to be in the top 15 to 20% of the Navy to be considered for submarines. That is true even for non-nuclear positions such as storekeepers, yeomen (admin) and cooks.
  • Submariners were – and are – an elite group. It was a chance to be part of something special.
  • The work was more interesting. Submarines often operated independently and without much direction from above or afar. Sailors on submarines couldn’t talk about much about where they were or what they did. Even the older boats could be doing interesting work such as training with divers or just practicing intelligence gathering and photo reconnaissance.
  • Sub sailors could learn something new nearly every day. Sailing a submarine in three dimensions was, and is, more complex, challenging and interesting.
  • Submarines were generally less formal than surface ships.
  • Submarine duty could be a faster route for promotions. For officers, it could be a faster route to commanding his own ship. (This was no longer as true after the war, particularly with the advent of nuclear power in the 1950s.)
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What was the best part of being on a boat?
title: What was the best part of being on a boat?
text: This varied for each individual. Possibilities included having a greater impact than many others in the Navy, the continued learning, the responsibility, having higher quality shipmates, an atmosphere of less formality, doing much more interesting work, or professional satisfaction. What would be your personal preference? Better pay and better food helped morale but weren’t usually the primary motivators after the U. S. came out of the depression.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How was a submarine less formal?
title: How was a submarine less formal?
text:
The main factor was that there wasn’t enough room for formality. On long patrols in the tropics, “uniforms” became much less uniform. In WW2 submarines, shaving generally wasn’t required. There were more informal conversations and banter. In quiet times, there would be verbal rehearsals for equipment failures or casualties. All of this was usually acceptable as long as everyone was also paying attention to their tasks and doing them well.

Another example was that “officers’ country” couldn’t be avoided as it could on a surface ship. There was only the one level that could be used to get through the boat. The crew had work to do or meals to eat that required passing through the officers’ and chiefs’ berthing in the forward battery.

However, being less formal did not mean that the officers or crew were disrespectful or less precise when doing their jobs.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What was the worst part of being on a boat?
title: What was the worst part of being on a boat?
text:
During WW2, the worst thing was, obviously, being attacked by depth charges or bombs. It is impossible to truly explain what it was like to someone who didn’t experience it first-hand. Depth charging has been described as similar to being in a drum that is being hit by a large hammer. The difference was that your life was in immediate danger, and your job was to be still and be quiet. The crew could hear the attacking ship – even without the aid of sonar – and could often hear the depth charges as they hit the water. If the depth charges were close enough, the crew would hear the click of the detonators right before the explosions.

After that, the worst part could be the smell, the inability to shower often enough, close quarters, lack of exercise or lack of sunshine. It depended on what was most important to each individual.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How long were the sailors assigned to a submarine in WW2?
title: How long were the sailors assigned to a submarine in WW2?
text:
There was a fair amount of variation here, but it appears that a man would typically be assigned to the same boat for about 15 to 18 months of combat. The Pampanito’s war patrols covered a period of 13 months and just 30 of her original crew made all six patrols. That would be consistent with about 15% of the crew rotating off after each patrol.

In peacetime, Navy men and women are typically assigned to the same ship for two to three years. Again, there can be a fair amount of variation.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How often did sub sailors get home during WW2?
title: How often did sub sailors get home during WW2?
text:
Not very often. The needs of the war came first. Sailors might have had a chance for leave and travel home when reassigned to another boat, particularly if it was to new construction. Leave would also be granted during shipyard periods. During overhauls, captains would try to give half the crew off at a time, usually starting with the married men whose wives were not nearby. Then the rest of the crew would get their chance to go home for a little while.

All of this was true of the rest of the Navy as well.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How were submarine sailors selected?
title: How were submarine sailors selected?
text:
Normally, the first requirement was that a sailor had to volunteer. He had to be different enough to want to be on a submarine. (We like to say that submariners’ brains are wired differently.) When someone offered an opportunity to be stuffed into a 16-foot diameter pipe with 79 of your closest friends and then go down 400 feet or more below the surface of the ocean, that had to sound like a good idea. In fact, sailors usually had to ask to be a submariner.

A sailor applied for submarine duty by sending a request up through the chain of command. His superiors would add their comments and recommendations.

The next step was to be selected as a possible candidate. For most of the war, there were actually more volunteers than there were billets (positions or spaces) in submarines. As a result, the submarine force had their pick of candidates. This was one of the reasons that submarine crews tended to be better than the average in the rest of the Navy. Selection depended on demonstrated skills and, perhaps, on the sailor’s rating (specialty).

Finally, the selected candidates were screened for even temperaments. There would be psychological testing if the Navy hadn’t already had a lengthy opportunity to observe them. The submarine force was looking for men (and now women) who were even tempered, who would “take an even strain.” Which candidates would get along well with others and pitch in when there was extra work to do? Applicants needed to be able to enjoy the banter and mild pranks of their shipmates while still being able to work hard as a team when needed. Could these candidates be a strong part of the team when an emergency or crisis arose?

Someone who was in your face (either angry or happy) or too retiring would not qualify.

Officers who came through the Naval Academy or Navy Reserve Officer Training Corps (NROTC) programs were already well known to the Navy and were not normally screened again for submarine duty. The same was likely true of enlisted sailors who had already served a few years in the Navy. Prior to WW2, an officer had to serve for two years on a surface ship before he could volunteer at all. That requirement ended with the war.

NOTE: Screening for nuclear power billets in submarines or carriers continues and is even more rigorous.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Was everyone on a U. S. submarine a volunteer?
title: Was everyone on a U. S. submarine a volunteer?
text:
Traditionally, everyone aboard a U. S. submarine was a volunteer. That has almost always been the case. The exception was early in WW2 when the submarine force needed to expand quickly. Some sub sailors at that time didn’t remember volunteering. (We like to say that the sailors didn’t back up quickly enough when volunteers were requested or that they were “voluntold.”)

However, if a sailor didn’t want to be on a sub, he didn’t have to. Submarine crews didn’t really want someone on board if he wasn’t comfortable there. A sailor could always request to “non-vol”, even if he volunteered in the first place. Being at sea in such close quarters and submerged for so much time can be very different from just a training dive or two. It might be much more uncomfortable than the sailor imagined. The Navy can always find another place for a quality, competent sailor to serve.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What kind of training did sailors get for submarine duty?
title: What kind of training did sailors get for submarine duty?
text:
Prior to the war, the usual program for diesel submariners was three months of sub school in New London for enlisted crew and six months for officers. This was in addition to any training for the enlisted crew in their ratings (specialties.) Once a sailor got to his submarine, the training began in earnest.

During WW2, the training in sub school was condensed and sometimes skipped completely. If a sailor went to sub school at all, it would be about half the normal time or about six weeks for enlisted men and three months for officers. For experienced sailors, sub school may be skipped altogether.

NOTE: The process for submarine school has changed, particularly for those who have been nuclear trained. The nukes will likely be sent directly to their boats after nuclear power school but without sub school. That way the nuclear power training doesn’t erode before the newly trained men and women can use it.

When the sailor got to his submarine, it was assumed that he actually knew very little. In fact, that was correct in that he had little or no practical experience on the boats. His first job would be to become a qualified watchstander so he could start to carry his share of the workload. The next thing would be to earn his dolphins, to qualify in submarines.

Qualifying usually required at least six months for enlisted men and at least a year for officers. He had to demonstrate knowledge of all the basic systems on the boat. For an enlisted sailor, this would mean passing an oral exam while going through the boat with the Chief of the Boat (COB) and then with the commanding officer or executive officer. An officer would qualify on another, similar submarine. That process would include a similar exam plus rigging the boat for dive, diving the boat and conducting a practice attack.

The key thing about submarines was that everyone needed to be able to respond quickly to any emergency. There were no designated damage control parties on a boat. It was up to whoever was in the space to respond and resolve an emergency. In order to do that, everyone needed to know the systems in every space.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did anyone ever stress out and need to get out of submarines?
title: Did anyone ever stress out and need to get out of submarines?
text:
During the war, there are a few instances of sailors stressing out when under attack. However, there were surprisingly few considering the stress of being depth charged.

In a few cases, the sailor might start yelling or trying to open a hatch to get out. In these cases, he would be forcibly subdued and then sedated. He might have to be knocked unconscious to render him quiet. He would usually remain sedated until returning to port. In a few other cases, the sailors froze and became very withdrawn, almost catatonic. In those cases, they might simply be relieved of their duties and replaced.

Submarine sailors rarely stressed out just by being submerged. There are very few, if any, cases like this in the literature. After all, he had volunteered to be under water. If someone thought there was a chance he might be claustrophobic, he wasn’t likely to volunteer for submarines in the first place.

That said, the policy was that a sailor could always “non-vol” and leave submarines. It would be reasonable to expect interviews to be sure that was really what he wanted to do. After all, the Navy has invested time and money in his submarine training.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How did submarine sailors deal with fear when they were attacked while submerged?
title: How did submarine sailors deal with fear when they were attacked while submerged?
text:
Some level of fear was a constant companion for submariners, especially during World War II. Crews lived and fought in a fragile steel tube, often hundreds of feet underwater, facing depth charges, flooding, mechanical failures, and long periods of uncertainty. The question was never whether fear existed, but how it was managed. Fear was managed through training, professionalism, discipline, and trust in shipmates and leaders. Humor and camaraderie also helped.

Training and professionalism were the first lines of defense. Submariners were rigorously trained to respond automatically to emergencies—fires, flooding, loss of power, equipment failures, or battle damage. They practiced drills every day. When something actually went wrong, there was no time to panic. Men fell back on practice from these drills, checklists, and muscle memory. Knowing exactly what to do reduced fear and replaced it with action. The story of the USS Puffer (SS-268) offered an example. When she was held down by enemy ships for nearly 38 hours, those who had something to do fared better. It was the sailors who wanted something to do who brought the boat home. (Refer to the category “Attacks and Battles, Small And Large” for more about the Puffer.)

Routine and discipline also mattered. Life aboard a submarine followed a strict rhythm of watches, maintenance, meals, and sleep. Even during combat patrols, maintaining routine provided psychological stability and a sense of normalcy in an otherwise extreme environment.

Trust in shipmates was perhaps the most important factor. Submarines operated with small, tightly knit crews where every man depended on everyone else. Submariners learned quickly that their survival rested on the competence and reliability of their shipmates. This mutual trust helped keep fear in check—each person focused on doing his job well so others could do theirs. In any combat, and not just on submarines, men were fighting for their fellow sailors, marines or soldiers, not just themselves.

Leadership played a crucial role. Calm, confident officers and chiefs set the tone for the entire crew. A skipper who remained steady during depth charging reassured the men throughout the boat. In most cases, the crew was confident that the captain would get them out of the situation and home safely. Panic at the top would spread instantly; calm professionalism prevented it.

Humor and camaraderie were common coping mechanisms. Gallows humor, pranks, nicknames, and storytelling helped release tension. Laughing together, even in dangerous circumstances, reminded the crew of their shared humanity and strengthened bonds.

Acceptance of risk was part of submarine culture. Many submariners understood that fear could not be eliminated, only controlled. As one veteran put it, fear was “always there—but he didn’t let it drive him.” He acknowledged it, compartmentalized it, and kept going.

It might be that in WW2, the bravest step sailors on submarines and ammunition ships took was just showing up when their ship was leaving port.

In short, submariners dealt with fear through training, routine, trust, leadership, humor, and an unwavering focus on the job at hand. Fear was real—but professionalism was stronger.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Was there a doctor on board these submarines?
title: Was there a doctor on board these submarines?
text:
No, there were no doctors assigned to U. S. submarines in WW2. The “docs”, as they were always called, were medics. These medics, called pharmacist mates at the time, were specially trained and qualified for independent duty. The medics were very good. They understood the art of medicine as well as the science and were very good at diagnosis and treatment.

Pampanito did have a doctor on board briefly. On her third war patrol, when she was headed to Saipan with the rescued British and Australian soldiers, she was met by a destroyer. A doctor and another pharmacist mate were transferred to the boat from the destroyer to help with the sickest soldiers. Unfortunately, the doctor appears to have spent most of his time doing paperwork and complaining that Pampanito, then well into the patrol, didn’t have enough fresh citrus fruit on board to prevent scurvy. As if it were possible to still have fresh fruit.

There are still no doctors on our attack submarines. The large missile boats are the only U. S. subs with doctors on board at this time.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What did the pharmacist mates treat?
title: What did the pharmacist mates treat?
text:
The main things that WW2 medics would treat would be minor injuries, a few broken bones, skin rashes, etc. A few needed to treat bullet wounds from surface attacks with guns since the enemy did tend to shoot back. There would probably be a few cases of venereal disease (now referred to as STDs or STIs) as well.

Colds and flu were relatively uncommon on submarines during WW2. Most sailors hadn’t had a chance to go home and be exposed to children who tend to spread such illnesses. If there was a cold or flu on board, it would probably spread rapidly because of the close living conditions and then die out completely.

Pharmacist mates did not expect to treat anything more unusual. As a result, they did not have the supplies to treat men with tropical diseases like those of the rescued POWs. Nor did the medics expect to do surgeries. However, in addition to the cuts, broken bones and routine illnesses, the medics did their best to handle whatever emergency issues came up.

For example, there were three known appendectomies done on submarines so the boats could stay on patrol. The first one was done on the USS Seadragon (SS-194) in September of 1942. The patient was in great pain and the medic thought he could do the surgery. The patient gave his informed consent. The operation took two and a half hours and was done “by the book”; the medic was following the descriptions and diagrams in his medical books. The patient recovered fully. A few notes:

  • The surgery was done submerged, at 120 feet, to provide a steady platform.
  • It was done on the wardroom table with the executive officer as the chief assistant.
  • Ether was used as the anesthetic which can be dangerous in the closed spaces of a submerged submarine with no access to fresh air.
  • Some instruments had to be devised from wardroom silverware. For example, a tea strainer was used as a mask to administer the ether and bent spoons were retractors.

Successful appendectomies were also performed on the USS Grayback (SS-208) in September of 1942 and on the USS Silversides (SS-236) in December of that year. After that, the Navy issued orders that pharmacist mates were not to perform any further appendectomies. It might seem unlikely that there were no more cases of appendicitis on board submarines, but there do not appear to be any records of other surgeries. However, by then we had established some forward bases with medical facilities.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Were there any women on board submarines in WW2?
title: Were there any women on board submarines in WW2?
text:
There were no women serving as crew on a submarine in WW2. There simply wasn’t any privacy. However, there were a few women as passengers when submarines rescued them or extracted key personnel from islands in the war zone. The same was likely true for other ships, not just submarines. However, hospital ships did have nurses aboard.

Although women have served in the Navy since 1917, when Loretta Walsh became the first woman to enlist, they couldn’t serve on ships or in combat in WW2. Fully integrating women into the Navy took time with women unable to join the Naval Academy until 1976 and unable to serve in combat until 1994. This was true of all our military services.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Was there an area on these boats that could be used for a jail?
title: Was there an area on these boats that could be used for a jail?
text:
There was no place for a jail on an operating submarine. There was rarely a need for one and, if there was, it wouldn’t usually be for the crew. Offenses that were serious enough to warrant physical confinement rarely, if ever, happened on a submarine during WW2. How could the Navy physically punish someone worse than putting him on a submarine in combat – where he already was?

However, there was an occasional need to confine someone. That would usually be Japanese POWs, although that didn’t happen very often. Japanese soldiers and sailors would usually swim away from a rescue. It was dishonorable to be captured. The few that were taken aboard, for intelligence purposes, would just be handcuffed to a bunk. Sometimes, the captured POW would want to contribute to the boat by helping with the cleaning. If the captain and crew believed that the POW was reliable enough, they could remove the handcuffs and let him help.

The assumption was that if a crewmember needed to be confined, it would be easy enough to cuff him to a bunk for the rest of the patrol.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Who were the officers on submarines?
title: Who were the officers on submarines?
text: Officers were the managers on the submarine. They managed the departments for operations, maintenance and training. They also led the watch sections, directing the operation of the ship under the guidance of the commanding officer.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Were officers on submarines all the same?
title: Were officers on submarines all the same?
text:
Yes and no. An ensign was an ensign and a lieutenant was a lieutenant. However, some were regular officers and some were reserves.

Regular officers enter the Navy through the Naval Academy or through the scholarship program of the Naval Reserve Officers Training Corps. (In spite of the name, the NROTC program graduated both regular and reserve officers.) Regular officers have a minimum service obligation but no definite end date. They serve at the pleasure of the president and may submit a request to resign after minimum service is completed.

Reserve officers enter the Navy through the non-scholarship part of the NROTC program or through various other reserve programs. Officers may have come through the Officer Candidate School (OCS). Reserve officers have a contract of a determined length but can be released early. They may apply to become regular officers.

A significant change during the war was the increase in the number of reserve officers. There were few reserves on boats when hostilities broke out. At first, reserve officers were looked upon with some skepticism. However, reserves proved themselves to be capable officers and the submarine force would have been much less effective without them.

It appears that nearly all submarine commanders were regular officers with most being Naval Academy graduates. It was late 1944 before the first reserve officer would command a submarine in WW2.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Were the officers on submarines specialists?
title: Were the officers on submarines specialists?
text:
Usually not, other than specializing in submarines. They were generalists who rotated through various assignments on the boats. If the officers remained in submarines for a career, they would probably hold most of the shipboard leadership positions at some point. However, there were some exceptions. There were Engineering Duty Only (EDO) officers who were sometimes assigned to ships and the boats. There were also, at times, warrant officers (WO) or limited duty officers (LDO) who were specialists. They were usually formerly enlisted, who were commissioned and part of the wardroom.

It should be noted that officers who are submarine qualified do have a special designation in their personnel records. This does not, however, limit their opportunities for assignments or command on other ships.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How many officers would be assigned to a submarine and what were their roles?
title: How many officers would be assigned to a submarine and what were their roles?
text:
There would normally be eight to ten officers on a boat like the Pampanito.

The captain and the executive officer were designated and assigned by the Navy.

  • The captain or commanding officer (CO) was the most senior officer assigned to the boat. He was responsible for the entire ship and all of its actions.
  • The executive officer (XO) was second in line to command. He supported the captain during critical actions. He was usually responsible, subject to the captain’s approval, for personnel assignments and most other administrative matters. He would normally have been qualified for command and able to assume command in case the captain was disabled or died.

The rest of the wardroom would be assigned to the boat by the Navy. Most of the rest of the assignments would change at the discretion of the captain and XO, although it would usually be by seniority. The most common roles, in general order of seniority, would have been:

  • The operations officer was responsible for navigation and preparing patrol and other operational plans. He may have also managed some of the other officers such as communications and electronics.
  • The engineer was responsible for propulsion, the battery and other mechanical equipment such as pumps and compressors. The engineer was often the battle stations diving officer.
  • The weapons officer was responsible for torpedoes, guns and related equipment.
  • The electronics officer would be responsible for radar, sonar and electronic counter measures (ECM) equipment.
  • The communications officer was responsible for the radio room, keeping the secret library current, drawing communications codes from base, issuing daily crypto codes and destroying them when no longer needed.
  • The supply officer was responsible for ordering needed equipment, supplies and spare parts. He also worked with the lead cook to develop menus and order the needed food.
  • The assistant engineer would support the engineer, usually by being responsible for the non-propulsion equipment such as the pumps and compressors.

These officers, with the likely exception of the CO and XO, would also be standing watches as the officer of the deck (OOD) or diving officer.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Was ”captain” a rank or a job?
title: Was ”captain” a rank or a job?
text: It could be both. The commanding officer of any ship, such as a submarine, was referred to as the captain regardless of his rank. Captain is also a naval rank just below admiral. Commanding officers of large ships may have been captain of that ship and also hold the rank of captain. In WW2, captains (commanding officers) of submarines almost never held the rank of captain. They were usually commanders or lieutenant commanders. However, they were always addressed as captain since they were the commanding officers.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Who or what were the Chief Petty Officers?
title: Who or what were the Chief Petty Officers?
text:
Chiefs, as they are known and addressed, were the senior enlisted on the boat. They were specialists in their ratings and were experienced leaders. Chiefs were, and are, often referred to as the backbone of the Navy and were generally acknowledged to be the people who enable its functioning. In WW2, there would be five or six chiefs assigned to the boat.

The chiefs’ quarters were in the forward battery compartment, across from the ship’s office. This space was referred to as the goat locker. (This naming was true of the entire Navy, not just submarines.) The space was so named because the chiefs were the “old goats” of the Navy. In WW2, many were as “old” as 28 or 30 years old.

In modern parlance, GOAT means the greatest of all time. Most chiefs recognize that would be a bit of an exaggeration when referring to the goat locker.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Who was the Chief of the Boat, also known as the COB?
title: Who was the Chief of the Boat, also known as the COB?
text:
This was a senior enlisted man who had a special assignment on the boat. The COB was often, but not always, the most senior chief on board. The Chief of the Boat, or COB, was the go-between for the captain and XO and the enlisted crew. Although the COB was not an officer, he was treated as the third most senior person on board. The COB monitored morale and was a key part of training the crew in submarine qualifications. The COB would try to defuse situations before formal punishment was required and could impose modest, informal punishment to keep issues off the record. This position had a long history on submarines and, in the early 1970’s, was implemented throughout the military as command master chiefs or command master sergeants.

In WW2, the COB was appointed by the CO and XO. They would select the chief who had the best leadership qualities. Currently, being a COB is part of a career track. The Navy offers specific training and qualifications. The COB is now appointed by the Navy, similar to the way the CO and XO are assigned. The COB is part of the command team and reaps the rewards for the success of the whole boat, as well as the discipline for significant failures.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Who were the petty officers who weren’t chiefs?
title: Who were the petty officers who weren’t chiefs?
text: These were the specialists who were assigned to submarines and were proficient in a certain area of expertise. Petty officers in increasing seniority were third class, second class and first class. As they rose in rank, they would have qualified as having increasing technical knowledge and leadership ability. That also meant these petty officers had positions of greater responsibility, such as being responsible for a torpedo room or an engine room.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What specialists (ratings) were typically assigned to submarines?
title: What specialists (ratings) were typically assigned to submarines?
text:
These are the typical ratings for these submarines in WW2. Since then, the names of some ratings have changed. For example, motor machinist mates became enginemen. Pharmacist mates became hospital corpsmen. Another rating, gunner’s mate, became no longer applicable to submarines when the guns were removed in the early ‘50s. However, missile techs have been added to submarines with Tomahawk or Polaris/Poseidon/Trident missiles.

Typical ratings aboard U. S. submarines in WW2 included:

  • Cook – prepared and cooked the meals. The overnight cook was the baker who made bread, rolls, cakes and pies. The senior cook worked with the supply officer to plan meals and order the necessary foods.
  • Electrician mate – responsible for maintaining electrical circuits and motors, and operating the cubicle in the maneuvering room. Also responsible for maintaining the battery cells, checking the specific gravity (estimating the power remaining) and adding pure water when needed.
  • Fireman – not yet a specialist, but a young sailor who was assigned to engineering and would eventually pursue a specific rating in that area.
  • Gunner’s mate – responsible for maintaining and operating the guns. Some of the work regarding the guns was also done by the torpedomen.
  • IC electrician – responsible for interior communications equipment including signaling systems.
  • Machinist mate - responsible for mechanical systems other than the engines, such as the air conditioning, pumps, motors and other smaller mechanical systems.
  • Motor mac – a motor machinist mate, responsible for the operation, maintenance and repair of the four main engines and the smaller “donkey” diesel which was in the lower level of the after engine room.
  • Pharmacists mate – the “medic” who cared for his shipmates’ illnesses and injuries. These men were specially selected and trained for independent duty since there was no physician aboard the WW2 boats.
  • Quartermaster – responsible for navigation and signaling between ships. Since submarines were often operating independently, signaling wasn’t often required. Assisted the navigator and tracked the ship’s position between fixes.
  • Radioman – responsible for sending and receiving messages as well as maintaining and repairing the radio equipment. Routed messages to the captain and other officers as appropriate. Alerted the communications officer when highly classified messages needed additional decoding. Responsible for keeping the crypto codes secure while in use.
  • Seaman – similar to a fireman, not yet a specialist, but a young sailor who was assigned to an operations department and would eventually pursue a specific rating in that area.
  • Sonarman – responsible for operating, maintaining and repairing the sonar equipment. Listened for the sounds of other ships in the area and alerted the officer of the deck (OOD) to any unusual or unexpected sounds.
  • Stewards mate – supported the officers; staffed the serving galley; provided the captain with coffee; etc.
  • Storekeeper – worked with the supply officer to submit the forms to obtain the food, spare parts and other supplies needed by the boat.
  • Torpedoman – responsible for maintaining and repairing the torpedoes on the boat. May have been part of the gun crews. Maintained the charge in the electric torpedoes. Maintained the torpedo tubes and associated equipment.
  • Yeoman – the administrative assistant. Maintained the records for assigned personnel and other records for the boat. Prepared the patrol reports as directed by the captain.
  • Mess cooks – these would normally be the newest and most junior members of the crew assigned to assist the cooks. They were most often seamen or firemen who have not yet been assigned to departments. (Mess cook was not a specialty or rating.) Mess cooks helped with meal preparation and with cleanup. It was equivalent to KP duty in the Army. However, on submarines this was not usually a punitive assignment.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did enlisted men have special designations as submariners similar to the officers?
title: Did enlisted men have special designations as submariners similar to the officers?
text: Yes, they did. Sailors who were qualified in submarines had an “SS” added to their ratings. For example, a third class radioman who had qualified in submarines would have his rating upgraded from RM3 to RM3(SS). This was a formal designation noted in the man’s service record. Similar to the officer’s designation, this did not limit their future assignments.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Were a sailor’s job or specialty his only responsibilities?
title: Were a sailor’s job or specialty his only responsibilities?
text:
No. Everyone was also responsible for their submarine qualifications, including the basics about the entire boat. This was particularly true of younger sailors reporting aboard their first boat. It was also true when reporting to a new assignment. Boats could be slightly different and the new command had to ensure that sailors transferred to the command knew what the new men said they knew. Obviously, requalifying on a different but similar boat would be fairly quick and easy.

There may be training across similar ratings such as electronics or mechanicals. In addition, it was the responsibility of everyone on board to help train and to mentor the newest submariners.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What was a “bubblehead”?
title: What was a “bubblehead”?
text: “Bubblehead” was probably intended to be a derogatory nickname for submariners. The name comes from the “bubble” in the inclinometer used to maintain depth. Even though it may have been intended to be somewhat derogatory, most sub sailors wore the label with pride. It was far better than being a “zoomie” (naval aviation) or a “skimmer”, a surface sailor.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What was “Liberty”?
title: What was “Liberty”?
text: Liberty was, and still is, time off for sailors when not on duty overnight or when visiting a port. Usually, one third of the crew will remain on board at any time so that the ship can get underway if needed during an emergency. The other two thirds may have had liberty. Liberty was usually just overnight or over a weekend assuming the sailor wasn’t part of a duty section. It was not time off counted against leave.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What was “Leave”?
title: What was “Leave”?
text: Leave was extended time off, similar to vacations or personal time off (PTO) in the civilian world. It was earned at a consistent rate and an individual’s leave balance was tracked. During peacetime, there was a limit as to how much leave could be accrued without losing the days over the limit. Leave not taken would be paid out when the sailor left the Navy.
category: Crews Aboard U. S. Subs in WW2

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What was a typical day for submarine sailors at sea on a U. S. boat during the war?
title: What was a typical day for submarine sailors at sea on a U. S. boat during the war?
text:
A typical day consisted of two four-hour shifts on watch plus time spent for maintenance, paperwork, training and studying for promotions. The time between 08:00 and 16:00 (8 AM to 4 PM) would generally be a work day, when maintenance, etc. was completed. Twelve hours was not unusual for a regular workday, and it could be even longer if the sailor was working toward his submarine qualifications or studying for a promotion.

Sundays were a day of rest. As long as there were no attacks in progress and no essential repairs, there would generally be no routine work on those days. In other words, on their day off sailors “only” stood eight hours of watch.

This assumes that there were three watch sections and the crew stood watches for four hours and then had eight hours off. If there were not three qualified watchstanders for a specific position, then watches were “port and starboard”, meaning four hours on and just four off duty. That lasted until a third watchstander could pass qualifications for that watch.

During the war, the routine was changed by attacks on enemy ships or by attacks from enemy aircraft and ships. Either attacks could last many hours and involved the whole crew. That would require changes to the normal schedule and the boats made whatever adjustments were needed for rest and food.

There were a few instances of captains reversing the day so that the crew was working at night when the engines were running (and noisy) and pulling fresh and, hopefully, cooler air into the boat. This also meant that the boat was submerged - quieter and calmer – during daylight hours while the crew was sleeping from 08:00 to 20:00. If this was done, it was only when the boat was in the tropics. In these situations, the workday was from 20:00 to 04:00 (8 PM to 4 AM) and meals were offset by 12 hours. For example, breakfast was around 20:00 rather than at 08:00.
category: Life Aboard U. S. WW2 Subs

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What did a typical day in port consist of?
title: What did a typical day in port consist of?
text:
The typical workday was from 08:00 to 16:00. That could be started and ended earlier, called tropical hours, so that the crew wasn’t working during the hottest part of the day. In WW2 it was often longer than eight hours as men trained or got the boat ready for the next patrol.

This assumes that there were no major problems to be corrected. If, for example, engines needed to be overhauled, then the enginemen (motor macs in WW2) worked many more hours. Others in the crew were assigned or volunteered to assist. The key thing was to get the boat ready for the next patrol. It is important to remember that sailors in the Pacific area did not go home at night. They may not have seen their families for a year or more at a time.

There was always one third of the crew remaining on board overnight. This was so that there were enough men on duty in case of emergencies and so the boat could get underway and change locations as needed. The duty section likely had some work to do to continue repairs or to clean up after shipyard workers.
category: Life Aboard U. S. WW2 Subs

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What is a “watch”?
title: What is a “watch”?
text:
A watch, in naval terms, is a normal shift for the routine operation the submarine. In WW2, that was normally four hours in length with eight hours off before the next watch. As indicated above, there would normally be three watch sections.

The routine was adjusted somewhat by dogging the watch about once per week. (See below.)
category: Life Aboard U. S. WW2 Subs

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What clock times did the Navy use in WW2?
title: What clock times did the Navy use in WW2?
text:
The Navy used, and still uses, a 24-hour clock. That is often referred to as military time or European continental time. Times from 1:00 PM and 11:59 PM between are expressed by adding 12 to the hours. Thus, 4 PM is 16:00; 8 PM is 20:00 and 11:59 PM is 23:59. Midnight is still 00:00. The hour until 01:00 is expressed as 00 plus the minutes, such as 00:30. Noon is still 12:00.

“Zero Dark 30” described any time in the very early morning when sensible people were still asleep. This was true no matter where the boat was.

For U. S. ships, times were local. As the boats headed west, the clocks were set back one hour as they crossed into the next time zone. This is what civilians do now, setting clocks back one hour three times as they drive from the East Coast to the West Coast.

NOTE: The German and Japanese navies did not use local time. Their clocks remained set to the time zones of their capitols.

If there was a need to specify a time regardless of where the submarine might be, that was stated as time zone Zulu. That is what civilians know as Greenwich Mean Time (GMT). This was used, for example, as the time for the cessation of hostilities, the end of the war. That way, everyone everywhere would follow the given order to cease fire at the same instant.
category: Life Aboard U. S. WW2 Subs

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How does dogging the watch work?
title: How does dogging the watch work?
text:
It means that one watch, usually the 12:00 to 16:00 was split into two shifts of two hours each. This had the effect of changing everyone’s watch forward by four hours. That way no one stood the same watches all the time. Boats would dog the watch about once per week.

For example, the schedule for watch sections to start would be:

08:00

12:00

14:00

16:00

20:00

00:00

04:00

Day 6

2

2

1

Watch section 2 in this example only stands half the 12:00 to 16:00 watch on day 7. Section 3 stands the last half of that watch, and will stand all of it on day 8. This gives section 2 a break from always standing mid-watches (00:00 to 04:00) and section 3 from always having the 04:00 to 08:00 watches. Everyone now stands watch four hours earlier than before they dogged the watch.
category: Life Aboard U. S. WW2 Subs

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What were the general living conditions on a submarine like this?
title: What were the general living conditions on a submarine like this?
text:
Living conditions were fairly rudimentary including the following, some of which are discussed further below:

  • A shortage of bunks.
  • A lack of fresh air.
  • Some temperature extremes.
  • Close quarters.
  • Limited fresh water.
  • A strong smell.
  • Little dedicated food storage space.
  • A lack of much personal storage.
  • A lack of privacy.

Sailors still thought sub duty was good duty. This list is just a statement of adverse conditions, not a list of complaints.
category: Life Aboard U. S. WW2 Subs

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Since the crew size grew, but not the number of bunks, where did they all sleep?
title: Since the crew size grew, but not the number of bunks, where did they all sleep?
text:
There were enough bunks. There just weren’t enough bunks for everyone to have a bunk to themselves. The numbers varied a little based on the actual number of men aboard for the patrol and the number of bunks available. Let us assume there were 70 bunks and 80 men. In that situation, 50 men had their own bunks. The other 30 men were assigned with three men to two bunks. They were assigned so that one of the three was on watch at any given time. They were each in different watch sections. That meant that if a sailor was one of the 30 junior men and had an opportunity to sleep – i.e. his work was done and his qualifications were current – there was a bunk available.

That was the good news. On the other hand, when they came off watch at midnight or 04:00 (AM) they were getting into the same bunk that their relief had recently gotten out of. It was called hot bunking for a reason. To further put that in context, it appears that the boats in the tropics were rarely, if ever, cooler than 90 degrees Fahrenheit or 32 degrees Celsius.

There was the possibility of some good news. If the captain had an opportunity and fired torpedoes from the after torpedo tubes, bunking could improve. The reload torpedoes were moved into the tubes, which were always kept full if possible. Now, for every torpedo fired, they could make two or three bunks on each empty skid. For every bunk that was created in this way, three sailors would no longer be hot bunking.
category: Life Aboard U. S. WW2 Subs

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Was there a best place to sleep?
title: Was there a best place to sleep?
text:
Submarines were relatively noisy at night. Engines were running and batteries were being charged. The boat was on the surface plowing through waves. People were on watch, operating the submarine. All of that made noise. Red lights helped make it easier to sleep, but the boat couldn’t go completely dark. As a result, nothing was as quiet and dark as your bedroom at home.

Most sleeping areas seemed to have advantages and drawbacks. The forward torpedo room was farthest from the engines, so that noise was at the lowest level here but the sailors there did hear the bow crashing through the waves. In addition, the bow, as well as the stern, experienced the most vertical motion - up and down - due to the swells of the ocean.

The after torpedo room had a little separation from the engines but did have the propellor shafts running under it with the screws not far behind. That generated noise while on the surface.

The after battery – crews’ berthing – had the least vertical motion. However, it was next to the forward engine room which normally had at least one engine running at night. (The water tight door to the engine room was normally closed unless someone needed to pass through it.) It also had a large fan pulling air out of the battery well during the battery charge. With 36 bunks in this space, the chances of at least one sailor snoring like a chain saw were close to 100%.

NOTE: The area on the port side of the crew’s berthing, away from the main passageway, was usually a bit better. There was normally a divider of some sort between the 18 port side bunks and the other 18. That area on the port side, called Hogan’s Alley, was then a little darker and a bit quieter.

The top bunks were usually preferred since no one stepped on that bunk as they climbed up to theirs. Sailors in some of the top bunks did have to watch out for all those little valves in the aft corners of the crew’s berthing area. They did not want to wake up with a start and imprint those valves on their foreheads.

The forward battery was likely to be one of the better places to sleep. There were still engine, fan and wave noises, as well as lights. But this space didn’t have the worst of any of the disadvantages. The key to having a quieter bunk may have been to become an officer or a chief petty officer and then sleeping in this compartment.

Finding a truly quiet place to sleep was very unlikely. The key was to get used to the noise and light quickly. It also helped to be tired after a long workday.
category: Life Aboard U. S. WW2 Subs

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What kept the crew from falling out of their bunks in heavy seas?
title: What kept the crew from falling out of their bunks in heavy seas?
text: This was mostly up to the individual sailors. They needed to find a sleeping position that was spread out enough so that they wouldn’t be as likely to roll over unintentionally. They may not get a very good night’s sleep but it was possible to sleep this way. In very heavy seas, they may have had to strap themselves into their bunk in order to stay put.
category: Life Aboard U. S. WW2 Subs

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How deep did they have to go to get below the effect of waves?
title: How deep did they have to go to get below the effect of waves?
text:
Of course, this depended on the size of the waves. In any case, it quickly became calmer than being on the surface. Even periscope depth was somewhat calmer than the surface. A depth of 100 feet made a significant difference. A depth of 150 or 200 feet was below most normal wave action. In large storms, captains went down to 300 or 400 feet and that was usually enough. That allowed the crew to eat, digest their food and get some rest.

Modern submarines need to be at 200 feet frequently to pick up any messages addressed to them via a trailing antenna. They have reported being bounced around quite a bit at 200 feet when they were in a typhoon. That isn’t surprising since waves in typhoons can be as high as 50 to 90 feet.
category: Life Aboard U. S. WW2 Subs

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What was the largest number of men on a U. S. WW2 submarine?
title: What was the largest number of men on a U. S. WW2 submarine?
text:
Again, the Gato/Balao/Tench boats generally had 80 to 85 men aboard. For the normal crew size, the largest number was likely the crews of the USS Argonaut (SS-166), the USS Narwhal (SS-167) and the USS Nautilus (SS-168). These were large, slow submarines built in the late 1920s. (These boats were about 35 feet longer, 6 feet wider and almost twice the displacement of the Gato/Balao/Tench boats.) They usually had crews of about 90 men. That increased briefly to nearly 100 in the middle of the war and then returned to 90. These submarines had two six-inch guns and were often used for minelaying and transport of small units of guerillas and regular troops.

There were situations when boats had extra passengers as the result of special operations, rescues or lifeguard duty. A small sampling includes:

  • USS Seawolf (SS-197) was lost in 1944 with 82 crew and 17 U. S. Army personnel aboard. (“Silent Victory” by Clay Blair Jr., page 737.)
  • At one point, USS Narwhal (SS-167) picked up 32 evacuees, including eight women and two children.
  • Overall, submarines rescued 504 downed aviators during the war with USS Tigrone (SS-419) rescuing 31 in a single patrol. That broke the record of 22 by USS Tang (SS-306). Some rescued airmen stood watches while on the boats.
  • USS Gato (SS-212), in 1943, evacuated 27 children, nine mothers and three nuns from Bougainville.
  • In September of 1944, USS Pampanito (SS-383) rescued 73 British and Australian soldiers from the South China Sea. The rescued soldiers were aboard for about five days. USS Sealion (SS-315) participated in the same rescue, picking up 52 soldiers.
  • When the USS Darter (SS-227) ran aground on a coral reef in late 1944, her crew was rescued by the USS Dace (SS-247). With two full crews, there were likely about 160 sailors aboard the Dace for approximately one week.
  • In February, 1942, the USS S-38 (SS-143) picked up 58 survivors from the British destroyer HMS Electra, sunk the day before at the Battle of the Java Sea. This was particularly noteworthy because the normal crew size for the S-38 was only about 42 men.
category: Life Aboard U. S. WW2 Subs

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How could they all move quickly when going to battle stations?
title: How could they all move quickly when going to battle stations?
text:
Submarine sailors quickly learned to get past each other in the narrow passageways. However, there wasn’t necessarily all that much movement going to battle stations, particularly during WW2. Some of the crew worked and slept near their battle stations. For example, torpedomen usually stood watch, worked, slept and had their battle stations in the torpedo rooms.

In addition, sailors typically had clues during the war that the captain was developing an attack. Smoke from potential targets could be spotted at least ten or fifteen miles away. Smoke was seen well before the ships themselves. If the target was a cargo ship or a tanker, which usually steamed at 10 to 12 knots, the tracking party was called away first. That could be an hour or more before going to battle stations.

In addition, there were very few secrets on a submarine. Word about a possible attack would spread through the crew quickly. Sailors would then have plenty of opportunity to drift toward their battle stations before the alarm was sounded.
category: Life Aboard U. S. WW2 Subs

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What was “battle stations”?
title: What was “battle stations”?
text: This was the condition when the ship was expected to go into battle. Every position was manned, usually by the best operators available. Crew members not at a specific battle station were available as reserves or for damage control.
category: Life Aboard U. S. WW2 Subs

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What was a “battle station”?
title: What was a “battle station”?
text: It was an individual’s job when the submarine went into combat. Some of the crew had different stations depending on whether the boat was attacking on the surface, preparing to use the deck guns, or attacking while submerged. This would normally be related to one’s rating or specialty. It could be as one of the primary operators, as a back-up, or available for damage control.
category: Life Aboard U. S. WW2 Subs

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Who was responsible for damage control?
title: Who was responsible for damage control?
text:
Most large Navy ships had assigned sailors for what were known as damage control parties. This was in addition to their regular assignments. Their roles, in the event of damage, a mechanical casualty or drill, were to report to the assigned damage control locker. From there, they grabbed the appropriate equipment and proceeded to fight the problem.

These submarines did not have assigned damage control parties. The sailors who happened to be in the compartment where the problem occurred were the damage control party. That was why every submarine sailor had to learn damage control techniques. That was why every submarine sailor needed to know the basics of every system on the boat. They had to know how to isolate problems and combat them effectively. This was all a part of submarine qualifications and earning dolphins.
category: Life Aboard U. S. WW2 Subs

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What was a tracking party?
title: What was a tracking party?
text:
The tracking party was the part of the battle stations crew that was determining the location and direction of the potential targets, often starting while they were still a distance away. This could be an hour or more before the rest of the crew went to battle stations, depending on the speed of the targets. The information gathered at this time would eventually be the basis for the attack and the final course of the torpedoes.

Obviously, the captain and executive officer were key members. They would also want the sonar and radar stations manned by their best people. The torpedo data computer (TDC) was used to track the targets’ progress and to begin to develop the firing solution for the torpedoes. Therefore, the TDC operator(s) were included. The plot teams were included to present and preserve a graphic account of the attack. In addition, the captain included anyone else he deemed relevant.
category: Life Aboard U. S. WW2 Subs

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Where did the submarines store all the oxygen for so many people?
title: Where did the submarines store all the oxygen for so many people?
text:
They didn’t. These submarines did not have the capability to make or store large quantities of oxygen or to remove CO2. (Modern submarines do, and that’s why they can be submerged for as much as three or four months at a time.) In the WW2 boats, the air that the sailors were breathing was the same air they had been breathing since the boat submerged. That air was intended to last 16 to 18 hours. Since most of the crew smoked, 16 hours might be more realistic. The normal procedure was to surface every night to get fresh air in the boat.

The best way to get breathable air in the boat was to run the engines to charge the battery. (To say it was fresh air might be a bit of a stretch.) The air system was set up so that most of the air for the engines went straight to the engine rooms. Also, some of it went to the ends of the boat and was pulled toward the engine rooms, refreshing the air in all the spaces. Running the low-pressure blower to push the last of the water out of the ballast tanks used the air in the middle of the boat, also pulling in fresh air through the conning tower hatch. The same thing would happen if the air compressors in the pump room were running to recharge the air banks.

The routine was to be on the surface every night. This would hopefully top off the battery for the next day while freshening the air in the boat. Being on the surface each night also allowed the boats to get their messages and, if the skies were cooperative, get position fixes using stars at dusk and again at dawn.

If the boat needed to remain submerged more than 16 hours - usually because it was being attacked - there were one-time measures that could be used. The first of those were the green oxygen bottles and the many CO2 absorbent cans in the overheads. The silver-colored cans in the overhead, labeled “DO NOT PAINT”, were the CO2 absorbent, typically lithium hydroxide. These would give the men a couple more hours of breathable air.

After that, the main option was to bleed air from the high-pressure air banks into the boat. This pressurized the boat somewhat, but improved the O2 and CO2 percentages. Even if the air in the boat was doubled, to two atmospheres, decompression would not be an issue. It was about the same as swimming and diving down to about 25 feet. To be clear, this air from the air banks wasn’t to be confused with fresh air, but it was air that allowed the crew to survive.
category: Life Aboard U. S. WW2 Subs

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Were these submarines hot inside?
title: Were these submarines hot inside?
text:
The temperature in the boat depended on where it was. Again, if they were in the tropics, it appears that the boats were rarely if ever below 90 degrees. Most of our submarine bases and patrols were in the tropics. A key factor was that the air and water temperatures were usually in the 80s. Then add the fact that the boat was constantly generating heat from cooking, running the engines and from charging or discharging the battery. As a result, the heat was not surprising. In the tropics, the engine rooms would easily reach 100 degrees.

When the engines were shut down when submerging, the cooling water to the engines was also shut down. Then the engine rooms could reach 120 degrees and the rest of the boat could be 110. It took some time for the warm ocean waters to cool the boat back down.

There was air conditioning, but it was really little more than a dehumidifier. (“U.S. Submarines Through 1945” by Norman Friedman, Page 200.) It helped but didn’t really cool the boat that much.

If the boats were in northern or southern latitudes, the temperatures were likely more moderate. This was particularly true in spring and fall.

If the boats were operating off Alaska, they might actually be rather chilly. The Japanese occupied the last two islands in the Aleutian chain at the time of the Battle of Midway. After that, the U. S. often had a submarine in the area monitoring any Japanese activity. In that area, the air and water temperatures may well be in the low 30s. If so, the boat could be cool or cold. The crew might be wishing for a little bit of that excess tropical heat. It would also be cold in the boats during the winter if they were being tested during sea trials off Manitowoc, WI; Portsmouth, NH; or New London, CT.
category: Life Aboard U. S. WW2 Subs

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Weren’t the boats crowded?
title: Weren’t the boats crowded?
text:
Submariners didn’t usually think so. No one thought a submarine was spacious when they volunteered. They knew it was small and was all closed up when submerged. Therefore, the boats did not seem that crowded to the crews.

Still, it’s really a matter of what they got used to and the crews quickly became accustomed to the conditions. It simply became the new normal. As Fletcher Pratt wrote about submariners in “The Navy’s War”, page 140: “It was a club of individuals with an almost incredible ability to treat every circumstance as normal.”

Even though the crew became accustomed to the close quarters, that didn’t make it ideal. Of course, carrying a significant number of extra passengers, such as rescued personnel or special operations troops would make it more crowded. The crew might have to work a bit harder to make that seem normal.

NOTE: It is sometimes noted that conditions on these submarines do not meet the minimum standards for U. S. prisons. Most of that is simply due to the lack of space per person and the fact that many of the crew would not see daylight for weeks. Some may not even see the sky at night. To be fair, conditions on most surface ships weren’t that much better.
category: Life Aboard U. S. WW2 Subs

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — There were showers on board.  Did the crew have an opportunity to shower every day?
title: There were showers on board.  Did the crew have an opportunity to shower every day?
text:
Generally speaking, the crew had an opportunity to NOT shower most days. On a submarine, there isn’t enough fresh water for everyone to take showers regularly. This varied from boat to boat, but the stills only produced so much fresh water.

The documentation (NAVPERS 16170) indicates that a submarine on a war patrol consumed an average of approximately 500 gallons per day of fresh water for cooking, drinking, washing and engine makeup water. (The internal cooling jacket for the engines used fresh water.) The ships battery used another 500 gallons per week. The battery actually had first claim on fresh water. That water was stored separately and may have needed to be distilled twice.

The Kleinschmidt stills produced 750 gallons per day when they were working at capacity. They were also famously unreliable. It was rare that both stills were working at capacity and, in the patrol area, they would not use the stills when submerged. They used too much power and made too much noise.

In theory, there was enough fresh water left over for the crew to shower every week or two. However, very few submariners remember taking showers on their boats. The literature is notable for the few times that it mentions anyone taking showers on submarines. What boat sailors remembered was not showering at all or getting a bucket of water from the air conditioning condensation to wash out skivvies and take a quick sponge bath.

The cooks and the pharmacist mate (medic) would usually be able to shower. After all, they prepared food and cared for the sick and injured. Showers, even if infrequent, for those crew members were a necessity.

Any showers were “navy showers”. Fresh water was precious throughout the fleet, even where it was more plentiful than it was on submarines. A navy shower means that the sailor stepped into the shower and got wet. Then he turned the water off. After applying soap and shampoo, he would turn the water back on to rinse off. Ideally, the total water usage was no more than three minutes.
category: Life Aboard U. S. WW2 Subs

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Why not take salt water showers?
title: Why not take salt water showers?
text:
An occasional salt water shower wouldn’t be a problem but regular showers with sea water irritate the skin. Soon sailors would be raising welts and getting infections. Because of the dangers, the boats were not plumbed to have salt water in the showers.

Fairly rarely, when returning from a patrol, if the boat was in a safe place and ahead of schedule, the captain would stop the boat and have a swim call. Anyone who wanted to could dive into the ocean and rinse off a few layers of grime. There might even have been enough fresh water for a quick rinse. On the other hand, most of the crew may have preferred to keep sailing toward home.
category: Life Aboard U. S. WW2 Subs

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — If no one could take showers, didn’t the submarine smell bad?
title: If no one could take showers, didn’t the submarine smell bad?
text:
Diesel submarines smelled awful, especially when at sea.

Again, most of the crew did not take showers. It would vary from boat to boat, but there just wasn’t enough fresh water for everyone to take showers regularly. Humans contributed significantly to the stench.

But human bodies were not the only source of odors on submarines. There was the all-pervasive smell of diesel, other oils and engine exhaust gasses. Paint smells lingered too. Paint might be a component of the odors on the Pampanito today. Most of the crew smoked since cigarettes were given away free to servicemen in WW2. (To be more accurate, most of the crew were active smokers and the rest were second hand smokers.) Yes, they could smoke inside the boat even when submerged.

Lastly, three of the four heads (toilets) drained to sanitary tanks. The good news was that these heads could usually be used when submerged. The less good news was that when the crew discharged something into the sanitary tanks, an equal amount of air was vented. That air would go through charcoal filters before venting back into the boat, but that only helped a little.

Yes, diesel submarines smelled very bad.

On the other hand, there still was some good news. Diesel submarines were like gardenias, night-blooming jasmine, tuberose and hydrogen sulfide. (Hydrogen sulfide is a poisonous gas that smells like rotten eggs. Submarines weren’t usually poisonous.) What all these things, and many others, have in common with diesel submarines was that after 15 to 30 minutes people no longer smelled it. Olfactory nerves were saturated and stopped sending signals to the brain. The nerves gave up. The crew didn’t get used to the stink; they stopped smelling it. They only noticed the new smells, like fresh-baked bread and rolls at night.

This is what makes hydrogen sulfide so dangerous. A sailor would no longer smell it but it could still kill him. Fortunately, it was very rare to have hydrogen sulfide on an operating submarine since it develops in closed spaces. Boats have very few of those and the crew almost never went into them when at sea. This was more of an issue on big surface ships.

Even if a sailor was up on the bridge for a watch, his olfactory nerves don’t normally reset that quickly. The lookouts and OOD were still mostly “protected” when they came down off the bridge. They didn’t smell the boat, at least not for long.
category: Life Aboard U. S. WW2 Subs

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How much food could these boats carry?  Where was the storage space?
title: How much food could these boats carry?  Where was the storage space?
text:
The boats were designed for patrols of about 75 days. Therefore, they could carry enough food to last for the full patrol.

There is not much dedicated pantry space. If the patrol was planned for 45 days or more, food was stored everywhere. Naturally, the limited pantry and cold storage spaces below the crew’s mess were full. Large cans of coffee, sugar and flour were stored outboard of the engines. Eggs, butter and cheese were stored in the forward escape trunk for as long as they lasted. As warm as it might have been, it was likely the coolest place on the boat.

Other canned goods were stored wherever there was room as long as they could be tied down securely and weren’t in the way of operating equipment. One logical place was the berthing space in the after battery compartment. Others were the showers, the pump room and the lower level of the forward torpedo room. The crew walked on their food – the cases of canned goods covered by cardboard or wood – until they ate the food down to the deck.

Sailors were often taking cans of peaches with them on patrol, as long as the cans fit in their individual storage.
category: Life Aboard U. S. WW2 Subs

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What kinds of food were served on submarines?
title: What kinds of food were served on submarines?
text:
The menu was fairly basic but generally tasty. The cooks were trying to keep 80 men happy even though they were from different regions of the country with different cuisines. Meat, potatoes and vegetables were the basic menus. That would vary some with regional specialties such as pasta and rice on the menu at times. Fresh bread or rolls were normal. In addition, the overnight baker may have made pies or cakes.

After the first week at sea, there were few fresh vegetables or salads. Fresh fruit might last a little longer. Fresh milk, cheese and eggs didn’t last long either. Powdered milk and eggs were available after that. Much of the meat was frozen or canned. Fresh food simply doesn’t last that long in a warm and humid submarine.

To be fair, the crews might still grumble about the food. It has been said that a sailor isn’t happy unless he is complaining about something. At times the crew would drive the cooks crazy. On one patrol, the main request might be for tuna salad. The cooks would then order more tuna for the next patrol. Of course, the crew would now want more strawberries on that next patrol and would complain about being stuck with all those stupid tins of tuna.

Much of this was also true of surface ships. Food on submarines was not much more limited than it was on surface ships. Still, the food on submarines was the best food in the seagoing Navy. That goes back to the earliest days on subs. President Theodore Roosevelt visited one of our first submarines in 1901 or 1902. It was apparent that there needed to be some added incentives to get sailors to serve on those primitive boats. The answers were to increase the pay and to increase the food allowance.

The Navy provided a certain amount per enlisted sailor for meals each day when assigned to a ship. The Navy provided a larger amount for those sailors assigned to submarines. Therefore, the supply officer and the cooks ordered special things from the standard stores list a little more often. Examples might be that they ordered more frozen shrimp for shrimp cocktails or they ordered better cuts of meat more often.

As a result of this incentive, the quality of the food on submarines became a fairly big deal. There were stories of captains fighting over good cooks, perhaps even physically. And you certainly didn’t want to be a bad cook on a submarine. You might not last long on the boats.

Here is just one positive example. There was one overnight baker on a submarine who asked his shipmates to write home for the recipe for their favorite cakes. The baker was asking for the recipes from his shipmates’ wives, girlfriends or mothers. Then, on that sailor’s birthday, he would bake that cake for dessert. This may not seem to be a big deal, but it mattered for morale. Scaling up the recipe may not have been as simple as it might seem since some ingredients, such as spices, can require different proportions.

The food on submarines really was better than on other ships.
category: Life Aboard U. S. WW2 Subs

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How could everyone fit in that small crew’s mess to eat?
title: How could everyone fit in that small crew’s mess to eat?
text:
There were four tables with three seats on each side. Therefore the crew’s mess seats 24, relatively comfortably. The crew eats in sections, one third at a time. Given the crew size of 80 sailors, minus the officers who eat in the wardroom and the cook and mess cooks, that leaves 22 or so who need to be fed at each seating.

Meals were tied to the changes of the watch. That means breakfast was at 08:00, lunch was at noon, soup down was at 16:00 and dinner at 20:00. The watch section that was going on duty ate first. During the time that the watch changes, the section not involved ate next. (The change of the watch was not instantaneous. The section coming on watch needs to be told about the current situation and any upcoming changes or expected operations.) Then the section coming off watch ate last. This was done so that no one needed to miss a meal. There was enough room since only one third of the crew ate at a time.
category: Life Aboard U. S. WW2 Subs

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Was that an ice cream machine in the crew’s berthing?
title: Was that an ice cream machine in the crew’s berthing?
text:
Yes, the tall, rectangular, metal box in crew’s berthing was an ice cream machine. Early in the war, there was no capacity to make ice cream on submarines.
