display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did using pure oxygen in a torpedo mean it couldn’t be detected?
title: Did using pure oxygen in a torpedo mean it couldn’t be detected?
text:
Because there was almost no bubble trail, it was much harder to detect the kerosene/oxygen torpedoes but not impossible. Torpedoes made a lot of noise. Still, it seems unlikely that it would have been detected in time to avoid being hit.

Bioluminescence may have also been detected at night. That too may not have been noticed soon enough to avoid being hit.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Didn’t Japan use mini submarines at Pearl Harbor?
title: Didn’t Japan use mini submarines at Pearl Harbor?
text:
Yes, they did. Japan sent five mini submarines to take part in the attacks. They were carried to the Hawaiian Islands on the larger submarines that were also part of the plan, but they were generally a failure. Our first warning of the attack – which we obviously didn’t take seriously enough – came when we discovered one of the mini submarines trying to enter the harbor and sank it.

It was originally thought that none of the mini submarines were able to accomplish their missions. However, recent video analysis indicates that one of the boats may have penetrated the harbor and successfully fired one torpedo against Battleship Row, hitting its target.

These very small submarines displaced only about 60 tons. They had a crew of two men and carried two torpedoes.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Were the Japanese mini submarines the Kaiten?
title: Were the Japanese mini submarines the Kaiten?
text:
No. The Kaiten were much smaller and were not developed and put in service until late 1944. They were developed as a modification of the Type 93 torpedo and had a crew of just one pilot.

The Kaiten were not very effective, although the Japanese certainly thought they were. The first Kaiten operations were delayed until November, 1944. The attack at Ulithi on 20 November sank the USS Mississinewa (AO-59). Our ASW forces then spotted the other Kaiten and sank them.

The Japanese claimed great successes by the Kaiten in the last three months of the war, but the claims of success were dubious: “[Japanese] Sixth Fleet Headquarters exaggerated the effectiveness of the Kaiten in the second Gen operation, especially before the loss of the I-48. Indeed, no ships were sunk, but as a U. S. naval intelligence officer noted, ‘The Japanese assessed the results as eighteen vessels sunk, including one converted aircraft carrier, nine large transports, one cruiser, and six other large ships including aircraft carriers, battleships and transports. Such optimistic estimates can only be the result of inexcusably poor staff work.” (“The Japanese Submarine Force and World War II” by Carl Boyd and Akihiko Yoshida, page 170.)

This is confirmed on page 256 of “Suicide Submarine” by Yutaka Yokota and Joseph D. Harrington, (also known as “The Kaiten Weapon”.) That text in the Epilogue indicates: “When World War II closed, the Japanese thought they had sunk some 40 Allied ships, including a British cruiser of the Leander class through their Kaiten effort. A check of all available sources reveals they sank only two U. S. Navy ships, the tanker Mississinewa in the Kikusui sortie and the destroyer escort Underhill. This second ship was actually sunk by friendly forces on July 24, 1945 after being hit by a Kaiten. Only one U. S. merchant ship, SS Canada Victory, was the victim of a Kaiten, going down on April 27, 1945. These three vessels, measured against the 8 submarines and nearly 900 Japanese lives lost in the Kaiten program, make the enemy’s sacrifice seem fruitless.”

Moreover, there was a great cost in development and use, “from the time of the first Kaiten sortie on 20 November, 1944 until the end of the Okinawa campaign, Kaiten took 7 lives in training and 48 in action, without achieving any significant confirmed results.” Further: “The cause of the failure was not the weapon, but rather the manner in which it was employed.”

(“The End of the Imperial Japanese Navy” by Masanori Ito, page 196.)

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Were there limitations or issues with the Kaiten?
title: Were there limitations or issues with the Kaiten?
text:
One problem was that the Kaiten could only dive to 80 meters (264 feet) while the submarines carrying the Kaiten could dive to 100 meters (325 feet). That meant that the depth of the submarine was limited by the Kaiten. Another was that the Kaiten was often unstable and training at 40 knots was “extremely difficult” and accidents were not infrequent.”

(“The Japanese Submarine Force and World War II” by Carl Boyd and Akihiko Yoshida, page 168-169.)

Although they may have had a long range for a torpedo, the range of the Kaiten was short compared to a submarine. They had a telephone connection to the mother submarine and a gyroscope, but lacked sonar, radio and navigation equipment. That meant it was difficult for the Kaiten to be truly effective. (“Submarines of the Imperial Japanese Navy” by Dorr Carpenter and Norman Polmar, page 137.)

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Were the Kaiten “suicide submarines”?
title: Were the Kaiten “suicide submarines”?
text:
There are indications that the pilots theoretically had an option to escape the Kaiten before it exploded. “They were allowed to build a prototype with the understanding that a means be provided for the pilot to be ejected before the torpedo struck.” (“Submarines of the Imperial Japanese Navy” by Dorr Carpenter and Norman Polmar, page 137.)

That may not have been practical. The Kaiten was traveling at 40 knots and it was very difficult, if not impossible for a pilot to escape. In any case, being as close to the target as the Kaiten pilot was expected to be, the explosion would likely have killed him even if he got free. For comparison, many survivors of sinking ships later died from the concussion of depth charges while they were in the water. The Kaiten warhead was much bigger than that of a depth charge leaving the pilot with an even smaller chance of survival. As a result, the Kaiten may not have been designed as a suicide submarine, but it almost certainly turned out to be so.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How did Pampanito rescue POWs?
title: How did Pampanito rescue POWs?
text:
Pampanito pulled 73 Allied prisoners of war out of the South China Sea in September 1944. It is the event she is best remembered for, and it began with a tragedy she was part of.

On 12 September 1944, Pampanito was operating in the South China Sea with Growler and Sealion, a wolf pack the crews called "Ben's Busters." They attacked a Japanese convoy running from Singapore to Japan. What none of the American crews knew was that two of the transports, Rakuyo Maru and Kachidoki Maru, were carrying more than 2,000 British and Australian prisoners of war, survivors of the Burma-Thailand railway. Sealion torpedoed Rakuyo Maru. Pampanito torpedoed Kachidoki Maru. Both ships sank, and the prisoners went into the water.

Three days later, on 15 September, Pampanito came back through the area and found men clinging to rafts and wreckage, covered in oil, many too weak to move. The crew realized who they were. Pampanito pulled 73 men aboard. Sealion, Barb, and Queenfish, called in by radio, rescued more: Sealion took 54, Queenfish 18, and Barb 14. Between the four boats, they saved 159 men. (“Silent Victory” by Clay Blair Jr.)

A submarine had no room for 73 extra men. The crew gave up their bunks, cut up clothing for the survivors, and fed them slowly. Pharmacist's Mate Maurice Demers worked without rest treating oil ingestion, exposure, malnutrition, and wounds. Pampanito ran for Saipan and delivered the survivors on 20 September. (“Silent Victory” by Clay Blair Jr., and the Dictionary of American Naval Fighting Ships entry for Pampanito, US Navy.)

Many more prisoners were not found. Some were picked up by Japanese ships and returned to captivity; hundreds died in the water. The rescue is remembered because of what the crews did once they understood what had happened, and because it is one of the few times in the Pacific war that submarine crews met, face to face, the people on the other end of a torpedo.
category: Attacks and Battles, Small and Large

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How did submariners sink the boat?
title: How did submariners sink the boat?
text: Submarine sailors did not want to “sink” their own submarine. Sinking usually meant putting a vessel on the bottom of the ocean and that was reserved for enemy ships. Sub sailors spoke of “diving” or “submerging” their own boat.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How did the boat submerge?
title: How did the boat submerge?
text:
When the chief of the watch opens the vents on the ballast tanks, water starts to fill the tanks. That is because the tanks are open on the bottom. (Previously, there were valves on the bottom but they had been removed for faster diving.) Since the ballast tanks were partly submerged already, water rushes in at the bottom of the tanks and the boat gets heavier.

The crew sets the bow and stern planes on dive and the boat takes on a down angle. Forward motion is now driving the boat deeper.

The negative tank was already full while on the surface. It was intended to help the boat to submerge more quickly. It provided additional weight forward of amidships, pulling the bow down. It was normally blown “to the mark” as the submarine reached periscope depth.

The negative tank could also be flooded again to get deeper quickly, typically from periscope depth, in case of an emergency. It would be blown “to the mark” again once the boat was at a safe depth.

NOTE: Blowing the negative tank to the mark meant blowing most of the water out of the tank. The mark is a point on a gauge or sight glass indicating that a consistent amount of water remains in the tank. A known amount of water remains so that high-pressure air wasn’t wasted and there was no air bubble escaping from the tank.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What steps did the crew need to take to submerge the boat?
title: What steps did the crew need to take to submerge the boat?
text:
Again, the simplest description is that they filled the ballast tanks with water to make the boat heavier. That would get the submarine near to neutral buoyancy. In addition, they used the bow and stern planes to put a down angle on the submarine so that their forward motion took them deeper into the water. When they reached the desired depth, they took the down angle off the boat.

However, there was much more to diving the submarine than that. Many different steps had to be completed, mostly at the same time, to dive the boat quickly:

  • The officer of the deck on the bridge sounded the diving alarm twice and announced “Dive, dive” over the 1MC announcing system.
  • The chief of the watch opened the ballast tank vents.
  • The engines were shut down.
  • The engine exhaust valves were closed.
  • The air intake flapper valves in the engine rooms were closed.
  • One machinist mate moved from an engine room to the control room to man the trim manifold.
  • A machinist mate from the other engine room moved to the control room to man the air manifold.
  • The electricians in the maneuvering room took the generators off line.
  • The electricians switched the power source to the battery.
  • The lookouts came down to the bridge from their perches on the periscope shears and proceeded through the hatch to the conning tower and on down to the control room.
  • The lookouts rigged out the bow planes and manned the bow and stern planes.
  • The bow and stern planes were set to full dive position as long as the propellers are not raised out of the water by the down angle on the boat.
  • The officer of the deck verified that no one was left topside.
  • The OOD then dropped down into the conning tower and pulled the bridge hatch shut behind him.
  • The quartermaster dogged (secured) the bridge hatch shut.
  • The OOD reported to the new officer of the deck, submerged, that the bridge was clear. He then proceeded to the control room and became the diving officer.
  • When the engines were shut down, the chief of the watch shut the main induction valve hydraulically. This was the 36-inch valve aft of the conning tower that fed air primarily to the engine rooms.
  • The cook or mess cook locked the main induction valve shut once it was closed.
  • The chief of the watch monitored the “Christmas tree” looking for all the red lights (open valves or hatches) to go green (closed) See below for the description of the Christmas tree..
  • The chief of the watch reported the status of the Christmas tree to the diving officer. Usually, it was already a green board by the time the diving officer arrived in the control room, indicating that all critical valves and hatches were closed.
  • When the boat was at or passing through periscope depth, the chief of the watch would “blow negative to the mark.” See below for information on the negative tank.
  • Once the boat was submerged and leveled off at the desired depth, the diving officer worked to get the boat to neutral buoyancy or neutral trim quickly, so the speed of the boat could be decreased if desired. At times, higher speed might have been needed so the planes had more effect in keeping the boat at the desired depth. At neutral buoyancy, the planes weren’t needed to maintain depth and could be at 0 degrees, with no up or down angle on the boat.

All of this happened at once or in rapid succession. The goal during WW2, and after, was to submerge the boat to periscope depth within 30 seconds and to be able to be at 150 feet within one minute. Most of the above steps had to be completed in 15 seconds or less to allow the boat to be at periscope depth in 30 seconds.

Modern submarines take much longer to submerge. A YouTube video shows a missile submarine taking about six minutes to dive. However, modern boats normally only dive once after leaving port and they do so in safe waters. As a result, there is no urgency like there was during WW2 war patrols.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How did they learn to do all of the steps in the right order to dive the boat?
title: How did they learn to do all of the steps in the right order to dive the boat?
text:
The same way that musicians get to Carnegie Hall – practice, practice, practice. Experienced crewmen had probably submerged submarines hundreds of times. They trained the new submariners, a few at a time, in how to do their tasks so all of these steps were done quickly and efficiently.

“It was only when they did this thing as a sort of second nature and in teamwork with everybody else that they can be called a first-class crew. Such a routine as that was not learned overnight nor out of books.” (“Battle Below” by Robert J. Casey; Bobbs-Merrill Company; New York; 1945.)

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What information will be helpful for the rest of this category?
title: What information will be helpful for the rest of this category?
text:
Here are some things that may be helpful. Submariners already speak a strange language. That gets even worse when explaining something that many people find very strange: deliberately submerging a perfectly intact vessel only to bring it back up to the surface later.

The next questions address the concepts of buoyancy and a few definitions such as the planes and ballast tanks.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What is buoyancy?
title: What is buoyancy?
text:
Buoyancy is the force that pushes up on a vessel. Merriam-Webster defines it as the upward force exerted by a liquid or gas upon a body in it or on it.

Perhaps we can think of it as the force that the water exerts as it tries to resume its normal position that the ship has displaced. Buoyancy is what keeps ships on the surface as long as buoyancy exceeds gravity.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What is neutral buoyancy or neutral trim?
title: What is neutral buoyancy or neutral trim?
text: This is the state where the buoyancy forces pushing the boat up equals the forces of gravity pushing it down. In this condition, a submarine hovers at the current depth, neither rising nor settling in the water. This is the desired state since it was easier to dive quickly and reach or maintain the desired depth safely.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What were the bow and stern planes?
title: What were the bow and stern planes?
text:
These were small wing-like structures at the front and back of the boat that rotated up and down. They were used to change and maintain depth while moving through the water. The bow planes were rigged up to the side of the boat when on the surface. (The starboard bow plane on the USS Pampanito is visible from the pier.) The stern planes were always rigged out and were protected by guards. They were under water and not normally visible.

The bow planes were normally used for small changes in depth. Perhaps the captain or officer of the deck wanted to see something farther away. That meant that the periscope needed to be higher. They couldn’t just raise the periscope or the officer wouldn’t have been able to reach the optics. Instead, they decreased the depth, raising the whole submarine.

Stern planes put an angle on the boat, up or down. Stern planes were used for larger changes in depth, for example from 63 feet (periscope depth) to 300 feet. That way, the forward motion of the boat generated the change more quickly. It was similar to an aircraft taking off or landing.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What were ballast tanks?
title: What were ballast tanks?
text: Ballast tanks were tanks that would be filled with sea water when submerging the submarine. They provided the additional weight the boat needed to submerge.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Where were the main ballast tanks?
title: Where were the main ballast tanks?
text: The main ballast tanks were on the side and below the pressure hull. They were mixed among the fuel tanks and could be seen on the side of the boat. The outside of the ballast tanks was made of thinner steel than the pressure hull since they were not subject to sea pressure. Because they were open on the bottom, pressure inside the tanks increased the same as the pressure of the surrounding sea.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Were there other ballast tanks?
title: Were there other ballast tanks?
text:
Yes, there were specialty ballast tanks including the bow buoyancy tank, the safety tank and the negative tank.

The bow buoyancy tank was also outside the pressure hull and was flooded along with the main ballast tanks. It provided added lift when surfacing and added downward momentum when diving since it was located just behind the bow.

The safety tank was inside the pressure hull and held about as much water as the conning tower. It was normally full of water. Should the conning tower be seriously damaged and flooded, the safety tank could be blown dry to get the boat close to neutral trim again. It was also used to offset flooding elsewhere in the boat. The safety tank was rarely blown dry.

The negative tank was also inside the pressure hull. With this tank, the crew usually did not have to race toward the bow when submerging quickly as the German sailors often did, as seen in the movies. As described above, it was located forward of amidships and provided downward momentum when diving.

There were also fuel ballast tanks. These were on the side of the pressure hull, like the main ballast tanks and normal fuel tanks. They held fuel at the start of a patrol, but could be reconfigured as ballast tanks after the all fuel in them had been used. When used as ballast tanks, they allowed the boat to ride higher and more efficiently on the surface and they helped the boat dive more quickly.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What was the Christmas tree?
title: What was the Christmas tree?
text:
The Christmas tree was a panel of lights at the chief of the watch’s station. It displayed the status of critical valves and hatches. A red light meant the valve or hatch was open. A green light indicated that it was closed, as it needed to be in order to dive safely. A completely “green board” was critical to diving.

The panel is not shaped like a tree. The name comes from the colors used.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How deep did these submarines go?
title: How deep did these submarines go?
text:
The prewar classes of these submarines were tested to a depth of 250 feet. This included the Porpoise, Perch, Salmon, Sargo and Tambor classes which were slightly smaller than boats like the Pampanito. The boats the U. S. built just before and during the war did go deeper. The Gato class was tested to 300 feet. The Balao and Tench classes were tested to about 400 feet. The Pampanito is a Balao class boat.

Test depth was not the same as design depth. Design depth would be about 50% deeper. In other words, the design depth of the Gato boats would be 450 feet. For the Balao and Tench boats, it would be 600 feet. Fortunately, the design depth was a conservative estimate. Many of these boats did go deeper than design depth, often unwillingly. Fortunately, the boats were built well and were often able to survive the greater depth. Of course, we only know about the boats that made it back to the surface.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How was depth measured, relative to which part of the submarine?
title: How was depth measured, relative to which part of the submarine?
text: The depth of the submarine was measured from the keel or bottom. Periscope depth was around 63 feet. That meant that the bottom of the submarine was 63 feet below the surface but the periscope could still be extended to be able to see above the surface.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What did it mean to rig the submarine for dive?
title: What did it mean to rig the submarine for dive?
text: It meant that certain valves and tanks were configured so that the submarine was able to dive when desired. For example, the safety tank and negative tank were full of water. Various safety valves were opened.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Why did submarines need to rig for dive?
title: Why did submarines need to rig for dive?
text: Some valves and other fittings had been secured when the boat came into port. This prevented errors that could have submerged the boat at the pier. For example, ballast tank vents would be secured to prevent water from filling those tanks. That needed to be changed so that the vents could be opened when it was time to dive.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What was the diving officer’s checklist?
title: What was the diving officer’s checklist?
text:
The diving officer’s checklist is to ensure that the rig for dive checklists for each compartment had been completed.

When going back to sea, the various configurations needed to be reversed. The routine was that a sailor would use the “rig for dive” checklist for a given space, and set everything to the configuration that allowed to boat to submerge safely. Then one of the officers would use that same checklist for that compartment to confirm that everything was set properly. At that point, the officer would notify the control room that the space was “rigged for dive.” Every space on the diving officer’s checklist had to be confirmed and marked before the boat could submerge.

The diving officer’s checklist also includes settings for five items in addition to each of the compartments.

  • Safety and Negative Tanks were flooded.
  • Hull Ventilation valves.
  • Flood valves and vents.
  • Hull openings.
  • Radio trunk.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Were the main ballast tanks always full when submerged?
title: Were the main ballast tanks always full when submerged?
text:
Normally, yes. The main ballast tanks were full of water when the boat was fully submerged. However, some dives did not use all of the ballast tanks. For example, the captain might only want to go to “radar depth”. In other words, he wanted to be able to use the radar while showing as little of the boat as possible. As a result, he didn’t want the boat fully submerged. A ballast tank may not be full of water. The radar masts had to be out of the water so they were still operational. The rest of the boat would be submerged and very difficult to see at a distance.

The captain might also want the decks just to be awash for some operations such as launching small boats or bringing swimmers back aboard. In these cases, a few ballast tanks would remain dry or only partially filled.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — When did the boats do a trim dive?
title: When did the boats do a trim dive?
text:
A trim dive was particularly important for the first dive after leaving port to make sure the boat had been compensated for the recent weight changes. There was normally a trim dive each day while in transit to and from the patrol area. The weight of the boat would have decreased because of the food that was consumed, any ammunition used for target practice, supplies that were used, and so on. That was offset by the increased weight of the boat as fuel was used.

NOTE: Yes, the boat got heavier as fuel was used. As diesel was burned in the engines, it was replaced by the compensating system feeding sea water into the bottom of the fuel tanks. This allowed the fuel tanks to remain at sea pressure, similar to the main ballast tanks. Sea water is about 1.5 pounds per gallon heavier than diesel fuel.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did they have to calculate the change in the trim after taking on supplies?
title: Did they have to calculate the change in the trim after taking on supplies?
text:
Absolutely. The change needed to be calculated the night before going to sea. This was done by the officer on duty on the last night in port. It was important enough that it was also checked by another officer. Then the duty officer who did the calculations was the diving officer for the trim dive the next day, for added motivation.

The calculation needed to include any crew members, and their gear, coming aboard or leaving the boat. An average number was used for the weight of a sailor and his gear. The calculation also included any added ammunition, food or supplies, and any changes to the number or types of torpedoes. The calculation also needed to include the decreased weight from taking on fuel which replaced the heavier sea water in the fuel tanks.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Why did the weight of the submarine matter?
title: Why did the weight of the submarine matter?
text:
The objective in WW2 was to have the submerged submarine weigh as much as the water that it displaced. In that condition, the captain could order the propellers stopped. When the boat stopped moving, the bow and stern planes had no effect on depth. If it was in neutral buoyancy, the boat would not rise or settle.

That was important to the safe operation of the submarine:

  • The boat could submerge quickly when needed.
  • It could submerge safely, without going deeper than intended.
  • It was easier to maintain depth while submerged.
  • It was far easier to maintain desired periscope depth without showing too much of the scope or dipping it. Obviously, this was very important during an attack.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Why did the weight of the submarine, or trim, change?
title: Why did the weight of the submarine, or trim, change?
text:
The weight of any ship changed as it was operating. Fuel was used, food was eaten, supplies were used and ammunition was expended. All of that made the ship lighter. Resupplying, in port or at sea, replaced some or most of that weight. The weight of submarines also changed for those same reasons.

However, submarines were different in a couple important ways. The most important difference was that the weight of the boat mattered much more. If a cruiser got much lighter, it might just ride higher and more efficiently. If a submarine got lighter, it might have had problems submerging quickly or staying submerged. The boat might have needed to add some water to the trim tanks to offset the weight loss.

NOTE: Surface ships could have problems if they got too light. They might have had problems riding out a big storm unless they took on some ballast water for stability.

Another difference is that submarines actually got heavier as they burned fuel as described above. Fuel was burned when the boat was on the surface, and it was important to be mindful of that when diving the next time. This design was very helpful in that the weight gained by burning fuel helped offset the weight loss from other changes.

A third difference is that the salinity and temperature of the water also mattered much more to submarines. If the water was less dense, as when the water was warmer or mixed with fresh river water, the submarine weighed the same but appeared to be heavier. Again, the same thing happened to surface ships but didn’t usually matter as much.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How did they adjust the weight or displacement of the submarine?
title: How did they adjust the weight or displacement of the submarine?
text:
Submarines have trim tanks. These are internal tanks that the diving officer uses to add water, pump it out, or move it fore and aft to get to neutral buoyancy. He estimates the changes needed based on the settings of the bow and stern planes needed to maintain depth. He then has the trim manifold operator move the desired amount of water. If his estimate is correct, the boat would be in neutral buoyancy. This could easily be a multi-step process.

Again, the test is to let the boat drift to a stop so that the planes have no effect. If it doesn’t rise or settle, the boat is neutrally buoyant.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What was a trim party?
title: What was a trim party?
text:
At some point, soon after the young diving officer mastered neutral trim, the crew conducted a “trim party”. The diving officer was focused on the planes and the depth gauge. At some point, he noticed that the boat was suddenly heavy forward. He wasn’t aware of any changes. Since it didn’t resolve itself, he moved water from forward trim to aft. Then, a bit later, he would find that the boat was heavy aft. He still didn’t know the cause. After a while he moved water from after trim to forward. This would repeat, heavy forward and then aft, until the diving officer turned around and saw the ten big sailors going toward the forward torpedo room and then aft to the after torpedo room.

That was the trim party. It was, and remains, a submarine institution. It accomplished two important objectives. First, it deflated the ego of the young diving officer. More importantly, it was an object lesson about changes in the weight of the boat. For example, if the captain fired all six torpedoes forward, that was about 18,000 pounds ejected from the boat. The water filling back into the tubes and drain tanks helped offset some of that weight. But the diving officer had to react quickly to keep the boat from broaching.

We are told that trim parties continue to this day, although computerized controls may have removed most of the entertainment value. Since many diving officers today are experienced chief petty officers, they are likely to quickly figure out what’s happening.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How did the diving officer know if the boat was heavy or light?
title: How did the diving officer know if the boat was heavy or light?
text: As stated above, he would know because the men on the planes had to use up or down angles to maintain depth. The boat itself might even need to be at an up or down angle to maintain depth.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Where was the trim manifold?
title: Where was the trim manifold?
text: The trim manifold is in the control room on the port side. It is just aft of the bow and stern plane control wheels in an alcove with some radar equipment.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What were the holes or windows on the side of the submarine?
title: What were the holes or windows on the side of the submarine?
text:
These are called limber holes. They allowed the empty space below the deck and above the pressure hull to flood and drain quickly. They allowed the crew to dive the boat in 30 seconds or less and to surface quickly. Without the limber holes, the air and water would push against each other trying to get through the openings in the deck and neither would move efficiently.

NOTE: This is not the same as filling the ballast tanks. This is just filling the free space under the deck quickly so there wouldn’t be a bubble of air keeping the boat light or on the surface.

Instead, when they submerged the boat, the water flowed into that empty space through the limber holes while the air escaped through the various openings on the deck. When the boat surfaced, the opposite occurred with the water flowing out of the limber holes and the air filling the space through the deck.

When submerged, the limber holes did add drag to the boat. A smooth superstructure would have been more efficient. However, the ability to dive quickly was more important.

Modern submarines do not need limber holes since they dive only once and remain submerged most of the time they are at sea. They also do not have all the open space between the deck and the pressure hull that would need to fill with water.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Why was it important to submerge quickly?
title: Why was it important to submerge quickly?
text:
It was a matter of safety. During WW2, lookouts could spot most Japanese planes at a distance of four or five miles. That meant that, assuming the Japanese pilot spotted the submarine, at WW2 speeds he could be attacking the boat in about one minute. In that one minute, the boat wanted to be at a depth of 150 feet or more. At that depth, it would probably be below the kill radius of the Japanese depth bombs. The boat could still be damaged and would be bounced around, but it would likely survive. In order to get that deep, the submarine would need to be completely submerged in 30 seconds and headed deeper. As indicated above, many things had to be done quickly.

Prior to the war, the process took much longer and the dive itself was significantly safer. In those days, when the order was given to submerge the ship, the bridge was cleared and the hatch to the conning tower closed and dogged. Engines were shut down and air intakes and exhausts were closed. When the Christmas tree was all green, air pressure was added to the boat to verify that everything was closed. If the added pressure held, only then was the alarm sounded and the ballast tank vents opened. This obviously took much longer than the minute that they had in WW2.

U. S. submarines began to consistently use “crash dives” during WW2. The change was that the OOD would announce the dive and sound the diving alarm right away. The chief of the watch would open vents immediately and the boat would start to submerge while all the other steps were still being completed. All dives were done in this manner, even if there were no aircraft in the area. It was good practice.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Why were there different handles on vent controls for the Chief of the Watch?
title: Why were there different handles on vent controls for the Chief of the Watch?
text:
This was done so that the chief could tell them apart by feel. In normal operation, the different shapes provided confirmation that the chief had the desired valve handle even if the control room was dark. The handles were for very important valves and the shapes provided added assurance.

Different shapes were also on the air manifold used to bring the boat back to the surface. One of the main valves has a square at the end of the handle. Another has a triangle and the third had a round shape. This allows the operator to know which handle he has even if the control room is dark or full of smoke. In normal operation, the different shapes provided confirmation that the operator had the desired valve handle.

To qualify to stand this watch, the operator was blindfolded and he brought the boat to the surface.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How did they change depth when submerged?  Did they pump water in and out?
title: How did they change depth when submerged?  Did they pump water in and out?
text: No. Depth changes were done with the bow and stern planes. However, it might have been necessary to add water to the trim tanks or pump it out as a result of the depth change. Differences in temperature or salinity may have made the boats seem heavier or lighter. Trim might have needed to be adjusted to get back to neutral buoyancy.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did the crew feel the pressure when submerged?
title: Did the crew feel the pressure when submerged?
text:
The crew was not subject to sea pressure. Nor did they feel much pressure from the compression of the hull. The pressure hull kept the atmosphere inside the boat close to what it was at sea level. It was similar to, but the opposite of what you feel in an airplane. The atmosphere in an airplane is less than sea level but you don’t generally notice. The important thing was that sailors did not need to decompress when the boat came up from the depths.

There were times when air was added to the boat and that could be noticeable. For example, if many torpedoes were fired, the air and water needed for that process would be captured and brought into the boat. That added pressure to the air in boat. However, it still wasn’t enough to cause the sailors to need to decompress.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did the added pressure ever cause an issue?
title: Did the added pressure ever cause an issue?
text:
It did provide a challenge, but it wasn’t hard to solve. The situation was that the entire boat may have had a slight overpressure after firing many torpedoes. That was in the whole pressure hull that was about 16 feet in diameter and about 275 feet in length.

When the boat surfaced, it was important to get eyes on the bridge quickly, to see what sonar and the periscope may have missed. When the hatch to the bridge was opened, all of the slight overpressure in the boat tried to vent through that hatch. That was happening while a crew member was going through the hatch. It was important to not let that crew member be ejected.

The usual way to do that was to get a large, strong shipmate to hold on to the ankles of the crewman headed up on deck and keep him from being ejected. Seriously!

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did the boat make noise when going deeper?
title: Did the boat make noise when going deeper?
text: It probably did make some noise as it compressed due to the increased sea pressure. However, it soon became a normal noise. The crew didn’t need to pay much attention to normal noises. It was the unusual noises that raised concerns.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — There was a small box in the control room that recorded temperatures.  What was that for?
title: There was a small box in the control room that recorded temperatures.  What was that for?
text:
That was a bathythermograph. As the name suggests, it recorded water temperatures at various depths. Submarines changed depths regularly just to see what the temperatures were. They were looking for abrupt changes in the temperature of the water.

Those abrupt changes are called thermoclines or layers. Changes in temperature also meant changes in density and that distorted sonar. If the temperature difference was large enough, sonar was reflected and a submarine could hide below the layer. In either case, anyone above who was searching for the boat probably had an inaccurate picture of where it was.

However, if sound was being distorted or reflected by a layer, the crew may not have had an accurate picture of what was above them. Caution was advised.

The bathythermograph (BT) was first developed in 1934 by Woods Hole Oceanographic Institute. It was first tested for submarine use in 1942. It could locate a “shadow zone” for a submarine to hide in. (“USS Pampanito, Killer-Angel”, by Gregory Michno, page 66; University of Oklahoma Press; Norman, OK; 2000.)

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How long could these boats remain submerged during WW2?
title: How long could these boats remain submerged during WW2?
text:
The record during the war was just short of 38 hours by the USS Puffer (SS-268). She was a Gato class boat built by Manitowoc Shipbuilding. She was being tracked and depth charged by Japanese ASW vessels. At about 38 hours, the battery was nearly discharged, oxygen was low and CO2 was high. The captain decided that his choices were to either suffocate submerged or take a chance on surfacing and fighting it out with the Japanese ships. (The latter was usually a very poor option.) Puffer was fortunate in that the currents had carried her a few miles away from the hunters. The captain then presented the stern to the hunters so it showed the smallest profile. He was able to use an island as a backdrop to make the boat even harder to see. The boat was then able to make repairs and escape back to base.

That was the longest submergence during the war and very unusual. Normally, these boats would be on the surface each night. They wanted to recharge the battery and get fresh air in the boat. While they were on the surface, they also wanted to get a star fix and pick up their messages from the fleet broadcast. The air in the boat was the same air the crew had been breathing since they submerged. It was expected to last 16 to 18 hours. (Since most of the crew smoked cigarettes, we probably should call that 16 hours.)

There were some things that could be done to extend the air if needed. There were five or six oxygen bottles on board. There were also multiple cans of CO2 absorbent in the overheads. (Those were the cans labeled “DO NOT PAINT”.) The oxygen and CO2 absorbent would extend the air a few hours. After that, if needed, they would bleed some high-pressure air into the boat. It wasn’t fresh air, but it improved the percentages and sustained life.

But air wasn’t the only issue. The other was battery power. How long the battery could last would depend on how fast the boat was going. The battery was rated at 48 hours if the boat was going two knots. (That is about 2.25 miles per hour.) However, if they doubled the speed to four knots, they had to divide the time the battery would last by eight. It was a cubic relationship. At four knots the battery would last about six hours. Double it again to eight knots, nearly the maximum speed the boat could go submerged, and the battery would last less than one hour. It was called the “one-hour rate”.

Clearly, it was important to use the battery and air conservatively when the boat was being attacked. Slow and silent was the best way to conserve the battery and to escape. To use air more efficiently, they put all non-essential crewmen in their bunks. The men used less oxygen when resting.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did they pump out water in order to surface?
title: Did they pump out water in order to surface?
text:
The water was removed from the ballast tanks, but it wasn’t pumped out. The crew blew the water out using high-pressure air. That air was stored at 3,000 PSI in bottles in the ballast tanks. To surface, the air was stepped down to 600 PSI and dumped into the ballast tanks. Once the bridge hatch was out of the water, the high-pressure blow would be secured and the low-pressure blower was used to blow the rest of the water out of the tanks. The low-pressure blower was run until bubbles appeared from the ballast tanks. (The low-pressure blower ran at 10 PSI.) This eliminated the need to use any more of the stored high-pressure air.

The air used to surface the boat would be lost when they dove the next time. It was just vented so that the ballast tanks were filled quickly.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How did they replace the high-pressure air?
title: How did they replace the high-pressure air?
text:
They replaced the air in the storage bottles by running air compressors as needed when on the surface. There was usually enough air in the bottles to surface the boat about seven times.

There were two 3,000 PSI air compressors in the pump room below the control room. The low-pressure blower was also in the pump room. The high-pressure air manifold and the controls for the low-pressure blower are both in the control room.

It was possible to surface the boat without using any high-pressure air. The boat was driven toward the surface with the planes. Once the bridge hatch was out of the water and opened, the low-pressure blower was used to blow all of the water out of the ballast tanks. It was slower, but it worked. This was done most often when training new diving officers and lookouts to submerge quickly. There was enough high-pressure air in the tanks to surface the boat multiple times in routine operations, but perhaps not enough for all those training dives.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Where was the air manifold?
title: Where was the air manifold?
text: The air manifold is in the control room on the starboard side. It is forward of the brass tubing for the low-pressure blower and aft of the electrical distribution panel.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What was the low-pressure blower?
title: What was the low-pressure blower?
text:
The low-pressure blower was located in the pump room. It took air from inside the boat, compressed it to about 10 PSI and dumped it into the ballast tanks. The manifold was in the control room just aft of the high-pressure air manifold. This allowed them to save some of the high-pressure air used to surface. This process also took some of the stale air from inside the boat and dumped it into the ballast tanks, which started refreshing the air in the boat.

The low-pressure blower was usually run until all the main ballast tanks appeared to be dry. This didn’t cost any high-pressure air and ensured that the boat was fully surfaced. When the ballast tanks were empty, the boat rode more efficiently on the surface.

As indicated above, it was possible to surface the boat using only the planes and the low-pressure blower.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Was it important to surface quickly?
title: Was it important to surface quickly?
text: Not normally. It was usually more important for the OOD (or captain) to take his time in order to surface safely. The boat would come up to periscope depth carefully. The OOD wanted to be sure that there was no danger of collision with other vessels and, in WW2, no immediate danger of attack by the enemy. Then, when they saw nothing through the periscope and heard nothing on sonar, they dumped air into the ballast tanks. They also put rise on the planes. That brought them to the surface.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did they ever want or need to surface quickly?
title: Did they ever want or need to surface quickly?
text:
Yes, there were some times when it was important to surface quickly. That would generally be when they were going to battle stations, guns in WW2. The most common example was when they were going to use the guns against small shipping late in the war. The smaller ships were not worth the cost of an expensive torpedo. In addition, since torpedoes would normally need to run at a depth of at least six feet, they would likely pass under these small ships without exploding.

In these situations, coming up to periscope depth was still done carefully. Then, when it was nearly time to surface, some air was added to the ballast tanks while the bow and stern planes were holding the boat down. Then, when the command to surface was given, the planes went to full rise and more air was dumped into the ballast tanks. The goal was to get the first rounds fired in less than a minute after the order to surface was given. The target was likely to be shooting back, so speed and surprise were of the essence.

Many things needed to be done to fire the first rounds in less than a minute:

  • Enough air had to be dumped into the ballast tanks to get the main deck out of the water.
  • Gun crews needed to open hatches and assemble on deck.
  • The guns needed to be unsecured. (They were tied down so they would not make noise when submerged.)
  • Ready storage for ammunition had to be opened. The ammunition was in the barrel shaped structures around the sail.
  • The gun(s) had to be loaded with the ready ammunition.
  • The gun(s) had to be aimed.
  • The gun(s) would be fired when the boat was steady enough.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What else was the high-pressure air used for?
title: What else was the high-pressure air used for?
text:
High-pressure air was used for many purposes on the boat. It was used to:

  • Charge the air flasks in the Mark 14 steam torpedoes to 2,800 PSI.
  • Blow the water out of the main ballast tanks to surface. The air was stepped down to 600 PSI for this purpose.
  • Launch torpedoes from the tubes. This air was stepped down to 300 PSI.
  • Roll over the diesel engines to start them. The air was stepped down to 50 PSI.
  • The air could be bled into the boat if needed when the oxygen content got too low or the CO2 content got too high. This pressurized atmosphere inside the boat somewhat and the air was far from fresh. However, it supported life.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did the crew need to decompress when coming shallow?
title: Did the crew need to decompress when coming shallow?
text: No. The pressure inside the boat had increased only slightly and was hardly noticeable. There was no need for decompression.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What was the big handle near gyrocompass table?
title: What was the big handle near gyrocompass table?
text: That was a manual backup valve for the negative tank. Remember the rule: everything that was important on the submarine had a backup – except for the ice cream machine.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What did the Pampanito do after commissioning and on the way to Pearl Harbor, Hawaii?
title: What did the Pampanito do after commissioning and on the way to Pearl Harbor, Hawaii?
text:
NOTE: The following information in bold text is summarized from the War Patrol Reports by LCDR Summers.  The summarized information from “USS Pampanito, Killer-Angel” by Gregory Michno and “Silent Victory” by Clay Blair Jr. is in italics and indented.

 6 November 1943 and following: LCDR Charles B. Jackson was in command at commissioning.

The boat completed various tests and sea trials.  They also completed a practice patrol.  Minor issues were identified, the most significant of which was a noisy propeller shaft.  Repairs would be completed at the Electric Boat Company at Groton, CT.

Training was conducted at Newport, RI for torpedo maintenance and firing.

The repairs on the propeller shaft bearing were completed in Groton which required 11 days.

There often was tension between LCDR Jackson, the captain, and LCDR Summers, the executive officer or XO.  There were more than the usual discipline problems which Summers blamed on Jackson.  Some of the crew thought Jackson would not “cut it”.

5 January 1944: Left New London for Pearl Harbor, T. H. (Territory of Hawaii).

Two nights before arriving at Panama, in nearly the same place as the USS Dorado (SS-248) was lost three months earlier, the bow of the submarine cut through the track of a torpedo wake.  Pampanito dove.  Later, sonar heard a submarine surface.  The two boats went in opposite directions.  (This was normal procedure at the time due to the limitations of sonar and torpedoes.)

24 January: Arrived at Panama Canal Zone.  Undergoing repairs there until 29 January

About one week into the trip from the Canal Zone to Hawaii, Pampanito submerged at high speed.  LCDR Jackson had put two inexperienced men on the planes to help them qualify in submarines.  The boat took a steep down angle, went past four hundred feet and was still going down.  The captain froze.  Two chiefs added air to forward ballast tanks.  Then the boat took a steep up angle.  Not everyone remembered the incident, but LCDR Summers did.

14 February: Arrived at Pearl Harbor.  Undergoing repairs on propeller shaft bearings again until 22 February.  Also installed new equipment.  Pre-patrol training.

There was a circular run by a MK 14.  (It almost certainly was an exercise torpedo.)  Pampanito went to flank speed and hard rudder to avoid the torpedo.  This was not LCDR Jackson’s fault, but it was another mark against him.  In training runs, he again froze.  The evaluations of Jackson’s training trials were less than satisfactory.

6 March: Change of command to LCDR Paul (Pete) Summers.

LCDR Jackson was furious when the orders came but he was relieved of his command.  Jackson went to work for CAPT Charles “Swede” Momsen and LCDR Summers assumed command of Pampanito.  An unspecified illness was given as the reason.  “Silent Victory”, by Clay Blair Jr., states that it was due to exhaustion.  (Blair, page 577).

Summers, as the new captain, seemed to think that everything would suddenly be fine.  That didn’t quite match the view of the crew.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Does this category cover all of the history of the USS Pampanito (SS-383)?
title: Does this category cover all of the history of the USS Pampanito (SS-383)?
text: This category covers the history of the Pampanito other than the war patrols. That information is included in a separate category, “Pampanito War Patrols”. This was done in an attempt to make the history more manageable.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Where was the Pampanito built?
title: Where was the Pampanito built?
text: The USS Pampanito (SS-383) was built at the Portsmouth Naval Shipyard (PNSY). Although it is named for Portsmouth, the PNSY shipyard isn’t in New Hampshire. It is located across the Piscataqua River from Portsmouth in Kittery, Maine.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — When was the Pampanito built?
title: When was the Pampanito built?
text:
Construction was started on 15 March 1943. It is customary on larger ships to say that the keel was laid when construction began. However, submarines are built differently since they are round. They don’t have a wide, flat bottom although they still have a keel. As a result, they are built in sections and then the sections are welded together.

At the time, some shipyards would start two or three submarines together in a drydock and finish them at about the same time. Pampanito was started in the same drydock with the USS Picuda (SS-382). The boats were launched together on 12 July 1943. That means that the hulls were completed enough so that they would float and many of the major systems were installed. The boats could then be completed alongside a pier.

The Picuda was finished before the Pampanito. Picuda was commissioned on 16 October 1943. She remained in the Portsmouth Navy Shipyard to complete fitting out until 18 November 1943, when she commenced sea trials. Pampanito was commissioned on 6 November and began sea trials on 29 November 1943.

Generally, after sea trials, there were construction issues to be fixed. For Pampanito, those corrections were completed at the Electric Boat Company in Groton, CT. Then it was on to Pearl Harbor on the island of Oahu, Territory of Hawaii (TH) to prepare for war patrols.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How was the Pampanito named?
title: How was the Pampanito named?
text:
Submarines were named after sea creatures. Many were named after fish such as the Perch, Bullhead, Cod, Flying Fish and Halibut. Some were named after marine mammals such as the Whale, Porpoise, Finback (a whale), Sea Cat (an otter) and Sealion. And others were named after unusual sea creatures, such as the Seahorse and Skate.

The Pampanito is named after a smaller version of the pompano fish. The name is Spanish for “little pompano”. A pampanito is a flat fish that is about 18 inches long and weighs a little less than 3 pounds. It is a rather mild-mannered fish that is brown or black on top and silver underneath.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How much did the USS Pampanito cost?
title: How much did the USS Pampanito cost?
text: It appears that WW2 submarines built in Navy shipyards were estimated to cost about $5 million during WW2. That would be the equivalent of about $100 million in 2025. The contracts with Navy shipyards were for time and materials, not fixed price.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Why does Pampanito have the number 383?
title: Why does Pampanito have the number 383?
text:
That means that Pampanito was the 383rd submarine ordered by the US Navy. The first mechanically powered submarine ordered by the U. S. was the USS Holland (SS-1), purchased in 1901.

Although the Pampanito was the 383rd submarine ordered, that does not mean that it was the 383rd submarine built. In WW2, submarines were ordered in groups. Contracts for groups of submarines were let to the various yards building the boats. As a result, the boats were built in a sequence different from that in which they were ordered. In this case, boats in the contract to the Portsmouth Naval Shipyard (Picuda, SS-382 and Pampanito, SS-383) were started more than a year before the last of the boats in a prior contract to the Electric Boat Company, such as the USS Diodon (SS-349) and USS Dogfish (SS-350), were begun. In addition, ten boats in a prior Electric Boat contract were cancelled. There was also a prior contract for 20 Manitowoc boats, not all of which would be built.

Late in the war, contracts for over 100 submarines were cancelled. Currently, the newest submarine commissioned, on 28 March 2026, was the USS Massachusetts (SSN-798). She was the 798th submarine for which a contract was signed but many fewer were built.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What class of submarine is the Pampanito?
title: What class of submarine is the Pampanito?
text: Pampanito is a Balao class boat. She has the thicker hull and can dive deeper than the preceding class of Gato submarines. However, she is sometimes called a Gato class boat by those who lump the Gato and Balao (and even the Tench) classes together because they are so similar. All three classes are the same length and width and have a similar layout.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How large is the Pampanito?
title: How large is the Pampanito?
text:
The Pampanito is just short of 312 feet long. She is 27 feet at her widest. That includes the ballast and fuel tanks outside and below the pressure hull. The actual pressure hull is about 16 feet in diameter in most places and doesn’t extend the full length of the boat. It is about 280 or 290 feet long and is tapered at the ends. The torpedo tubes are placed only partly inside the pressure hull. That explains much of the difference between the length of the pressure hull and the overall length of the boat. The conning tower, above the main pressure hull, is only about 10 feet in diameter and 20 feet long.

When fully configured and loaded, the Pampanito displaces (weighs) about 1,550 tons on the surface and about 2,400 tons submerged. Currently Pampanito is much lighter. She does not have batteries, a full complement of torpedoes, 80 men with their personal effects or any food on board. She has very little fuel so most of the fuel tanks are empty. As a result, she now weighs less and rides higher in the water than she did during the war.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How thick is the hull?
title: How thick is the hull?
text: The main pressure hull is 7/8 inch (2.22 cm) thick. The conning tower is one inch (2.54 cm) thick for added protection since it is closer to the surface and more vulnerable. The Balao boats were also a higher tensile steel than the Gato predecessors, which had hulls of 11/16 inch (1.75 cm) steel.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How deep could the Pampanito go?
title: How deep could the Pampanito go?
text: That sounds like a simple question but the answer is a bit more complex. Balao boats, such as the Pampanito, were designed for 600 feet but would be tested only to around 400 feet. 600 feet is known as the calculated crush depth. (Think of that as the depth where the “shipyard guarantee” runs out.) Limiting the normal operating depth to 400 feet gave the captain and crew a 50% margin of error. However, we know that the Pampanito was at or below 600 feet on at least two different occasions. She is likely to have been down at least to around 650 feet at one time, but the deep depth gauges only go to 600 feet. Pressure gauges could be used to estimate depths past 600 feet.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — How fast could the Pampanito go?
title: How fast could the Pampanito go?
text:
Like most Balao class boats, Pampanito had a top speed of around 21 knots on the surface (about 24 mph or 39 km/h) and 9 knots submerged (about 10.5 mph or 16.5 km/h). However, there were caveats.

Surface speeds depended on the number of engines on the line. A speed of 21 knots required flank speed with all four engines on line. A more typical (and more efficient) cruising speed was standard speed on two engines or about 12 knots. A captain would order additional engines on the line if he needed to go faster.

Submerged speeds determined how long the battery would last. The maximum speed of 9 knots depletes the battery in less than an hour. It is called the “one hour rate”. However, if the boat was just going 2 knots, the battery was rated at 48 hours. The relationship of speed to battery was cubic. If the speed was doubled, battery duration was divided by eight.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Who was the captain of the Pampanito?
title: Who was the captain of the Pampanito?
text:
Pampanito had four captains in the short time she was in commission.

Her first captain, taking command at commissioning, was LCDR Charles B. Jackson Jr. Jackson commanded the Pampanito through sea trials and the ensuing repairs. He also took the boat to Pearl Harbor. However, at Pearl Harbor, he was not successful in pre-patrol training. He was relieved and the cause was said to be due to illness. Clay Blair Jr., in “Silent Victory” described the illness as exhaustion.

LCDR Paul E. (Pete) Summers had been executive officer on the Pampanito under Jackson. He fleeted up to captain when Jackson was relieved. He took the boat out for five of the six war patrols. He had requested a break after three patrols and was relieved for the fourth. Summers resumed command for the fifth and sixth patrols. He was formally relieved in normal rotation after the sixth patrol when Pampanito went into the shipyard in early May of 1945. Summers was then assigned as captain of the new construction USS Cusk (SS-348). The war ended before the Cusk needed to make a combat patrol.

CAPT Frank (Mike) W. Fenno Jr. was a much-decorated officer who had commanded the USS Trout (SS-202) and the USS Runner (SS-275). He was commanding a division of submarines in Hawaii when he volunteered to take the Pampanito out for her fourth patrol.

CDR Donald A. Scherer had been captain of the USS Permit for her last three war patrols. Permit (SS-178) was then retired for training duty. CDR Scherer was assigned to relieve CDR Summers and assumed command of the Pampanito while the boat was still in overhaul. The war ended while CDR Scherer and the Pampanito were in Hawaii preparing for a seventh war patrol. He then brought the boat to San Francisco to be decommissioned and placed in the reserve fleet at Mare Island.

Summers and Fenno were both decorated captains. Jackson had earned a Silver Star for bravery during a rescue while serving as a LT aboard the USS Spearfish (SS-190) in 1942.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Where did the Pampanito serve?
title: Where did the Pampanito serve?
text:
Pampanito completed all six of her war patrols in the Pacific. After she was built at the Portsmouth Naval Shipyard and had completed her shakedown, sea trials and repairs, she sailed through the Panama Canal and then on to Hawaii. Her first war patrol was off the island of Yap in the Caroline Islands. Her second was off the east coast of Japan. The last four patrols were in the area of the South China Sea.

After her sixth war patrol in April of 1945, Pampanito came to San Francisco for an overhaul. This was for a major upkeep with equipment upgrades and was normal after six war patrols. Pampanito was back in Hawaii, training for her seventh war patrol when the Japanese surrendered in mid-August of 1945.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — When were the war patrols and how long were they?
title: When were the war patrols and how long were they?
text:
Most of Pampanito’s war patrols ranged from 42 to 63 days. However, her fifth patrol was only a bit over two weeks. (Sources differ on the exact length.) She was almost out of torpedoes and had a very short transit to her next port, Subic Bay in the Philippines.

From the war patrol reports:

  • The first war patrol was from 15 March to 8 May 1944.
  • The second war patrol was from 3 June to 23 July 1944.
  • The third war patrol was from 17 August to 28 September 1944.
  • The fourth war patrol was from 28 October to 30 December 1944.
  • The fifth war patrol was from 23 January to 12 February 1945.
  • The sixth war patrol was from 25 February to 24 April 1945.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did anyone die while on the Pampanito?
title: Did anyone die while on the Pampanito?
text:
One of the rescued POWs, John Campbell, a Scot and a Gordon Highlander, succumbed to his injuries and poor health while en route to Saipan. He died on 16 September 1944, the day after he was rescued, as a free man. He was buried at sea with dignity.

None of the crew perished while serving on the Pampanito.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did the captains know about the POWs on the Japanese ships?
title: Did the captains know about the POWs on the Japanese ships?
text:
The submarine captains did not. The sources of the ULTRA intelligence were not made known to submarine captains. There were two dangers in telling them. One was that they might give up the information under torture if captured. The other was that captains would behave differently if they knew, and that behavior could tip off the Japanese that their codes had been broken. Refer to the movie “Imitation Game” about the breaking of the Enigma codes.

It is possible that the code breakers knew of the cargo before the attacks. They certainly knew about the POWs from Japanese message traffic after the ships had been sunk.

It is useful to remember that the Japanese only needed to request safe passage for the POWs or put them on hospital ships and the U. S. would not have attacked. We did grant safe passage to such ships during the war, but Japan normally did not make requests until late in the war. At that time they began requesting safe passage for a number of vessels that they said were hospital ships. Safe passage was granted even though the U. S. was skeptical.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Is there more information about the rescue on the third war patrol?
title: Is there more information about the rescue on the third war patrol?
text:
Yes, there is. A supplemental narrative to the war patrol report was submitted by Pampanito with greater detail. It is quoted, with minimal editing, as follows.

On the afternoon of 15 September 1944, while patrolling on the surface on an easterly heading from HAINAN ISLAND in the South China Sea, at Latitude 18° 42' N., Longitude 114° 00' E., the O.O.D. and bridge lookouts sighted a lifeboat and a large quantity of debris floating on the surface of a calm sea. This spot was a little to the north of where an enemy convoy had been intercepted and attacked by our submarines on the night of 11-12 September 1944. There was a possibility of the lifeboat being occupied so course was altered to go alongside, only to find it abandoned. At this time, 1610(I), a lookout reported that there were two rafts on the horizon with men on them. It was naturally believed that these would be Japanese, so small arms were broken out and preparations made for taking prisoners.

On the approach to the first raft, which was a makeshift affair of hatch covers and timbers, it was noted that the fifteen men it contained were thickly covered with crude-oil and were clothed very scantily, though some had nondescript hats and a few wore the regulation Japanese soldier's caps. They were waving frantically and all shouting at will so that no words could be distinguished, although one voice was finally heard to speak distinctly in English. While getting the raft alongside, orders were given to bring aboard the English-speaking man, and by the time the first line was over the amazing announcement came to the bridge, "They are British and Australian Prisoner-of-War and shipwreck survivors.”

All hands went into action immediately; those below decks sent up bales of rags and began preparing hot soup and tea in quantities; the pharmacist's mate assembled his gear for immediate treatment, and the rescue party commenced bringing the survivors aboard. The poor fellows were so frantic with joy at this unbelievable piece of good fortune that they began jumping from the raft and trying to clamber up the sides of the ship. Members of the rescue party dived over the side to make the raft fast, herded the survivors back onto the raft and aided them up to the ship's deck. The weakened condition of these men, as well as their covering of slippery crude-oil, made the actual recovery quite difficult. Some of them could help themselves, but the majority had to be lifted and dragged aboard bodily.

The next problem was to clean some of the oil from their bodies and to treat their immediate needs before sending them below. While this job was being done the second raft was reached and the true bearings taken of three others within sight. The second raft contained nine men who fortunately were comparatively free from oil, making the problem of bringing them aboard much easier. While heading for the next group, a small raft was passed close aboard with its single occupant dead with part of the head gone (Probably by a shark). Recovered third and fourth raft-loads of eleven emaciated ex-prisoners-of-war. Another small raft was sighted with one figure lying motionless on his back. He seemed to be still alive and when one of the ship's crew dived into the water with a line, he sat up, startled and started to go over the side. The man in the water persuaded him to remain seated until he could be helped aboard. This man was almost blind and in a semi-conscious condition when brought aboard and remained unconscious almost continuously until he died the following evening.

While the eleven men from the next raft were being brought aboard the after lookout reported "Three planes in formation astern". There were approximately fifty men topside at this time including bridge personnel and the rescue squad as well as many survivors who had as yet not been lowered down the hatch. Fortunately, one of the planes was seen to flap its wings proving the formation to be large birds gliding in perfect order.

This completed the rescue of all survivors in the immediate vicinity, but a bearing had been taken on a raft now out of sight to the south, so the ship was headed in that direction at high speed. At 1810, two rafts were sighted ahead and soon thirteen more survivors were being rescued. While getting the men from the last of these two rafts the high periscope watch sighted another raft at 020° T. and also what appeared to be a ship's masts bearing 037° T. at the extreme range of vision. While unable to verify this report of the raft, the ship was identified as a submarine that appeared to have a gun aft, making us very suspicious, since one of the survivors had stated that a German submarine was somewhere in this area (later proved to be SEALION with men on deck aft), we dived to periscope depth and after identifying and watching the submarine for a few minutes through the periscope and noting that it was practically dead in the water, decided that it must be the SEALION rescuing survivors. We had sent a message to her earlier requesting that she come over and assist in rescue. So surfaced and resumed searching. It was almost completely dark by this time. A single man on a small raft was seen waving what appeared to be a white flag, but he was at some time, but later proved to be his "bleached hand". He was recovered and course was set for the last raft that had been sighted before diving. This raft was luckily located in the dark and another twelve men were rescued and stowed below making a total of seventy-three (73) survivors on board.

Once below decks the main problem was the examination to determine the injuries and sicknesses. In this respect, DEMERS, M.L., PhM1c, USN, showed tireless energy and outstanding professional knowledge of the highest order. The survivors most acute need was water, which they were given in small quantities through the rags followed by hot tea, soup or broth for those who were conscious. As all these men were suffering from acute exhaustion, exposure, shock, starvation, dehydration and skin sores, their needs were many, but since the ship had necessarily to retain its military efficiency, and since it was not known what contagious diseases some of them might have, it was decided to place all but six of the most critical cases in the after torpedo room (the six were put on bunks in one corner of the after battery compartment) where, even though it was more difficult to tend their needs, they could be isolated until given a more thorough examination. One head was set aside for the use of the survivors; they were given separate eating utensils which were washed and stowed apart from those of the crew, and two officers and several crew members were assigned the nursing detail. The entire crew showed an exemplary attitude and volunteered cheerfully to do all tasks and make any sacrifices that would help the survivors in any way.

The PAMPANITO was now headed East and stayed on the surface until the next afternoon when a four engined bomber was sighted. A short dive was made and when the bomber had cleared the area, the PAMPANITO was brought to the surface and the voyage to base was continued.

At 2030, on September 16, 1944, the survivor, JOHN CAMPBELL, Lance Corporal of the Gordon Highlanders, British Army, died, and two hours later while passing through BALINTANG CHANNEL, his body was committed to the deep.

By noon of the 18th of September 1944, when rendezvous was made with the U.S.S. CASE, to receive medical aid and supplies, most of the survivors had recovered sufficiently to be on their feet and able to make their way to the forward torpedo room. This was accomplished so that our men plus a few of the healthiest survivors could do some cleaning up in the after torpedo room.

Their spirits were gratifyingly high and they enjoyed to the fullest the food allowed them, the telling of their experiences, listening to the phonograph and radio and most of all the friendliness and kind treatment so long foreign to them.

On the morning of the 20th of September 1944, land was sighted, and within a short time we were standing up the channel to the tender, U.S.S. FULTON. All survivors except five stretcher cases were by this time on deck aft, each man fully clothed and looking quite respectable.

While the small boats for the transfer were arriving, ice cream and fresh oranges were brought aboard, giving the survivors their finest treat in over two and one-half years. The five stretcher cases were moved first, then the two boats carrying the remaining sixty-seven men ashore were loaded and shoved off with cheers, thumbs-up and a mutual feeling of friendliness that will be hard to exceed anywhere.

The general condition of the survivors when rescued was critical, with every man suffering from acute exhaustion, exposure, shock, starvation, dehydration and salt sores. About seventy percent of these men had drunk sea water, urine or blood during their four days on the rafts, and nearly all were covered with fuel oil.

As the survivors were brought aboard, they were treated on deck as follows: the crude-oil was wiped and then sponged off with diesel oil, and morphine was administered to those suffering from extreme shock (15 syrettes being used in this time). As soon as emergency cleaning and shock treatment were given, the men were lowered through the after battery hatch, given a cup of hot tea, a sip of hot vegetable soup, after which each was given an eye irrigation followed by Butyn Sulfate and Boric Acid Ointment was applied to ease the irritation on the skin of each man's scrotum. This irritation being caused by the crude-oil.

Six of the more critical cases, who were given bunks in the after battery compartment, had their sores and ulcerations cleaned with Azochloramide in Triscetin 1:500 and dressed with Sulfathiazole Ointment 5%.

About one quarter of the survivors were given sedatives of Phenobarbital or Sodium Amytal, depending upon each one's condition. Three men had rather severe cases of malaria, one of whom was in a state of delirium for four hours after being rescued. These men were given Quinine Hydrochloride grs. XX followed by grs. X every four hours. Two men found to have severe Cellutitis infections were placed in bunks with parts elevated and dosed with Sulfadiazine grs. XV with Sodium Bicarbonate at four-hour intervals rather than the prescribed dose of 4 gm. of Sulfa, because of their condition. One man was found to have an injured back and a broken rib, but due to the acute tropical dermatitis infection which covered fifty percent of his body no strapping was done. This dermatitis infection was treated with Sulfathiazole Ointment covered with cotton dressing to make the man more comfortable in his bunk.

By twelve hours after the rescue every man had received an examination and had had his worse sores cleaned with Azochloramide in Triscetin 1:500 and dressed with Sulfa-thiazole Ointment 5% or Sulfadiazine powder depending on each individual's condition. Upon questioning the men, it was found that during their two and a half years of imprisonment all had had some degree of malaria; seventy percent had suffered from Pellagra or Beri Beri [sic]; fifty percent were affected by tropical dermatitis infections and all but three or four had Gingivitis or Vicents [sic] Angina. It was also learned that all had been exposed to Cholera, Dysentery, Typhus Fever, and other types of contagious diseases, so that although, during their time on board, no one showed any signs of having contracted any of these diseases, precautions were taken to keep isolated all cups, utensils, the head, etc. Within three hours after examination each survivor was receiving one cup of either water, tea with sugar and milk, cocoa or soup every hour for twenty-four hours.
