The only casualty occurred the day following the rescue. This man died of acute exhaustion, exposure, shock, dehydration and possible internal hemorrhage. He had been in a state of delirium almost continuously since being brought aboard. Intravenous injections of Dextrose and Saline Solution were attempted, but without success due to the failure to locate a vein or even a drop of blood; the injections finally being given in the buttocks, but to no avail.

From the second through the fourth day all but the six men who were critically ill were given baths, shampoo and shaves by members of the crew, while the six bed cases were bathed in their bunks. The officers and crew all donated clothing so that every survivor had underwear, trousers, shirt and socks and most had shoes or sandals.

The diet was gradually increased to include beef boullion [sic], bread and butter, chicken broth and crackers, tomato consommé [sic], egg-nog [sic], canned fruit and finally soft-boiled eggs and hash. Two multiple vitamin pills were given every fifteen hours, as well as a small amount of soft chocolate. Fruit juices, although given at first, were discontinued when they proved to be irritating.

On the final days aboard, those men with the most aggravated eye conditions were given more frequent eye irrigations followed by Sulfathiazole Ophthalmic Ointment, and all patients were given 1½ gr. of Atabrin.

By the time of transfer at our base the morning of September 20, five stretcher cases remained, although every survivor showed great improvement and was well on the way to complete recovery.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What did the Pampanito do after her sixth war patrol?
title: What did the Pampanito do after her sixth war patrol?
text:
Shortly after arriving at Pearl Harbor following the sixth patrol, Pampanito proceeded to the Bay Area in California for an overhaul. On 3 May 1945, Pampanito passed under the Golden Gate Bridge and tied up at Hunter’s Point Naval Drydock.

There is no seventh patrol report since Pampanito wouldn’t need to do one. Most of the following information is summarized from Michno’s “USS Pampanito, Killer-Angel.”

During the overhaul, Pampanito received various upgrades including a five-inch cannon and a load of the new acoustic torpedoes.

When she went into drydock, they discovered a dent in the ballast tank outboard of the maneuvering room. Something had hit the boat on the previous patrol and it wasn’t an amorous dolphin. Most of the crew were surprised by the dent, except for those who heard or saw the torpedo while they were patrolling around Wake Island.

Most of the “plank owners” (members of the original commissioning crew) had been transferred by the end of the overhaul. That included CDR Summers who had been relieved by CDR Donald Scherer. CDR Scherer had commanded the USS Permit (SS-178) for three war patrols. CDR Summers was assigned to command the new submarine USS Cusk (SS-348). Neither commander would need to make another war patrol.

Pampanito completed the overhaul at Hunter’s Point and sailed for Pearl Harbor, Hawaii on 20 July 1945.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What happened in August of 1945 while Pampanito was at Pearl Harbor?  If Pampanito was training for another patrol, why didn’t she make one?
title: What happened in August of 1945 while Pampanito was at Pearl Harbor?  If Pampanito was training for another patrol, why didn’t she make one?
text:
Pampanito was in Hawaii getting ready for a training run when the news arrived about a new kind of bomb being dropped on Hiroshima on 6 August. It was followed by another bomb on Nagasaki three days later. Most people expected that this would mean the end of the war.

On August 14th, our time, the Japanese announced their surrender. A major celebration ensued. “’Sailors at the barracks were raising Cain’ said Weaver, ‘and the sub base commander drove up in his jeep to try and quell the noise. They picked him up and threw him in the swimming pool. He crawled out, got back in his jeep, and left them to their celebration.’” (Michno, page 367.)

The rumors were that submarines would act as pickets to draw out kamikaze boats and aircraft. There was some truth to the rumors. The Navy ordered 24 submarines to be converted to radar boats. However, those boats may not have been fully ready until 1946.

Pampanito does not appear to have gotten any new equipment for radar duty. Instead, there were reports that she may have been scheduled to receive the new FM sonar for mine-detecting. In that case she may have been assigned to the Sea of Japan. She would have needed the FM sonar to transit the Tsushima Strait which was heavily mined. Then she likely would have been assigned to continue the naval blockade and provide lifeguard services for aviators. Fortunately, none of that was needed.

Three weeks after the surrender, Pampanito was on her way to San Francisco for decommissioning.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — When was the Pampanito decommissioned or taken out of service?
title: When was the Pampanito decommissioned or taken out of service?
text:
Most of the crew had been discharged or reassigned shortly after Pampanito arrived at the Mare Island Reserve Fleet. Those who remained on board were “mothballing” the boat – sealing and preserving it. Pampanito was the first of the Balao boats to be decommissioned. That occurred on 15 December 1945 while at Mare Island.

“The men had done their duty. Most of them had a hard time explaining why it was that they fought in the first place. Certainly they were patriotic, but they were not zealots. They were fighting for their country, true, but not for any idealistic reasons such as making the world safe for democracy. They fought for their families, girlfriends, wives and buddies. As one man worded it, they fought ‘for the smell of fried chicken, or a stack of Dinah Shore records on a phonograph or the right to throw pop bottles at the umpire at Ebbets Field.’ The war was an aberration – a disrupter of normality and an unpleasant task that had to be finished before they could get on with their lives. Not facetiously, they had to fight so they could quit fighting. The war was over – at least the combat part. Later would come the remembering.”

(Michno, page 368)

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What happened to the Pampanito after she was decommissioned?
title: What happened to the Pampanito after she was decommissioned?
text:
Pampanito was inactive, as part of the reserve fleet, until the 1960s when she became a dockside trainer at Mare Island, north of San Francisco. She then returned to the reserve fleet in the early 1970s until she was selected as the museum boat for San Francisco.

Pampanito was turned into a memorial and museum on 21 November 1975 and transferred to the San Francisco Maritime Park Association (formerly the National Maritime Museum Association). Then the work needed to make her ready for visitors began.

It then took some time to restore the boat. Safety features, such as plexiglass panels and grates, had to be installed for visibility and to protect visitors and the submarine. The torpedo loading hatches were removed and more accessible ladders (stairs) were added for visitors and old submariners to enter and exit. Other than that, the goal has been to display the submarine as it existed at the end of the war. This work was completed on 20 May 1976.

Due to some political infighting, Pampanito did not arrive at Pier 45 until 1982. The political problem appears to have been with a union, rather than elected officials. It was related to the sinking of the Kachidoki Maru with the POWs on board. As a result, Pampanito spent time in Stockton while waiting to come to Pier 45. Pampanito opened to the public in San Francisco on 15 March 1982.

CDR Paul (Pete) Summers went on to various positions in the Navy after the war, including executive officer of an NROTC unit, submarine division commander, and executive officer at a naval powder factory. He was promoted to captain in 1955. He received a tombstone (honorary) promotion to admiral when he retired in 1957.

He was then involved with the Polaris missile program at Lockheed until he retired again in 1978. He attended only a few of the Pampanito reunions. He died in 1993 and is buried in Arlington National Cemetery.

The last surviving Pampanito crew member was Spencer Stimler, who had been an electronics technician. He was aboard for patrols 2 through 6. He passed away on 4 September 2023, on his 100th birthday.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did the crew stay in touch with each other?  Did they stay in touch with the rescued men?
title: Did the crew stay in touch with each other?  Did they stay in touch with the rescued men?
text:
Yes they did. There were a number of reunions, which was fairly common for the crews of World War II ships. Not everyone would attend. Some of the reunions were held here in San Francisco in conjunction with the museum.

Some members of the crew did stay in touch with some of the rescued POWs. Those in the crew who visited Australia would contact the rescued soldiers. The reverse was also true and some of the rescued men would attend Pampanito reunions. One of the rescued men, Frank Farmer, would call Pampanito crewman Bob Bennet each year on 15 September, the anniversary of the rescue, and say “Thank you for another year of my life.” (Michno, page 371.)

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Are there more reminiscences by the crew available?
title: Are there more reminiscences by the crew available?
text:
Yes. Some follow here. However, we recommend the full last chapter, “Exeunt Omnes” of Gregory Michno’s book “USS Pampanito, Killer-Angel” which is referenced and quoted often in this Pampanito history.

Some selected reminiscences, quoted from Michno’s book:

Hubert Brown: “At first he thought it would be a rousing good time, but he found out ‘that I had a lot of maturing to do.’ He was satisfied with the service, with that he had seen and accomplished, but also gave him some of the ‘most scary’ experiences of his life. ‘I thought it would be exciting’, he said, ‘but I guess being 19 years old had to help.’ Although he doubted he’d do it again, Hubert said ’I was never sorry I did it. It was a good experience. As a matter of fact, it was probably the highlight of my life.’” (Michno, page 378.)

George Moffett: “The populace has little or no concept of the major foe for all sailors: the power of the ocean. The ocean is relentless, without compassion or remorse; it does not forgive mistakes and it takes no prisoners. This is a fact of life for every vessel that sails upon it and is especially true for submarines. War simply increases the hazards that a submarine and her crew face on a daily basis. We lost submarines prior to the war, and I suspect during the war, not from enemy action, but due to the power of the ocean and mistakes made by unknown crewmembers.” (Michno, page 349)

Paul Pappas: “If you missed the war, don’t regret it. It was a good experience. I wouldn’t trade the experience, but if I missed it, and know what I know now, I’d say, ‘Paul, use your head, you didn’t miss anything.’ You got boredom. You got heartache. The biggest thing you looked forward to was getting home. You planned, waited, and hoped to get home. The war came third; home and family were on top. If you missed the war – no matter how they talk at the reunions – you didn’t miss anything. I made terrific friends, it educated me, but don’t regret having missed it. Then again, I wouldn’t take any amount of money for my memories.” (Michno, page 383.)

Norm Arcement: “’I wouldn’t take a million bucks for the experience I had in World War Two, but I wouldn’t give you a dime to go through it again.’ Then, after a few seconds of silence, he added, ‘At least I’ll keep the memories of it.’”

Norm kept in touch with some of the rescued men, particularly around the Christmas holidays. (Michno, page 388.)

Charlie McGuire: “’It was only in old age, when they didn’t care so much what people thought, that they finally admitted they were frightened.’ The experience was indelible. ‘You change when you go through a depth charging. No doubt about it.’

“As for his years in the Navy, Charlie had dichotomous, but concise thoughts: ‘I dislike the Government, but I wouldn’t hesitate to give my life for my country. I was glad I was in the submarine service; but I’d never do it again.’

“Charlie and his wife once traveled to Scotland. In a chapel in Edinburgh was a listing of all the Scotsmen killed in World War II. Charlie looked but could not find any reference to John Campbell. He informed them about the Gordon Highlander, his POW experience, and how he had been committed to the deep in the South China Sea. Campbell’s name was added to the list.” (Michno, page 380.)

Roger Walters: “’I would never have done anything differently. I don’t have any regrets about it at all. It was the most exciting, greatest experience of my life, bar none. I will never forget it. I will never regret it. War is hell, and when I hear threats of war and think of all the young men who might have to war to defend their country it just brings me to tears.’ Roger concluded: ‘With all the horror and all the glory, and everything that went with it, it was something that made an impression on us that would last a lifetime. Yet, we don’t consider ourselves as heroes at all. We just did our job. But I would not have missed it for the world.’” (Michno, pages 390 to 392.)

Mike Carmody: “’A man’s memory was pretty selective’, he said. He thought it was strange how one person would remember things a certain way when the fellow standing next to him would have a completely different recollection. Paul Pappas thought it was weird how something could happen on such a small boat and some men would never know about it. For example, he knew they were hit by a dud torpedo, but the first time he heard about the torpedoes paralleling them off Japan was at a reunion almost forty years later.” (Michno, page 384.)

LT William Ruhe: LT Ruhe served on the USS S-37 (SS-142). Although he didn’t serve on the Pampanito, this officer has an interesting insight. He said “ said that most sailors felt snug and secure while aboard a submarine, almost ‘like a child in a mother’s womb that is safely protected from the outside world’. The men felt a sense of well-being while on submerged patrol and more comfortable and free of concerns than while on a surface ship. To many civilians it was a mystery how a man could like being on a submarine, but liking it, feeling comfortable, and having the camaraderie of shipmates was taken for granted by almost every submariner.” (Michno, page 353.)

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — What did the crew think of CDR Summers?
title: What did the crew think of CDR Summers?
text:
CDR Summers was not a popular captain. He could be petty and he was slow to forgive. “’He might have been a bad egg’, they said, ’but at least he brought us back.’ It was more than could be said for some of the other poor sailors.” (Michno, page 381.)

Apparently, the sailors on the Cusk, who served with Summers after the war, thought more of Summers and came to his defense when the crews were together. (Michno, page 379.)

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Why did Pampanito serve on active duty for only two years?
title: Why did Pampanito serve on active duty for only two years?
text:
The literature is unclear as to exactly why this was so. What is clear is that, at the end of the war, the U. S. had a huge Navy and was only going to keep half of it in active service. We were keeping half the carriers, cruisers, destroyers and submarines that we had at the end of hostilities.

“After the war, the [N]avy immediately scrapped 20 fleet submarines, placed 106 in reserve, and kept 19 as trainers.” (Michno, page 392.) Shortly after the war, there were three training submarines in the Bay Area but not the Pampanito. That would come later. The earlier training boats in the Bay Area were the USS Dentuda (SS-335) in San Francisco from 1946 to 1967; the USS Parche (SS-384) in Alameda and Oakland from 1948 to 1969; and the USS Sunfish (SS-281) in Vallejo from 1949 to 1960.

Most of the decommissionings occurred in 1946 and 1947. Some of the boats in the reserve fleet were brought back into service for the Korean Conflict in the early1950s. Most of these then went back into the reserve fleet after the conflict ended.

As new as Pampanito was at the end of the war, she was near the median age of our remaining submarines. That may have made her more susceptible to being put into the reserve fleet. But the question remains as to why Pampanito was taken out of service so soon. The answer isn’t clear. After all, her sister ship., the Picuda, was upgraded and active until 1973. There are two possible theories, although we have found no evidence for either. One is that the damage from the first war patrol was a factor. However, that damage wasn’t structural and Pampanito made five more war patrols without any real problems.

Another theory is that the Navy wanted to preserve the option of using the Pampanito as a museum boat because of her history. Some of today’s museum boats had particularly interesting histories. Some had been very successful, such as the USS Bowfin (SS-287) in Hawaii and the USS Silversides (SS-236) in Michigan. The USS Batfish (SS-310) in Oklahoma was reported to have sunk three Japanese submarines in 72 hours.

But these are nothing more than two unsubstantiated theories. In any case, we are proud to have the USS Pampanito, the “Killer-Angel”, here in San Francisco.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Did the Pampanito have a good combat record?
title: Did the Pampanito have a good combat record?
text:
Other than the rescue, Pampanito’s record seems to be just above average. When all the WW2 US submarine war patrols and all the ships they sank are added up, the numbers are about the same. There were about 1,474 patrols and 1,392 ships sunk, for an average of about 0.94 ships sunk per patrol. Pampanito sank six ships in six patrols, so her record was slightly above average.

However, that may not tell the whole story. The six sunken ships credited were after an audit or reconciliation of our records with the Japanese records after the war by JANAC, the Joint Army–Navy Assessment Committee. Japanese records were often incomplete and generally did not include vessels under 500 tons. Many captains believed that they were not credited with all of the shipping that they had sunk. Some combat records, such as the USS Tang (SS-306), have since been adjusted upward.

In any case, Pampanito has the distinction of rescuing the 73 British and Australian soldiers who had been POWs and getting nearly all of them to Saipan alive for medical evaluation, care and the return home.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Why is there a broom at the top of the submarine?
title: Why is there a broom at the top of the submarine?
text:
As much as we would like to say that it is up there to tickle Santa’s butt on Christmas Eve, that would be a “sea story”. In fact, the crew was bragging. This tradition actually goes back to the 1600’s when a Dutch admiral literally swept the bits from defeated British ships off his. He then flew the broom as “bragging rights” when he returned to port.

The symbol was reinstated, likely in early 1943. It was resurrected by submarine skippers such as Dudley “Mush” Morton, skipper of the USS Wahoo (SS-238) as a symbol of their successes. The standards for the boats were that they had to have fired all or nearly all of their torpedoes (there were not enough remaining to safely start another attack) and that the boat had been successful in sinking and damaging ships. “I have swept the oceans clean of all the enemy I could find.” The broom was apparently only good for bragging about that patrol. It would have to be earned again on a future patrol.

We believe Pampanito earned the broom on her fifth war patrol. She returned with just one torpedo remaining. She had sunk two ships. It was not her best patrol, but it met the criteria for the broom with nearly all torpedoes fired.

Submarines today continue the tradition of the broom, but it is obviously not about firing all their torpedoes. As of May of 2026, only one torpedo has been fired in anger by the U. S. submarines after WW2. Now it is more likely to be about Tomahawk missiles and land targets.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Can the Pampanito still run?
title: Can the Pampanito still run?
text:
A majority of the equipment on the Pampanito can run. For example, the hydraulic pumps do work and at least one engine is usually started on Memorial Days during our Lost Boat ceremony. Other engines would require some work in order to be able to run them. The TDC does work. It is hard to say how much of the electronics would work and whether it might matter. If the radio were to be working, is there anyone out there who could answer with similar equipment?

The Pampanito radio club uses different, CB equipment.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Can the Pampanito submerge?
title: Can the Pampanito submerge?
text:
The Pampanito certainly could submerge once more. However, unless the water were very shallow, it is unlikely that the boat would be able to surface again on its own. The gaskets on the various hatches are likely to be old, and you probably don’t want to trust your life to them. Pampanito has no battery nor does she have propellers. She doesn’t have air in the air banks. That means there would be no lights, propulsion or other important equipment when submerged.

Another important factor is that the torpedo loading hatches have been replaced with the housings and stairs that we now use to enter and leave the boat. Those doors are not designed to withstand significant pressures. That just makes them two more things to which we wouldn’t want to trust our lives.

However, there is nothing to worry about. The ballast tank vents are welded shut and the associated levers in the control room are padlocked in the closed position. At present, the normal mechanisms that were used to submerge the Pampanito are not operable. In addition, Pampanito isn’t in water deep enough for her to sink. The water near Pier 45 is shallow.

display_citation: SubmarineDocent FAQ — Can you recommend books about the history of the USS Pampanito?
title: Can you recommend books about the history of the USS Pampanito?
text:
The best book about the wartime history of the Pampanito is probably “USS Pampanito; Killer-Angel” by Gregory Michno. The author is the son of Frank Michno who served on the boat from commissioning through the second war patrol.

A recommended book that tells the story of the rescued soldiers is “Return from the River Kwai” by Joan Blair and Clay Blair Jr. Clay Blair Jr. has written many books about submarine history, including “Silent Victory”.

“USS Pampanito: A Submarine and Her Crew” by Carl Nolte. Mr. Nolte is a local journalist with a lengthy association with the museum. This book may be available at the USS Pampanito visitor center.

Another book about the history of the Pampanito is “Steel Shark in the Pacific; USS Pampanito SS-383” by Capt. Walter W. Jaffee. This book is a bit more basic with extensive definitions and photos. It provides the most detailed information about the postwar transformation of the boat into a museum along with the related political issues.

The book “Hellships Down; Allied POWs and the Sinking of the Rakuyo Maru and Kachidoki Maru” by Michael Sturma. This is a fairly recent book and covers more “hellships” than just the two mentioned in the title. The author is Australian, and the book may be a bit harder to find.

Another book about the rescued soldiers is “Lucky 73; USS Pampanito’s Unlikely Rescue of Allied POWs in WWII” by Aldona Sendzikas.

All of the above books are likely to be available through used-book vendors such as A Libris, ABE Books, Thrift Books and Amazon, among others.
